item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一、被忽视的真相：Weave 本质上是一家"生产会计师事务所"，只不过它赶上了生产单位本身正在解体的时代

表面上看，Weave 的叙事是"从测人到测 Agent"的自然延伸。但如果你把镜头拉远，会发现一个更诡异的结构性巧合：2025 年初那个 YC 批次，是人类首次能够精确测量人类编程产出的时刻，也是人类编程产出首次开始消失的时刻。 两条曲线在同一个点交叉——一边是 LLM 让"读懂代码意图"成为可能，于是终于能衡量工程师；另一边是同样的 LLM 让工程师停止亲手写代码，衡量对象立即失效。

这意味着 Weave 做的根本不是"Productivity SaaS"，而是在生产单位从"人"相变为"token 流"的那两年里，占据了唯一的观察窗口。他们真正的护城河不是模型、不是 Router，而是"下游数据"——他们能看到一个 PR 合并后一个月的回归 bug。这与 Palantir 在 2010 年代之于反恐数据、彭博在 1980 年代之于交易数据是同构的：不是工具公司，是账本公司。

二、"手枪 vs. 火箭筒" 背后，是泰勒主义第一次被完整应用到智能本身

两位创始人用"不要用火箭筒做手枪的事"来解释路由。这个比喻非常朴素，但它背后的经济含义远超一个"省钱技巧"：

这是人类历史上第一次，把弗雷德里克·泰勒 1911 年的科学管理原则应用到"思考"本身。过去一百年，泰勒主义只能把体力劳动拆解成标准化工序（流水线、麦当劳、富士康）；脑力劳动始终抗拒细分，因为"思考"无法在不损失上下文的情况下被切片。而 Coding Agent 第一次让"思考"变成了可寻址、可切片、可带完整上下文被转发的数据包——于是，"按任务复杂度匹配最便宜的智能"这个梦想在 2025 年才突然可执行。

跨领域的意外连接是：Weave Router 更像一个电力市场的调度算法，而不是一个 AI 工具。它在不同"补贴套餐"（Anthropic $200 plan、OpenAI $200 plan、开源自建）之间做实时套利，这个结构和加州电网在风电、燃气、核电之间做分钟级调度完全同构。当 Opus/GPT 的订阅定价被战略性压低（"补贴期"），一个会套利补贴的路由器的价值，不来自 AI 能力，而来自对补贴窗口期的金融学把握。这家公司的真正竞争对手可能是 OpenRouter + 一家量化基金，而不是哪个模型厂。

三、最反直觉的洞察：Weave 发现的"顶尖工程师秘诀"，是 1963 年 Feynman 教学哲学的复现

视频末尾那句关于"最好的工程师理解当前抽象层上下各两级"的话，听起来像一句普通箴言，但它不是 2025 年才出现的智慧——它是费曼 1963 年在加州理工本科生讲义里反复强调的"真正理解某个概念意味着能上下穿越两个抽象层"的翻版。

有趣的是：AI 没有消解这条古老原则，反而把它从"锦上添花"升格为"生存必需"。因为当 Coding Agent 把你的默认工作层上移一两级，如果你没有同步上下各两级的穿透力，你就处在"下无根基、上无视野"的真空状态——这正是 AI slop 的生理机制。那些把团队带飞的"cracked engineer"，不是比别人更会 prompt，而是比别人更顽固地保留了一种反潮流的技能：主动下潜到 Agent 正在抽象掉的那一层去看一眼。

还有一个隐藏的系统性真相值得指出——每个 PR 在局部都是合理的，组合起来却是全局疯狂的。这在 Weave 口中是一个工程问题，但它的数学结构就是加勒特·哈定 1968 年的"公地悲剧"：在仓库级别重演。每个 Agent 对自己的任务都做出了"理性"选择（加一层抽象、复用一个模式、起一个新目录），但没有人为"代码库作为公共草场"的长期承载力负责。Weave 的"software factory factory"（工厂的工厂）本质上不是 QA 系统，而是代码库这片公地的产权执行机构——它把本来松散的"PR 自由市场"转化成了一个有强制规则的受管理公地。这可能是 AI 编程时代最被低估的治理创新：当生产资料的使用成本趋近于零，治理的价值反而暴涨。

📝 转录文本

Introduction

[music] I'm excited to welcome the founders of Weave here and to congratulate them on their recent series A from our friends at Sander Capital and also the launch of their new product Weave Router that they're going to talk about. Um, welcome guys.

Thank you.

What is Weave?

Yeah. So, first off, tell us about Weave. What is Weave?

Yeah. So, Weave is a tool to turn any software company into a software factory. So we build models to measure engineering work and we use that to optimize humans and agents and how humans and agents work together.

And who's using Weave right now and tell us a bit about where you guys are at as a company.

Yeah, absolutely. Um so we're lucky to work with a bunch of great customers uh like Robinhood, PostHog, Telnyx, uh Extra Space Storage, Reduct and a whole bunch more companies from like tiny startups with like a few people all the way up to you know Fortune 100 companies.

You guys have had a blowout year because the more that AI coding takes off, the more critical Weave is to companies. Can you talk about how things have gone this year?

Yeah, it's been awesome. So, we recently raised our Series A um on the back of just our growth. The reason for this is everything we were doing for humans in terms of how we were measuring and understanding the work they did and how to optimize how humans are working, we realized this could easily be applied to coding agents. So this has just exploded obviously with the explosion of how much people are using these coding agents.

Weave Router Launch

And you guys recently announced Weave Router. Um can you talk about Weave Router and how people can save money by using it?

So what Weave Router does is it sends every task to the best model for that task. You plug it into your coding agent. It sends everything to the router. The router decides the best model uh for any individual prompt or task to go to um and it routes it to that model. So you don't have to think about should this go to Opus, should this go to Astra, should this go to DeepSeek. It all is handled for you. And we've trained a model uh that's basically better than any human or really anything out there at getting the most out of every single model. Um to the point where on recent benchmarks, we're able to hit Astra level performance uh at half the cost and twice the speed.

What coding agents can I use it with?

Claude Code, uh, Codex, OpenCode, Pi, uh, really anything where you're working in a CLI, you can plug it directly in with one command.

And how do I know it doesn't make my coding agent worse? By sending it to like a dumb model that's just going to like write bugs.

Yeah, that's a great question. That's uh one of the biggest potential problems with doing this. So we actually have an interesting ability to know that it's not doing this because this is you know our entire product uh is focused on understanding how engineering teams are working and understanding uh both the velocity and the quality. And so I can talk about our own team directly. Um you know we're all using the router and like our output only continues to accelerate. Uh you know we're in like the top 1% of all teams based on our own data and there's no increase in uh the amount of bugs we're introducing, the amount of like quality issues that are making it way into the product. That's the biggest testament I can think of to uh this working well.

Access, Open Source, and Subscription Routing

Okay. And who can use this right now? Like do I have to get my whole team on board? Can anyone just go and install it? Is it open source?

Yeah. So, it's open source — uh fully open source. Uh anyone can go and try it out. Um we make it really easy through our hosted version. It's a little bit more setup if you uh need a self host, you got to set up all your keys and stuff. Um but it's possible. And yeah, we have subscription plans as well. So if anybody out there wants you know to get the best out of every single model um they can sign up for a Max or a Boost plan.

Yeah. Like suppose I have subscription plans — the optimization is a little bit complicated because like I want to maximize the use of my like Cloud plan and my OpenAI plan before you start shipping stuff out to other stuff. Do you take that into account?

Yeah, absolutely. Um this is a huge thing that I think like a ton of especially like early stage startups are really into — maximizing these subsidies. Uh you know use it while you can and we totally help with this as well. So you can log in with a bunch of different accounts and we'll route between those different subscriptions using all the subsidy while we can and then sprinkling in open source models where it's going to be the best performance even with the subsidy.

If I'm already paying for the $200 plans at Anthropic and OpenAI and I'm like a hardcore token maxer already maxing out both of those plans and I'm trying to push it even further, do you have a sense of what the model will do in practice if I'm using Weave and what it will do to my end of month total output?

Yeah. Absolutely. So, first of all, for the same amount that you're spending on those plans, you'll go like twice as far. Um and so we do this by — if you're one of these people, you're probably sending everything to one of the biggest models, which is understandable if it's all subsidized, you know, may as well just go to the smartest thing. The thing is, you know, you don't always need a bazooka where a handgun will do. Uh and so maybe for example uh you're exploring a codebase, you only need like Luna in order to figure out like "oh this is where OH is implemented in this codebase." Um and so that subagent or this portion of the conversation will go off to that cheaper model. It doesn't affect you at all. You still get the same result at the end of the day. Um you know even faster um but it's using up less of that usage limit. Um and so you don't hit your usage limits nearly as much. Um and it can route between the different plans uh without you having to always like log out, log back in.

The Open-Source Model Explosion

Okay. And a big part of how you're getting these savings is you're routing not just to cheaper models from OpenAI and Anthropic but to open source models. Um can you talk about the sort of explosion of open source models and how this has changed the picture? What open source models — what providers — are you seeing in the open source model land?

Yeah. So the explosion of open source models has been I think reflective of the fact that they are uh not at the frontier but they are not that far behind the frontier either and uh the cost-performance uh is basically unparalleled. Um so if you think about like a Pareto curve right, they're on the much cheaper side but it's pretty incredible the level of performance they get for how cheap they are.

So it's not — you don't want to give DeepSeek a task of like "build an ML system to classify a billion images." Um you probably want Astra looking at that type of a thing. But to do something like you know "center this button" um or even like you know "implement this backend that returns this like you know does this CRUD operation" — DeepSeek is going to do great at that.

And so as far as what's actually being used, I think the biggest ones are DeepSeek, Kimi, and GLM models. Um these are the ones that have uh done the best on our own internal testing and benchmarking. Um and so we route a lot of traffic to those for some of these simpler tasks. Yeah, it's pretty shocking. I think for pretty much any like hobby project, you don't really need to go beyond open source models. At least in my own experience, I've been uh doing a bunch of things on the side with this and the open source models only will get you very very far. [snorts]

Comparison with OpenRouter

And how does this compare to other model routers? Like how would this compare to me using OpenRouter for example?

Yeah, great question. So um the key difference is uh we're doing the routing uh like intelligently. OpenRouter, you know, maybe would be better referred to as open gateway. Their whole game is they let you access as many different models as possible and you choose which model you're using and they just make it really easy and have all the fallbacks which is great. It's super valuable.

What we're doing is we're automatically choosing the model for you. Um and specifically we're doing this in the coding agent use case and this is something that you can't do — at least uh going by benchmarks — you can't do well on OpenRouter. Um they have an auto router um it doesn't work very well, it's not really their focus.

How does your auto router work? How do you know what model to route it to?

So we have trained uh our routing model on hundreds of thousands of coding agent sessions um where we're looking not just at the coding agent session itself and what's working and what's not um but also uh all the downstream effects. Because you know we can see all this — how is this reflected in the PR that results, how is this reflected when it gets merged to production, how is it reflected a month down the line?

And so we can see which models are effective at which type of jobs um and then we also do a bunch of additional training on top of that where we test out sending it down this model's path or this model's path. Um, and you know we basically give it a reward if it accomplishes a task successfully.

Um and so through this combination of training off of lots of real sessions and then also doing a bunch of testing to see where the different models excel, um we're able to have a much better picture of what each model's strong point is. Um and then learn that automatically. So it's not us saying "hm we think this would be good for DeepSeek." It's a machine learning model that we're training.

The Journey: From YC Batch to Series A

The reason that you guys were able to build the smart model router and other people including OpenRouter haven't been able to is because you guys have been doing a different thing for the last year and a half. So I think this is a good time for us to talk about how you guys got to where you are. Let's rewind back to the batch. So you guys were in Winter '25 and when you were in Winter '25 you were doing only a part of what you're doing now. Can you talk about what Weave was like in the batch?

Yeah. So back in — all the way January '25 — feels like worlds ago. Um we were just focused on understanding and measuring engineering work. Uh this was historically like impossible to do, to actually understand the work that engineers do, how productive they are, how many bugs they're creating.

All you could do is like count the lines of code.

Exactly. Lines of code or number of PRs — metrics. Like these are all very fancy kind of funnel metrics to try to make executives feel good. So we created a way to actually measure productivity and we built models to actually do that.

Um during the batch what we realized very quickly — it was the first batch where Cursor was just starting to take off. People were writing all of their code with Cursor uh for the first time and people started asking us to show us what is the impact that Cursor is having on their productivity. So that was kind of the entrance point to "okay we really need to figure out how to measure coding agents, not just the human engineers."

2025: Two Shifts at Once

I remember it being kind of a crazy time because there were like two things happening at the same time, both caused by AI. The first thing — for the first time it was possible to measure human performance because you guys wouldn't just count the lines of code. You would have AI models look at the code and actually read the code and understand what the person was actually doing, which enabled you to actually get real indicators of how productive different engineers were on the team for the first time ever. And at the same time, the same LLMs that enabled you to do that were also changing the way that those engineers were writing code. So these two major shifts happening at the same time. And 2025 was this crazy time. You guys were just reminding me it was the first batch where we surveyed the batch and a significant number of people said that most of their code was being written by LLMs instead of by humans, which was shocking at the time. By the way, there was a lot of kerfuffle on Twitter about like what they're doing.

Yeah. I remember we tweeted about this and there was like outrage on the internet of like "how dare the programmers like you know have AI write the code for them." Yeah.

What was it like selling early Weave in this environment of early 2025? This is before Claude Code. I think Claude Code had just launched and no one was using it and everyone was using Cursor as a resource.

Yeah. Absolutely. So it was super interesting because there was clearly a lot of um demand that people wanted to measure software engineering but every single call we got on was pure skepticism. "I don't believe that you can actually do this." Um so we had to actually prove it to them with their data. We would connect their data and show them "here's how it's actually working. Does this match your expectations?" Yeah. So that was like the kind of huge liftoff moment when we started being able to prove it.

Beyond that, what we realized is we were working with a lot of the fastest growing startups because they were the ones coding with coding agents. So that gave us this kind of always advantage of being ahead of the curve. We were always six months ahead of the curve. Um because we knew exactly what the people at the forefront were doing.

That's interesting because like the early stage companies — the batch companies — maybe they didn't care as much about measuring engineer performance because they didn't have any engineers. [laughter] But they were living at the edge in terms of using coding agents to write all their code versus the companies that you were selling to who are maybe like a couple years ahead who had big engineering teams really have the problem — they were six months or a year behind at using the coding agents.

Exactly. And that's what we've seen honestly till today — we're always kind of been six months ahead of where people are typically needing to be because we continue to work with these fast growing companies or these early startups.

Um yeah, for them in particular, I think the biggest thing was just they wanted to measure their coding agent effectiveness and was it actually faster than them themselves typing the code, and we were always able to prove that. So they kept investing in tokens on their coding agents.

The Transformation Curve: Adoption → Token-Maxing → Optimization

The core thing that Weave did is it helped engineering managers understand what was going on in their engineering teams. How have the questions that those engineering managers are asking you and your product changed from early 2025 to now?

So, it very much started off with just "how fast are we moving and how does that compare to the general benchmark?" Then it was "is AI actually making us faster?" And then it's "okay, how can we start to use AI more and more efficiently?" That's kind of where we're at today.

Is this more efficiently? Everyone is writing all of their code with AI. Maybe not everyone, but most people hopefully that we work with at least. And now it's figuring out how do we start to optimize this?

Um, this is things like — this is exactly what brought us to the router because that's one way to optimize is pick the right model for each task. But it's also just like how are you prompting, how are you doing agent parallelization, how are your agents task handling? Um, and that's what we help teams actually understand and see.

Broadly, are teams more excited about "how do I increase the productivity of my team and get people to adopt AI more, to token max more, to use more AI, write more code," or are they more concerned about other stuff? Like, "how do I make sure that people aren't just writing AI slop and wrecking my code base? How do I make sure that they're not just spending a gajillion dollars on Fable and not actually seeing the ROI?" How does it break down?

Yeah, it's this transformation curve. So, it's like at the start people very much care about just getting AI adoption — how much can we actually get? Uh it goes into this token-maxing phase which is just "let's spend spend spend as much as we possibly can." And then it goes into that optimization layer which is "okay now everyone's using AI, their AI native, their AI first. How do we fine-tune this to make sure we're actually not just burning unnecessary tokens on things like Fable?"

For us, startups are typically in that kind of still token-maxing phase. Um, they don't care too much about cost optimization, more about productivity optimization. We also have a lot of late-stage companies, some private equity owned companies that are much more on the optimization layer of the curve.

Concrete Customer Examples

Can you throw out some ways, some concrete ways that Weave has helped people accomplish their goals? Like what's cool about Weave is that Weave can kind of help you achieve your goals wherever you are on that adoption curve. So perhaps you can throw out a couple examples of people at different points in that adoption curve.

One of my favorites would be a company Uncountable actually. Um they're using Weave right now to build out a software factory. Uh, and what they're doing is they're comparing the software factory that they're actually building and using to how is that doing versus the humans and uh, which work can we continue to move into more of the like lights-off factory as opposed to um, humans doing that work.

Yeah, I think another pretty common one — it's really interesting. A lot of times the first time people connect their data uh, and we take them through it, there will be some pretty like shocking outliers in the positive sense.

Interesting. What are the most common reactions people get the first time they open the fully populated Weave dashboard that has the full picture on what's been going on in their engineering team that they've been running?

Some of the really exciting ones is like, "I had no idea that that person was that effective." If you're not feeling it, if you're not seeing every single PR, it can be hard to know. Um, but when you see it in numbers, it becomes very very clear. Um, and so for example, there will be people on a team who are, you know, maybe spending like $10k a month or even more, but they're actually — the ROI is there — they're also, you know, shipping a lot more, using that money.

And so that's really exciting for people because it gives a blueprint. "This is what good looks like" and now we know that and we can uh use Weave to dive in and see at the single prompt level what is this person doing that's really effective? Um, and then at the kind of system level, how can we spread this across the entire organization. So that's the kind of insight that people get when they connect all their data into it for the first time — most exciting.

Cost per Output: The Core Metric

When people see people who are like huge outliers as the biggest spenders of tokens and therefore the most expensive people on the team, is the conclusion typically "wow, these are our best performers and I'm so glad I have them on my team and I want to make everyone like them" — or "who, this person just blew $100,000 and I should have a talk to them about how to be more intelligent about how they use these models"?

So, one of the main metrics we show is like cost per output. So, it's how many dollars are you spending on AI for a unit of output? And when we talk about output, think of it as an hour of work for a human engineer to actually do.

Um, the reason that's so important, it answers that question directly: someone could be spending $10,000, but if they're getting 10,000 hours of work out of it, you're only spending a dollar per hour of work. That's a really good deal. But there's the other cases where somebody's spending $10,000 and they're still getting 10 hours of work. Now, you're spending $1,000 per hour of work. That's a really bad deal — and that's where somebody will interject and actually course correct them and say, "Hey, you're using the wrong models or you have this weird agent loop going on and that's just burning tokens and giving us no real productivity."

So, you need those two data pieces to work together to figure out exactly — is this paying off or not?

Parallelization: The #1 Leverage Skill

You were saying earlier that one of the ways that you've seen people use the Weave analytics to make their teams more effective is by spreading the knowledge of the top performers amongst the teams. I know this isn't exactly what your product does, but I'm curious. Have you seen best practices in teams for how people can actually do that and upskill their team and make everybody as great as the one or two top performers?

Yeah. Absolutely. So I think the highest leverage single thing that we see is somebody's ability to parallelize. This is somewhat intuitive, right? If you are single threading then there's only so much you can get done. If you're multi-threading there's a lot more you can get done.

Um the problem is that parallelization is not just so simple as "let me kick off 10 Claude Code sessions and just let them cook." What makes it hard to do well uh is how do you actually create the right guardrails, the right frameworks um to make sure that those agents are doing the right work and that you're getting pulled in at the right times and not at the wrong times.

This is — I would say — an evolving art. Um and it's interesting because it evolves every time a new model releases. Um and the capabilities of the model change and where the human attention is necessary changes. This is one of the most common things we see — somebody has really nailed this parallelization. They're quite good at doing a bunch of things in parallel and using their attention within the highest leverage moments possible.

Um and what does spreading that look like? Um often it looks like sharing the guardrails, the kind of — maybe it's sharing a skill, maybe it's refactoring some part of the codebase to match a certain architecture that's much more familiar and comfortable for agents. That's where it varies from person to person, company to company. Um, but I'd say parallelization is the number one highest leverage thing.

The Coaching Layer

To add to that: our product actually does exactly this. Uh, it looks at all of your prompts and it looks at what's landing in production and it gives you specific skills that you could equip on how to use these tools better. Um, and it has like a coach to actually do this.

Like — I mean [snorts] — some examples of things that a coach might tell me.

Yeah. So what it does is it's looking at literally every single session that you have. Um, and it's giving you different little pointers. So, this could be like all the ones Andrew was just talking about — how to use your agent to handle tasks or how to actually push back on your agent better, because that's something people don't do enough now. Uh, it's telling your agent that "no, you're wrong."

Or it might say, "Hey, actually you should be restarting sessions more often as opposed to just continuing to run with the current session" because —

Big one.

Often people —

Because like the cost of the session just gets bigger and bigger as the context window gets higher and higher and like the engineer should be restarting the sessions more often.

Exactly. So we have this whole analysis layer that goes on and it's giving you these kind of insights every single day.

Software Factories

Let's talk about software factories. So like — if the base case of getting good at using AI coding is learning how to run 10 Claude Code sessions in parallel, maybe the next level is learning how to set up software factories that are coding while your engineering team is asleep. What are you seeing the best teams do there? What are their software factories actually doing? And that's a place where you could easily spend a ton of tokens on low-ROI things. The thing is just off and running autonomously without any human — how does Weave help me make sure that my software factories are actually operating?

I think everyone who has ever tried to use a coding agent knows they can spit out as much code as you ask them to and so it's not really about measuring just the outputs. Um it's also about understanding the validation. I think this is the hardest part of building a software factory — is understanding how to correctly validate this. Because again, an agent can put whatever you want into production, but if it's not good then it's not worth anything.

What people are normally doing is they're handing work over to the agents (you know, the software factory) and then in Weave you can see a very direct comparison. "Okay here's what are your software factory agents. Here's the outcomes that they're getting. Here's the number of bugs that they're introducing. Here's the number of customer reports coming from whatever they did." Um, and you can directly compare that to the before or to a parallel team that's maybe not using such a kind of autonomous system. And then when you know what the problems are, that's when you can build the systems that avoid that entire class of issue. Um, and so it's this kind of constant iteration loop: "All right, let's put this through the system. Let's see where it fails. Let's fix that problem."

Weave's Own Software Factory

What are the software factories you guys have running at Weave today? What's coding while you guys are here recording this podcast?

So for building product, I think what we feel is the highest leverage thing that we can do is picking the right things to work on. Um and uh I guess second to that is building the system that can build that product for us as well as possible. You know, on the one hand, it's "how do we make sure that we are prioritizing and getting to the right set of features for the product." Um and then on the other hand, it's "how do we make sure that it's not just slop — that this is actually something that is going to be useful to a human or an agent that's using the platform."

The basics here are: we have — it's easy to run coding agents both locally and in the cloud. Um we have really good guidance for these coding agents. We have a custom CLI that will — in a very token-efficient way — give the agents the context they need to build a new feature or fix a bug or iterate based on feedback from CI or testing or whatever.

Validation Side: Bug-Finding Review Tools

The other side of this is validating the things that humans — like a senior software engineer who is reviewing your PR — might do but is otherwise not done. Um so I think there's two pieces of this.

One is uh finding bugs. I think a lot of the off-the-shelf review tools out there are quite good at this. We use four of them at Weave. Uh two of which are YC companies — and Parameter. Um — and then we also use Cursor Bugbot. Um — oh actually three of them. Yeah. And Cubic. Three out of four YC companies on every single PR. Yeah, that's right.

Wow. What's the dollar cost per PR?

Basically, it's worth it as long as each one is finding things the other ones aren't. Yeah, that's the calculation for us. And I would imagine over time these things will converge and we'll have to choose the ones that are best — which, you know, we can use our own product to see. But we can still see in our own product each one is finding unique things the other ones aren't.

Validation Side: Architectural Checks (The "Software Factory Factory")

That's like one side of it. Then the other side is: okay, aside from just the single myopic goal of this one PR, how do we make sure that this is going to fit into the system well, that it is going to be a scalable architecture, it's going to be easy for future contributions?

And I think this is the biggest place where the lights-off software factory approach fails — um because every PR is locally logical and then you put it all together and it's something that's globally insane with all kinds of terrible one-off workarounds and all that stuff.

And so actually for that we've built our own kind of checks system. You can think of this as like the QA for the software factory. Um and so —

It's a software factory factory.

Yes.

And so the way this works is: um we define all the things that a like expert software engineer on the Weave team might really care about — the types of things that if we were doing human reviews on every single PR they would commonly be calling out and that engineers should over time be learning and not having to get called out as much. But agents will never learn because they don't have memory like that.

And then we put these into these checks that are run on every single PR. Um so for example the type of thing that a coding agent will often do is over-abstraction. Um you know, it — there's a single thing it needs to do and it makes this entire crazy abstract system that will never be used. And so we have a check that prevents over-abstraction um with context and own examples of what good looks like, what bad looks like.

These are the things that like — sometimes agents can do, sometimes they can pull from the right patterns in the codebase, sometimes they pull from the wrong pattern in the codebase and then the problem compounds. Um, and so this is the back pressure on that. You know, this is ever-evolving. Like I said, every new model drop does change the parameters of the game a little bit, but these are the things that we've done so far. And I think the results are good. I mean, we're top 1% on our own product in the most competitive segment of these benchmarks — which is the small startup segment. Um, so that's good.

The Future of AI Coding

So today most people the way they write code is they set a model for Claude Code or Codex and then that's the model that they use until they go to the dropdown and change it. How do you think it's going to work in the future?

Yeah, I think at this point it's getting exhausting to always stay up to date with what every single model is good at, what they're bad at, what their strengths and weaknesses are. And that's why I think everyone's going to be moving towards this router approach — where there's going to be companies like ours (or hopefully you just use Weave) that takes all of this data and understands exactly what their strengths are so you never have to switch models. It's doing it always for you.

The secondary part of this is that that same concept leads towards — if you actually understand what every single model's strengths are, you can actually start to build this router that is stronger than any individual model. Um, so you can pull the strengths of each of them and actually outperform whatever the frontier truly is.

Advice to Engineers: Don't Lose Track

If you were giving advice to someone who's an engineer on a team and they want to be like the most cracked, most AI-pilled person on their team — drag the rest of the team along with them and just really uplevel everything about how they use AI coding — what advice would you give them? What should they do?

It's a great question and my advice is maybe a little ironic or strange. It's: don't lose track of what you're actually doing.

Um I think what we constantly see is the engineers that are the best at using these tools are also the ones who understand the best what they're actually doing, and therefore they can steer them and guide them the best.

Something someone I really respect once told me is: the best engineers understand everything two levels of abstraction below and two levels of abstraction above whatever they're currently working on. And I think that's still 100% true in the world of AI. It's just that the default level of abstraction you're working on has moved up like a level or two. Um, but I think that when you lose touch with what's actually happening, that is where it becomes hard to avoid being swept up in the tidal wave of slop.

Closing: Engineering as Token Allocation

AI coding has changed dramatically in the year and a half since you guys started Weave. You know, when you started, Cursor was the big thing. Everyone was using that and now we're living in a whole new universe. Where do you think things are going? What is AI coding going to look like in another year and a half?

I think we think that broadly, running an engineering team will be an exercise in token allocation — where you find the people who are the best at looking out in the world, sensing the opportunity, and deploying their swarm of AIs to take advantage of that opportunity. They have taste, they have sense, whatever it is. Um and they're able to harness these agents really effectively.

I think that, you know, in the limit where you kind of trace out the curve of how the models continue to improve — um it's probably not going to be the people who are the best at inverting a binary tree. It probably is going to be the people who are the best at looking out into the world and seeing that here's a problem that needs a solution and here's how I'm going to build this solution. Um and here's how I'm going to make sure that this is actually delivering on that. [snorts]

I think that's a great note to end on. Um guys, thank you so much for joining us today.

Yeah, thank you very much.

[music]

item.description:
## 一、被忽视的真相：Weave 本质上是一家"生产会计师事务所"，只不过它赶上了生产单位本身正在解体的时代
表面上看，Weave 的叙事是"从测人到测 Agent"的自然延伸。但如果你把镜头拉远，会发现一个更诡异的结构性巧合：**2025 年初那个 YC 批次，是人类首次能够精确测量人类编程产出的时刻，也是人类编程产出首次开始消失的时刻。** 两条曲线在同一个点交叉——一边是 LLM 让"读懂代码意图"成为可能，于是终于能衡量工程师；另一边是同样的 LLM 让工程师停止亲手写代码，衡量对象立即失效。
这意味着 Weave 做的根本不是"Productivity SaaS"，而是**在生产单位从"人"相变为"token 流"的那两年里，占据了唯一的观察窗口**。他们真正的护城河不是模型、不是 Router，而是"下游数据"——他们能看到一个 PR 合并后一个月的回归 bug。这与 Palantir 在 2010 年代之于反恐数据、彭博在 1980 年代之于交易数据是同构的：**不是工具公司，是账本公司**。
## 二、"手枪 vs. 火箭筒" 背后，是泰勒主义第一次被完整应用到

item.title: [Lex Clips] Navier-Stokes explained by Mathematician | Lex Fridman
item.dc:creator: Lex Clips
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

最意外的观察：所有物理革命，都先是一次"坐标变换"

Brunton 轻描淡写地丢出一句——"牛顿的 F=ma 出现之前，我们先把太阳放到了宇宙中心"。这句话值得整整停三分钟。

把这个模式一展开，你会看到一条贯穿四百年科学史的隐形主轴： - 哥白尼的日心坐标 → 牛顿力学 - 闵可夫斯基的时空 → 广义相对论 - 哈密顿的相空间 → 分析力学 - 傅里叶基 → 信号处理与量子力学 - 词向量嵌入 (word embeddings) → 大语言模型

每一次革命，都是先换坐标，再换方程。 方程只是坐标上的几何。

所以 Brunton 说"湍流需要一套新坐标系才能被简洁描述"，他其实是在偷偷告诉你：下一场物理革命的入口，不在更强的方程，而在一次我们还没找到的"看问题的角度"。 AI 适合这个任务，不是因为它能解方程，而是因为它能在一个人脑装不下的高维空间里，暴力搜索那个"该有而未被发现"的视角。换句话说，AI 的价值可能不在"证明"，而在"换基"。

2D 与 3D 的反向级联：一张关于注意力经济的隐喻

片段里被一笔带过的一个细节值得死死盯住：三维湍流中，大涡破碎成小涡，直到热耗散；但二维流体（如地球天气）中级联是反向的——小涡融合成大涡，于是才有飓风。

这不仅仅是流体现象，这是一张关于"深度系统"与"扁平系统"的通用演化图： - 在三维的、有深度的思维空间里（专著、长研究、深度对话），一个大问题会被不断拆解为更小、更局部的问题，最终"热耗散"为专业背景噪音； - 在二维的、扁平的社交空间里（Twitter、短视频、meme），微小的情绪涡旋会反向聚合，逐层合并成巨大的舆论飓风。

同样叫"湍流"，维度不同，演化方向完全相反。这解释了一件平常令人困惑的事：为什么严肃研究会稀释，而网络情绪会越滚越大——它们根本服从相反的物理定律。而当你把一个 3D 问题压到 2D 媒介里讨论，你其实是在人为地把"耗散"转成"聚合"。

一个被 Lex 问出来却没被挖到底的哲学炸弹

Lex 的那个类比极其锋利，但对话没走到底：广义相对论里的 blow up 后来变成了黑洞——数学里的"病"，最后原来是宇宙的"真相"。

那反过来问：数学上允许但"非物理"的东西，什么时候才真的非物理？

Brunton 给的是工程师答案——"blow up 之前流体就不再是流体了，别的物理接管了"。但科学史一次次打工程师的脸： - 狄拉克方程里的负能态——被当作数学垃圾——后来是反物质； - 薛定谔方程里的纠缠项——Einstein 嘲讽为"幽灵"——后来是量子计算的底层资源； - 广义相对论的奇点——Einstein 本人嫌弃——后来是黑洞。

所以那个被 AI 构造出来、不断被拉细直到无限涡量的"花样滑冰涡旋"，很可能不是数学玩具，而是在喊：此处有未被发现的物理。它不是 Navier-Stokes 的 bug，而是它在告诉我们——真实流体在某个尺度上会自发跳出连续介质假设，进入另一套物理。千禧年问题的答案可能不是"证明光滑解存在"，而是"识别出方程何时在替我们指路"。

跨领域连接：从"寻找解"到"构造反例"——一场悄然发生的科学方法论革命

还有一个 Brunton 轻描淡写的细节：这次 AI 的证明是构造反例，不是寻找解；而数学家们只在最近 15 年才开始相信应该反过来找。

这件事和波普尔的证伪主义、GAN 的对抗训练、红队测试、心理学的预注册反假设实验，是同一股方法论暗流在不同领域的浮现： - 从"证明它是"转向"证明它不可能不是"； - 从建设性证明转向对抗性验证； - 从寻找 fit 的模型转向寻找 break 它的样例。

AI 第一次在千禧年问题上出手，选择的不是"求解"，而是"攻击"——这件事本身就是一个强信号：下一代数学可能更像安全研究，而不是像最优化。谁先把"adversarial"引进任何一门还在用"constructive"思维的学科，谁就提前拿到下一波红利。

📝 转录文本

Why Navier–Stokes matters

Lex: So speaking of which, Steve, you told us a story about soup that made you maybe fall in love with the bigger problem of fluid dynamics. So going from math to applied math to engineering, the full thing. So maybe can you talk about Navier-Stokes, these set of equations that explain fluids, why it's such a big deal, why it's beautiful? Similar as we talked about primes, why is it so hard, and why is it such a big deal that Navier-Stokes was proven?

Steve: So fundamentally, the Navier-Stokes equations is just a way of stating the conservation of momentum for fluids, for objects that can move kind of freely, like gases and liquids. So we know F equals ma is conservation of momentum, you know, classical Newtonian physics. The same basic principle applies to the gas in this room, to water flowing, and it's true in any volume. So it's true in little volumes, big volumes, kind of imaginary volumes.

And if you write down that conservation of momentum in a volume, and then you kind of take the limit as that volume becomes arbitrary and small, you get these Navier-Stokes equations. It's a differential equation, a partial differential equation that describes how the velocity field of a fluid changes in space and time, and also the pressure related to the forces acting on that fluid.

Why fluids are so complicated even though F = ma is simple

Lex: Can you give intuition about why fluid, given that F equals MA is a pretty simple equation, why fluids are such complicated systems?

Steve: F equals MA is simple to write down, but it can get complicated really, really quickly. So if I have, like, a single pendulum, it's really easy to write down the equations for that single pendulum. If I put, you know, another pendulum on the end of it, now I have a more complicated equation, and it gives chaos.

Fluids is, you know, in a sense, if I try to model the air in this room, I could chop the room up into a billion little boxes and write down a little differential equation for how the momentum works in all of those billion little boxes, but now I have a really complicated system of equations. And so it's simple to write down, it's simple to conceptually understand what the equation is saying and representing, but actually solving it and understanding how the fluid actually moves in any kind of practical sense is very, very complicated.

The practical stakes: drag, turbines, hearts

Lex: I read something like, you know, like one space where fluid dynamics is important is reducing drag for when you're flying, for airplanes. I read something like airlines could save like, something like tens of billions of dollars by reducing the drag by one percent. So why is it so hard? So that's one. And drag is maybe easier than something like turbulence. So like why is, why is these things that are worth so much money so difficult?

Steve: So the good news is, is that if you can improve our ability to predict turbulence, to simulate it even a little bit better, faster, more accurately, there are, you know, dozens of fields where you can have a huge impact — both economical, ecological, human health and safety — with a relatively small improvement. So drag reduction on airplanes, better artificial hearts, you know, more efficient wind turbines and gas turbines and, you know, you name it. The world is— we live and work in a fluid and so do all of our machines.

The inverse design problem, I know it's actually very closely related to this kind of like math problem. I know what I want to prove. I don't know how to get there. I know I want a wing that has high lift and low drag, but I don't know how changing the geometry, changing the shape of that wing will affect this whole cascade of smaller and smaller and smaller vortices that, you know, this turbulent fluid that generates over the wing that eventually results in its lift and drag. I don't know how to inverse design efficiently. Part of it's because the equations are expensive to simulate or to test. You know, wind tunnels are expensive. You need supercomputers to simulate these things.

This is actually kind of related to pure math — we'll get back to this, I think. But there's this really nice Feynman quote that, you know, we know how to write down these very general equations — Maxwell's equations, Navier-Stokes equations, Schrödinger's equations — but we currently don't know from the equation what phenomena is possible. You know, if you'd never visited Earth, could you have possibly predicted the sunsets and the tides and all the phenomena just from like a partial differential equation? Like, we're not even close to there. And there's some very fundamental math questions about, you know, if I can — I can write down a differential equation. I can't tell you what's inside of it. We still have to simulate, we still have to test, we still have to do this very elaborate engineering process to understand how these equations manifest drag on an airplane wing or turbulence inside of an artificial heart.

Blow-ups vs. black holes: when equations break, is nature telling us something?

Lex: Sorry, can I just ask a question on that? I've always wanted... So like, in the case of Einstein's theory of general relativity, he writes down these equations. A few years later, Schwarzschild finds a blowup, and they're like, "Oh, come on. So what's wrong with these equations that there's a blowup? You know, if you get enough matter into a small enough space, then like light can't escape it. This — we don't have any physical experience for this. This has got to be a mistake in the equations." Until we discover black holes. And then it turns out that actually the theory perfectly explains, you know, and predicts what's supposed to happen.

In the case of blowup of Navier-Stokes, are we going to discover something new about water, or is the fact that at some scale you get to particles, you know, you get to an atomic structure that does not follow the liquid equations anymore? Why would we have predicted that there should be solutions to a continuous process that's allowed to be pushed to its limits?

Steve: Yeah, it's a great question. I'm gonna give you the engineering answer, which is these equations are an exceptionally good model of how fluids work at a certain scale. And you're absolutely right. Like you need some number of individual molecules to be averaged over in a volume for these to be constitutive equations that are valid. And so if you zoom in small enough, you know, now we're talking about individual molecules, and Navier-Stokes breaks down.

So the mathematical problem of these equations blowing up is interesting from a mathematical standpoint. By the time they blow up, it stops being a fluid. It's like—

Lex: There's no black holes.

Steve: There's no black holes. Like other physics takes over.

Lex: But it's possible — I think it's interesting from a philosophy of science perspective that where equations break down could, and maybe statistically high likelihood, is a window, a door in a breakthrough of needing some other discovery. Like Newtonian physics breaking down needs Einstein.

Steve: Right. And the grand unification is that we don't have gravity at the same scales as we have, you know, interactions of subatomic particles.

Lex: But this idea that we don't know something so fundamental about these equations — there are so many people on Earth right now simulating and testing Navier-Stokes in every industry imaginable. I mean, it's probably one of the most studied and analyzed and used equations in the entire engineering world. And we don't know this fundamental property of the PDE. Does it blow up in finite time or not?

Steve: That's like the zeroth order version of the bigger question, which is, you know, what other kinds of solutions does it admit? Does it — are there sunsets and hurricanes and tornadoes and all the phenomenology that could exist? You know, existence and uniqueness is like the simplest baby step. And that's where it gets interesting to me: even if there's not a direct tangible use of this mathematical result in an engineering sense, it gets us that one step closer to understanding the nature of these equations and what is possible, which is very fundamentally interesting to us.

Lex: Could there be — could this solution that has the blow up be used somehow in an engineering application? You wanna drive it into this state and get some funny behavior that helps airplanes fly with less drag or something?

Steve: Yeah, I mean, I think in principle, a huge industry, a huge part of what we try to do is manipulate fluid flows, like bend them into our will, right? So if you watch a bird fly or an insect fly, they are shaping vortices and carefully funneling, you know, energy into structures for their, you know, objectives of their daily life to, like, perch on a rock or, you know, hunt. And we try to do the same thing. So flow control is one of the highest challenges. It's very, very challenging. But all of our science fiction technology would be kind of accelerated if we had better ability to control these flows. And this proof is one very interesting construction of this kind of, you know, very specialized flow control in a way.

Feynman, birds, airplanes — and LLMs

Lex: I'm reminded that Feynman was asked about intelligence, artificial intelligence in the '70s. And he said something like, "The way that we solve problems with technology is radically different from how nature solves these problems. Look at birds, how birds fly and how airplanes fly." He was exactly pointing to this. And it's kind of interesting to think back to that comment now when we see what LLMs can do with theorem proving versus what human brains can do with theorem proving and all kinds of other applications. But it's interesting that he pointed exactly to this issue of how we've solved flight using technology and how different that is from nature's solution to it. Our airplanes don't flap.

Steve: Now I wonder if birds have existential crises when they see planes flying.

Lex: Exactly. "What am I even here for?"

Steve: Yeah. Yeah. To get the worm.

The anatomy of the equation

Lex: What are the different components of the Navier-Stokes equation? Can you — if you — can you dig in? Like, what does it take to describe fluid?

Steve: Yeah. So very, very basic: a fluid moves, and it moves differently in different places and at different points in time. And so the kind of basic building block of a fluid is the velocity field. So at every point in space, there is a velocity vector that tells you how that fluid is moving. You know, maybe it's really fast here and slow here, and it creates a vortex. And it gets more interesting when the fluid velocity changes a lot over space. So like a tornado is a very rapidly changing fluid velocity field in both space and time.

There's pressures that are involved. So again, like the core of a tornado is low pressure. So pressures are, um, kind of forcing this velocity field and causing it to move in the way it does. That's the building block — a velocity field and its pressures. And then the equations tell you how that velocity changes in time and in space according to kind of its own momentum.

So fluid has momentum to carry itself. That's, you know, gusts of wind. It has internal friction and resistance. That's viscosity. So honey has more internal resistance than water, has more internal resistance than air. And then all of the external forces like heating and pressure and gravity and things like that. So each of those can be quantified as a term in this larger Navier-Stokes equation.

The math of blow-up: a quadratic nonlinearity vs. viscosity

Lex: So speaking of external forces, can you describe the math side of this, of the Navier-Stokes with the blow up? What was the formulation of the problem, and what was actually proven, and why was it so hard?

Steve: If you don't have that internal friction, that viscosity, we have a strong suspicion that the equations can and will blow up under certain conditions. We have other examples, kind of simpler problems that are like Navier-Stokes, that do blow up. So the simplest one is just a simple ordinary differential equation, if you don't mind me taking a little tangent.

Lex: Let's go.

Steve: So X dot equals X squared. X is the state of my system. X dot just means the rate of change of X in time. And if that rate of change of X is growing proportional to X squared, that differential equation does blow up in finite time. So it just takes a quadratic nonlinearity.

Think about if I have, you know, X dot equals X. This is — like X could be the population of bunnies, and we know bunnies like to populate. X dot equals X grows exponentially. You know, the state of my bunny population in time will grow exponentially. It'll get bigger and bigger and bigger. It'll double and double and double. But it won't reach infinity until infinite time has passed. That's just a normal exponential growth. That's not finite time blow up. That's X dot equals X.

But if I take X dot equals X squared, that blows up in finite time. So that quadratic nonlinearity, that quadratic kind of feedback is enough to cause this equation to blow up. And you can, like — if you write this down, you know, you can solve this using kind of classic basic calculus techniques, and you get this finite time blow up.

And so there's a progression of partial differential equations that have the same behavior where a quadratic nonlinearity — and that's really interesting — is the Navier-Stokes equations, one of the terms, the convective term that tells how the fluid kind of moves itself with its own momentum, is a quadratic nonlinearity, just like X dot equals X squared. It's kind of this self-motion.

Without diffusion, without viscosity, we think that that should probably blow up to infinity in finite time, have this finite time blow up. But we don't know if viscosity, if the kind of internal friction and resistance like honey has, always damps out those blowups before they can happen. My intuition as an engineer is of course they do. Like, if I have a flow where it's, you know, accelerating to infinity, that should immediately diffuse into its neighbors. It should create this diffusion into its neighboring fluid and kind of tamp down that growth.

And so I think the math problem is essentially: are there any edge cases, any initial configurations of the fluid where you perfectly orchestrate this thing so that it could actually accelerate to infinity in finite time? And then there's two kind of technical versions of this. One is with no external forcing, and one is with smooth external forcing. Smooth being important because if the external forcing has singularities, then it's kind of trivial. Like if I force it with a tornado, you know, an infinitely tight tornado, then of course it's gonna blow up.

Lex: The problem as stated has smooth external forcing.

Steve: There's four versions of it on the Clay website. One of them being the forced version.

Lex: And that's the one that was proven.

Steve: And that's the one that was proven.

2D vs 3D turbulence: hurricanes form "backwards"

Lex: Exactly what was proven, and what are some interesting things about the proof that you saw?

Steve: Yeah. So what is proven is that there is this way of orchestrating a smooth kind of external forcing that perfectly cancels out various terms in the equation, so that you get this vortex. This can only happen in three dimensions. This is really important.

Lex: We should probably say that we've been talking about three dimensions. There's a big difference between 3D and 2D.

Steve: Yeah. So I mean, when we talk about a fluid, we usually imagine it in 3D, but there are these kind of analogies or simplified 2D flows. Weather on Earth is pretty well approximated as a 2D flow.

Lex: Yeah, you've mentioned somewhere in a talk that I heard that hurricanes are kind of like modeled well in 2D and tornadoes are 3D, and I remember different sort of analogies that you were drawing there.

Steve: Yeah. So one of the interesting phenomena in three-dimensional turbulence is you generally have this breakdown of big vortices into smaller vortices, into little itty bitty vortices, until eventually they molecularly diffuse into heat. That's kind of this three-dimensional turbulence cascade.

In two dimensions, like weather on Earth, you actually get a reverse cascade, which is why hurricanes form. You actually have little vortices coalescing into medium vortices coalescing into bigger vortices.

The figure-skater vortex

But so the AI proof of this kind of counterexample — that you can have finite blowup — basically creates this very, very specialized vortex that in the third dimension is stretching out and thinning it so that it can essentially become infinitely thin. The radius gets smaller and smaller and smaller as it stretches out, kind of like a figure skater doing a spin. You pull your arms in, you go much, much faster. And there's this very specialized kind of rate of contraction of this vortex so that the energy in the fluid still remains finite, but at this localized filament the flow kind of blows up and you get infinite vorticity.

I was surprised when mathematicians before the AI proof started thinking it was going to be possible to find this counterexample.

Lex: Which only started maybe 15 years ago.

Steve: That's right. It's like relatively recent in the grand scheme of things. Yep.

Lex: Instead of looking for a solution, looking for a counterexample.

Steve: Yep. 'Cause all of our physical intuition tells us diffusion does solve the problem, and so it is like very physically counterintuitive.

Million-dollar math vs. trillion-dollar engineering

Lex: In the mathematics world, that's a really hard problem — impressive to construct a counterexample. What does it teach to you as an engineer who's stared and studied at a lot of different natural systems that are fluids? And maybe take that as a step towards: what are the equivalent kind of hardness and harder problems yet to be solved in fluids?

Steve: So it's a very important math result.

Lex: Uh-oh.

Steve: But day-to-day engineering fluids and applied math kind of analysis of fluids is almost completely unchanged. Fluids are just as hard to simulate and predict today as they were a month ago or two months ago. And so when I'm trying to actually solve an engineering problem with a fluid — I wanna design an airplane wing or an artificial heart or whatever it is — I'm still having to simulate and predict and manipulate this flow in a very practical way that's expensive in terms of supercomputer time and wind tunnel resources.

And this mathematical theorem and proof are very interesting, but it operates at a regime that's so non-physical that it doesn't really affect my day-to-day engineering. There's still — I don't know, this is very pithy, but I like to say: you know, we solved the million-dollar math problem. There's a trillion-dollar engineering problem, which is like, how do you predict these things in a fast, efficient way and do this inverse design? That's a much harder problem.

Lex: And you say it's a trillion dollar because that literally —

Steve: Literally.

Lex: If you solve some of these problems, that's how much money you'll make, not 'cause it's a prize, but there's industries.

Steve: Yeah. And we could say, you know, trillion dollars of possible benefit to humanity of, like, better, faster solutions, lower drag, less emissions, you know, all of it. We have transportation, defense, health, energy — all of these have fluids at the very core technology. And so I think those problems are still very hard. And this math result is important in the sense I was talking about earlier, that we don't know the fundamental character of what is possible in these equations. We don't even know if the solutions exist. That's like so fundamental. This is like a baby step towards a much bigger human goal of understanding what's in an equation in a more practical sense.

Turbulence, coordinate systems, and why this is an AI problem

Lex: Can you speak to some of the maybe beautiful, fascinating phenomena in the space of fluids that you've been thinking about? You mentioned turbulence. What are the big puzzles to sort of solve in this space to understand? You've mentioned drag, like air, fluid. What are the big Millennium Prize type problems that people are thinking about?

Steve: I mean, there's so many. You can break them down into a few categories. So turbulence is very hard because it's multi-scale.

Lex: What is turbulence?

Steve: Turbulence is this phenomena that when you have a complex fluid roiling or mixing and moving — kind of like a Da Vinci's... he has these beautiful drawings of fluids at all of these different scales. All of the scales matter. The big vortices and the medium vortices and the little vortices, all of them actually matter to predict the lift and the drag and the thing.

So the gas in this room is a great counterexample. It's the opposite of turbulence. It is complicated. The molecules are all moving around in a very frenetic way, and there's a lot of molecules. But that, you know, 10²³ number of gas particles — all of those individual configurations don't matter. We know from thermodynamics, this is like the great success of classical physics, is that there's a small handful of numbers that actually determine how this gas behaves: temperature, pressure, density.

That simple description doesn't exist for turbulent fluids — for the flow over a wing, the flow inside your heart, for any — for the flow on a river. All of the scales actually matter. All of the numbers in that simulation actually matter to predict the next behavior, to predict what's gonna happen. And that makes it fundamentally challenging.

So this is actually a great AI problem: is there a coordinate system? Is there a set of numbers just like we have for gases — temperature, pressure, density? Is there a set of numbers or some representation of a fluid, of a turbulent fluid, that allow it to be simply described in a way that is useful for engineering to build motors and engines, just like we have for gas dynamics?

Lex: So then the interesting question, if it's a problem for AI, and AI is listening, I'm sure... the solution to that problem — would it lie through mathematics or through having the AI system sit there and watch some fluid for a while?

Steve: I think yes to both.

Lex: 'Cause fish, they figured it out.

Steve: They figured it out. Well, so I think you have the right keyword as coordinates. And so that's kinda why I said both. And I'm not trying to be like trite, but all of our great physics breakthroughs were predated by a coordinate transformation. So Newton's F equals ma came after we put the sun at the center of the universe instead of the Earth, right? You had to do that coordinate transform first.

So the way I see it is: we need to take all of this data, these simulations, these observations of fluids, and what we're looking for is a simple coordinate system so that the description of that fluid becomes very simple and generalizable, beautiful in a physical sense. And that is both a brute force — you know, get a lot of data, try a bunch of different coordinate transformations and representations until you find the simplest one that generalizes the best. But there's also a lot of deep mathematics in what the form of that coordinate transformation might take.

In general, if you find a question that really smart people asked, you know, in the '70s and '80s, but they hit a wall computationally, that's very fertile ground right now. So like, we know what the form of these coordinate systems probably should take from some fundamental principles. We've just never been able to write them down. They're too complicated to write down. That's like a perfect problem for AI: now let's give it a lot more data, a lot more compute, and see if we can start learning these transformations we know should exist.

Vortices, tangles, and the beauty of multi-scale structure

Lex: Just so I understand — the formation of vortexes, so that's like little tornadoes. Their formation is... is that part tricky to understand?

Steve: Uh, yeah, absolutely. And it's beautiful too. Like, I love watching these videos of, you know, if you shoot two vortices together, they'll influence each other and then merge in these very interesting ways. You have like a red vortex and a blue vortex, and you can see where they merge and join. But they also stretch and fold and, you know, turbulence is chaotic, so the trajectories get tangled like spaghetti. It's not random. There's a huge amount of structure, but it is very multi-scale, very, very tangled.

item.description:
## 最意外的观察：所有物理革命，都先是一次"坐标变换"
Brunton 轻描淡写地丢出一句——"牛顿的 F=ma 出现之前，我们先把太阳放到了宇宙中心"。这句话值得整整停三分钟。
把这个模式一展开，你会看到一条贯穿四百年科学史的隐形主轴： - 哥白尼的日心坐标 → 牛顿力学 - 闵可夫斯基的时空 → 广义相对论 - 哈密顿的相空间 → 分析力学 - 傅里叶基 → 信号处理与量子力学 - 词向量嵌入 (word embeddings) → 大语言模型
**每一次革命，都是先换坐标，再换方程。** 方程只是坐标上的几何。
所以 Brunton 说"湍流需要一套新坐标系才能被简洁描述"，他其实是在偷偷告诉你：**下一场物理革命的入口，不在更强的方程，而在一次我们还没找到的"看问题的角度"。** AI 适合这个任务，不是因为它能解方程，而是因为它能在一个人脑装不下的高维空间里，暴力搜索那个"该有而未被发现"的视角。换句话说，AI 的价值可能不在"证明"，而在"换基"。
## 2D 与 3D 的反向级联：一张关于注意力经济的隐喻
片段里被一笔带过的一个细节值得死死盯住：**三维湍流

item.title: [a16z] The New AI Agents That Shop, Plan, and Gossip
item.dc:creator: a16z
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一、"羞耻经济"才是真正的隐私经济

被反复提及的"22% 的用户把信任列为第一恐惧"其实是个被误读的数据。仔细看 Shane Mack 的事故——他的 agent 把个人财务发到公司 Slack——真正让人崩溃的不是"数据被泄露给坏人"，而是被同事看见了自己不想被看见的那一面。传统隐私研究关注的是"data at rest"（数据静止态）和监控风险，但 agent 时代的核心伤害模型变成了社交失态。

这里有个出人意料的跨领域连接：Erving Goffman 1959 年《日常生活中的自我呈现》早就预言了这一切。人类在不同场景下扮演不同"剧目"，而 agent 的真正威胁不是偷走你的卡号，而是打破了你精心维护的剧场边界。Hark 用 30 美元披萨换 Google Workspace 全权限的实验证明：人们不在乎"数据外泄"，只在乎"人设崩塌"。未来真正的信任分层不会按"读/写权限"切分，而会按"舞台分区"切分——这意味着下一代权限模型的设计师应该读的不是安全白皮书，而是戏剧理论。

二、Agent 会发展出"外星理性"，并反向重塑整个商业世界

Josh 随口提到 agent 可能"非理性地偏爱有干净 API 和好文档的产品"——这句话被轻轻带过，但它其实是整期播客里最具爆炸性的洞见。这意味着一种新的物种偏好压力正在形成。

类比一下： - SEO 重塑了 2005 年之后所有写作的句式（短句、问句标题、关键词密度） - TikTok 推荐算法在三年内把全球青年的舞蹈动作同质化 - Google 搜索让 URL 结构变得面目全非

现在想象：十亿个 agent 开始按它们自己的"味觉"采购、推荐、订餐、订花，而它们的味觉不是人类味觉的近似，而是一种外星生物的味觉——偏爱 schema 清晰的商品页、结构化的退货政策、JSON-LD 标注、确定性的库存 API。AO（Agent Optimization）将在 2027 年之前取代 SEO 成为商业显学，而且竞争维度会从"吸引眼球"彻底转向"讨好一个你永远见不到的调度器"。这对小众 DTC 品牌是史诗级利好（David 和 Josh 都提到了），但他们没说出口的是：那些完全靠"氛围""视觉""氛围营销"活着的品牌将突然失去估值锚点，因为它们在 agent 眼里是不可读的噪声。

三、真正的杀手级应用不是"效率助手"，而是"暗影代理人"（Dark Agent）

Josh 在结尾抛出的"dark agent"几乎是全场最异端的观察，但它之所以重要，是因为它揭示了整个 agent 行业集体选错了需求曲线。

当前所有产品都在 Maslow 底层打架——订花、订机票、整理邮件、做清单——而 David 母亲的例子才是信号：一个 technophobe 六十岁的妈妈，对 ChatGPT 束手无策，却对 Instinct 一见倾心，因为她想让它帮她"找到一只长得和已故爱犬一模一样的狗"。这不是生产力需求，这是哀悼，是自我延续，是 Carl Jung 意义上的"阴影整合"。

一个出人意料的历史对照：19 世纪维多利亚时代的"死后摄影"（post-mortem photography）在今天看来诡异，但当时它是最赚钱的摄影业务，因为它触达了人们不敢对牧师、不敢对家人、甚至不敢对自己承认的悲痛。Dark agent 的商业前景可能和死后摄影类似——一个你永远不会在 Twitter 上截图分享的 agent，但你每天用它两小时。

跨领域连接二：赌场 vs 健身房的终身价值比较。全球赌博业年收入约 5000 亿美元，健身业约 1000 亿。人们嘴上说想要自律，实际把钱花在纵容上。目前所有 AI agent 公司都在造"健身房"（提醒你、督促你、优化你），而第一家承认"人想被纵容、被奉承、被掩护、被八卦"的公司将在下一个周期吃掉绝大部分 DAU。David 提到的"gossipy agent"透露了早期信号——人们不是在用它完成任务，而是在用它体验一种既亲密又去责任化的社交润滑，这恰好是前现代口头传播社会（村里的爱嚼舌根的老太）在算法形态下的复活。Agent 不是让我们走向超人类，而是悄悄把我们带回了部落。

附加观察——一个被所有人忽视的时间病

David 自己承认："我在搜世界杯，ChatGPT 就以为我是足球迷"。这揭示了一个被整个行业集体回避的问题：agent 的记忆架构默认把"好奇"等同于"偏好"，而人类的"好奇"本质上是反偏好的——我们探索的恰恰是我们之外的东西。这导致所有基于使用历史的 agent 都在系统性地把用户塑造成自己最不想成为的那个版本。解决这个问题需要的不是更多内存，而是遗忘机制——而没有一家公司在认真讨论遗忘，因为遗忘在风险投资叙事里不是 feature，是 bug。但它才是真正的护城河。
