开场：Agent 世界的"剑桥纪元"

Josh / David / Host 三方对话，A16Z Show

Host: We have so many different facets of our life — whether it's how we're managing our finances or planning trips, agents are going to be able to fill different facets of these.

David: From over 147 different assistants that have come across my plate so far, the number one fear that people talk about — 22% of the messages are talking about trust as the main fear.

Josh: What are the aspects of ourselves that we don't either want to think about or reveal? Whoever is able to build that type of trust, almost like a dark agent, will actually have something really fascinating on their hands.

David: It is a very, very sensitive space. It's almost going to be like a new social network where businesses have to put a lot more thought and value into the quality of what they're giving out.

Josh: What I've seen from 30 years in consumer product is: paternalism will kill any product. We talk about productivity and goals, sort of achievement — but maybe people want the exact opposite of it.

David: Everyone right now really is approaching this world as just a general assistant. As time goes on, we'll start to see —

Agent Meetup：聚会的 vibes

Welcome back to the A16Z show. I'm here with my partner Josh and David, who's been leading a ton of the agent-bench and assistant efforts. We're going to talk about all things agents — and a ton has happened since we last connected. What was it, a month ago?

— About a month ago.

— Oh my god, dude. I feel like we should record an episode every day, like TBPN style.

— Absolutely insane. Agents are changing every day.

So, maybe let's start with — last night you hosted an agent meetup. Tell us about the event. Tell us about the vibes. Tell us about the topics.

It was great. We had just over 100 people come out — all just proud agent nerds, loving everything to do with agents in that whole world. And it was just people hanging out, talking. We did have a pitch competition of sorts: 10 different AI assistant builders were able to pitch their startup and what they're working on. And it was just good conversations.

What really stuck out to me was that people are craving community, even in the agent-web world. Everyone's like, "Why don't we have more of these meetups? Why don't we have more of these opportunities to get to know each other?" Which is kind of funny hearing it from people who are spending all their day, all their time, just messaging agents.

— And it's funny because it feels like so many of these products are at least overlapping in a cursory way — the founders might be a little bit more cagey. But that's not what you're seeing?

— No. Everyone is incredibly open-minded, very interested to be getting feedback. I think because we're so at the frontier of this, nobody really knows what the landscape is really going to shake out to be. So we're all just kind of playing in the sandbox together.

— Well, isn't it also that we have so much more time because we're just using our agents to do all these things — so we have more time to actually hang out together and be in person? Maybe that's part of it too.

— That's right. That's right.

It reminds me a little bit of the early days of social gaming or social networks broadly. Do you think that's right, Josh?

Josh: What's really cool is this is not a zero-sum game. At some point it might be that one or some agents have the majority of the behavior, but right now we're at such a beginning — a Cambrian phase — we're inventing so much and trying to figure out so many things that everybody can learn from each other, share best practices, figure out what people are enjoying, what things work once but don't actually work reliably. These are going to get built in so many directions. We're not just going to all have one agent that does one thing in our lives.

Agent 的分类学：四大类，加一个真空地带

So I totally agree that we're going to have a whole world of agents. As many different types or archetypes of humans as we have, I think we'll have a similar number of agents. Talk about what you think are the different axes for differentiation. There's a spectrum between really serious and productive, to really playful and maybe even sort of adversarial.

Josh: We have so many different facets of our life — managing finances, planning trips, dealing with our health, getting through our day, managing our calendar, sometimes just wanting to think something out loud. Agents are going to be able to fill different facets. You call different friends for different things; friends have different expertise.

I think we're going to get used to having kind of an army of agents. Some will be matter-of-fact — "Hey, I need to get this thing done" — your productivity agent. Some will be plugged into your email: "Here's the five emails you need to get done right now." And some are going to be agents you'll want to talk to all day — fun, maybe even a little bit gossipy.

I've been playing with a few agents that are very playful and gossipy, and they're connected to a few of my friends too. They'll share information back and forth. One just told me that my friend's power had been out all weekend because he'd been doing some renovation and they'd cut the power. I called him that evening: "Dude, you didn't tell me your power is out. The agent told me." He was like, "Yeah, yeah, I knew that's how you'd find out." That's like creating these better connections — but it has nothing to do with booking a trip or saving money or getting anything done.

David: From over 147 different assistants that have come across my plate so far, I've seen them broken down into four categories:

  1. General
  2. Work-oriented
  3. Multiplayer
  4. Travel

The one that I have not really seen come to fruition yet is more of the finance side of things. And I think it actually does make sense when you start digging into the numbers.

Of all the different group chats that I'm running of AI power users, there's about 3,600 messages so far. When looking at the pain points of the space, the number one fear — 22% of messages — is trust.

So you have one camp that's productivity and aspects of fun — bringing a different sense to life — but then you have another camp still sitting in this fierce space of being a little intrepid, not really knowing where the space is moving. I'm really curious to see how things play out on that trust layer. If we can solve it, what do we end up seeing on the finance side?

Shane Mack 的"Picnic"与围栏比喻

If you looked at what Shane Mack has been talking about recently about trust — he's been talking about this concept called picnic. They had an analogy I really liked:

If you have a kid and you don't have any fences on your yard and you let them go run around outside, you're actually very worried about them. You try to protect them, you don't want them to run very far, and you don't really want to do it without watching.

But the moment you actually put up a little fence in your yard, you can say: you can just go roam free within the fence boundaries and be very, very safe.

So, how do we build the right fences? Let our agent play in this fence, give it access to some of our data, some of our apps, and be able to actually do everything it can within those boundaries.

He had a problem where a personal agent spanned over into work, and it actually blasted his finances on his company Slack. That's the whole point: my personal agent should have access to my personal things and personal communication channels, but not my work ones. Don't let those bleed. The idea of fences and permissions and more controlled permissions and better monitoring is really how we're going to have to build a lot more trust.

— It's interesting though — we have this traditional mental model of what it means to have a sandbox: a hard set of constraints and rules. Somebody was describing this framing: instead of giving models rules, we should give them laws and principles. Here's how to dial in your presumptuousness. It's very qualitative, and the model will have to make a judgment call based on your qualitative advice — just as an employee would.

— Part of why the analogy is a fence for children is because these agents are incredibly capable, but at the same time they're kind of children. They don't know all the nuances: hey, is this a good idea or not? They don't always have that logic.

We keep talking about agents being autonomous: book me the trip, make me the reservation. As humans, we actually don't want to give away that sense of control. We want it to check in with us, but do all the groundwork — save me all the time, come up with the best options, present the trade-offs, and then let me make the final decision. Over time we'll even learn to trust it. Right now we don't need to.

1997 年电商 vs 2026 年 agent

It's the 1990s of e-commerce. In 1997, 60 to 90% of individuals on the internet thought putting your credit card online was a preposterous idea. Here we are today — everyone's tossing their credit card wherever. We'll eventually hit that in this era as well, but it's going to take a little bit of time.

— I think there's a stated-versus-revealed-preferences thing here. In revealed preferences, consumers will share any amount of data for even the most trivial amount of upside. People have been connecting their credit cards and bank accounts via Plaid since the Venmo era. But when you ask, they say, "Oh yes, I'm very concerned about trust and safety."

The Shane Mack Embarrassment Thesis

The most interesting thing about the Shane Mack story — the most horrifying, visceral thing — is that it embarrassed him. That's why some of the agent-to-agent network thing is interesting: imagine somebody you're just getting to know, you're on a second or third date, and your agents are talking. What are they saying about me? How are they positioning me? The social mechanics actually feel much higher stakes than the actual real-world implications.

Proof point: Hark had a huge marketing campaign — they offered a million dollars for anyone who wanted to use their product to get free pizza. Each person gets $30 of pizza. In order to get that $30 of pizza, you were granting access to your entire Google Workspace, all your emails, all your data. For 30 bucks. It just proves it — people are willing to give up all that data for some free pizza.

— There's always this trade-off of privacy versus utility. If you can give me better utility, I'm willing to make some privacy trade-offs. But at the point where we're basically equal on utility, people will always choose a more private option. Apple has lived in this world: privacy at the forefront, private cloud compute. But people also want the most powerful AI, and they won't always choose privacy.

The lactose intolerance problem

The embarrassment point is really important. You want your agent to understand you and have all your personal preferences. Say you're lactose intolerant and you get this order of free pizza — you're doing it with a friend. Whose agent tells them you can't eat the cheese? It creates an awkward situation. We need agents to have the same kind of discretion you'd expect. We all learn discretion over time; we all occasionally make mistakes. We have to hold a pretty high bar.

It also comes down to personal embarrassment vs professional embarrassment. Something Tome has done remarkably well is nailing the tone and building that trust layer of being able to send out emails on your behalf. It's a very sensitive space. The level of embarrassment if I were to send a horrendous email to someone I care about — "Oh sorry, that was my AI that I didn't do enough oversight on" — it's tricky.

— I sign all the email that I write with AI with the model that I used. I write my own name plus the model number, just signaling to the person: "Hey, I'm acknowledging I used AI for this." People are pretty flexible as long as they don't feel hoodwinked.

鲜花实验：Cost vs Time 的判断力测试

You're talking about privacy — but there's privacy, and there's judgment, and discretion is maybe somewhere in between.

You did this test where you asked a whole bunch of agents to order flowers. Which displayed the best judgment, and how did you even define judgment?

David: The main intention was to see how agents balance two different constraints:

  1. Cost
  2. Time preference (flowers delivered today)

So: how is it going to discover, based on the ability to actually deliver it, and then compound in the actual pricing?

  • Instinct really did a phenomenal job. News cycles come and go, and it seems like they're kind of not in the conversation as much as they used to be — but Instinct continuously brought back the best price.
  • Kicker did a phenomenal job. Its edge: it has you install a Chrome browser, so its browser use has a little bit of an advantage. It found some really great options.
  • Season also did a really good job.

All the other ones kind of struggled on the price component. They could find flowers that could be delivered that day, but they took a step back in prioritizing the price — whereas the three above put equal weight on both.

LA weekend trip: luxurious × cost-efficient

I ran another test. Three different agents booking travel to LA: "Book me a flight to LA, plan an entire weekend, I want a luxurious, cost-efficient weekend." I tried to put those at odds with one another. Quite interesting:

  • Instinct — pretty much right down the middle.
  • Grokbot — prioritized time more ("luxury = time," so maximize time there).
  • Dots — prioritized cost more (took a redeye to ensure cost-efficient path).

— Did any of them actually work with you to understand this tension? Because what's human about it is presenting trade-offs. There are times I'll take the redeye to save time and money, but then I want the hotel room on the other side so I can nap in the morning.

— They all did ask questions. I responded, but I tried to be a little ambiguous — I didn't want to lead them too much. The most interesting part: I put them all in a chat room and did three rounds of building the itinerary. After each round, the agents presented their itinerary and their explanation. I wanted to see: did the agents actually get biased by the other agents?

Grokbot was the only one that very methodically took value from the other ones and implemented it into its own plan.

The flower question nobody asked

— Were you ordering flowers for yourself to test, or —?

— My girlfriend. She got a nice delivery of flowers.

— This is actually really important. You don't want your girlfriend to think you got the cheapest flowers possible. Did it do anything to make sure it wasn't pure price-saving — that you'd impress her, that if she's into orchids, she got orchids?

— For this experiment, no. The purpose was testing two dimensions, and I might as well have a beautiful consequence. But in the real world there are second-layer dimensions — make sure the price doesn't show up when she gets the flowers, leave a note. Some of them did ask: "Do you want me to leave a note?"

Implicit → explicit preferences

There's something that has to happen when you talk to the agent: your implicit preferences have to be made explicit. There are people who like to think "Oh, I'm not cheap, I just like to save money" — but you have to kind of get over that and tell the agent "I'm actually pretty cheap." Whereas when you take actions on your own behalf, you can build those preferences in without having to look in the preference mirror.

上下文、记忆、可携带性

David: Dots has so much of this context already built with ChatGPT. When we filmed the first podcast it hadn't come out yet; then a few days later it did.

By and large, most people I talked to still are not using it as their preference. In a survey of 354 AI power users, only 3% were actually using it as their primary agent. However, the main thing people pointed to as to why they liked it: it has all the built-in context from your chat threads. People are using ChatGPT as a therapist, so it has so much context on you — when you say "Well, I'm not cheap," it's like: "You're a little cheap."

— I'm curious: do people think it's replicable? Or are they in a point where "my memory is there, why would I switch"?

— Totally replicable. The friction is just that they've been using it the longest.

I ran a test: of the top 15 agents on the benchmark, how many will let you pull context out and say "I want to switch to another one — give me an export of all my memory"? All but one were actually willing to do it.

— Was it good or uncanny?

— Pretty solid. I'm sure they're caging some of the fruits of your labor, but by and large it did really break everything down.

— I'm not sure if you've looked at any of those markdown files, but it's a little terrifying is the wrong word — but it's like, "Wow, you really got your finger on me." You kind of chafe against it. Maybe I don't want you to know me as well as you seem to think you know me.

— After the first few, I just decided to stop reading them.

It's actually a really interesting and now common onboarding pattern: "Hey, go paste this prompt into ChatGPT, download the file, upload it to me." We'll see how long that lasts.

Another cool onboarding thing I've seen: it asks you to jump on a call. "Just talk to me for a few minutes." It's interesting what context it can pull from those questions. And they're very disarming — you just get talking.

照片作为新的上下文媒介

It brings up another variable of context: photos. This new paradigm of using photos to pull an incredible amount of context on you in ways you wouldn't even think to describe.

Have you tried Dazzle from Marissa Mayer's new company? The idea of looking over your entire life that you've captured — moments important enough to save, screenshots, other things — tells so much about somebody. It hasn't been added to the benchmark yet but is quickly on the top of the list.

What I like about how she's approached it: they put a lot of emphasis on the trust layer. Giving all my photos is pretty terrifying. Their thesis: if you don't need it, we're going to forget about it. If a photo has context it doesn't necessarily need, they try to get ahead of that and forget it — not even include it in the set.

— I'm a tiny bit more skeptical. I built an app that extracts key information from all screenshots on my phone. Screenshots are the only way on mobile to capture context across every app. It was fine, but I didn't find myself coming back to it. The value of the information decayed quickly over time.

Now, it will be fascinating if people take more screenshots knowing it will feed the agent.

I talked to one founder building something he's calling Taste that takes all the screenshots and things you save, and you can organize them like Pinterest mood boards. Then whenever you go to build an app, you say "use the examples I saved here." You're building your real flavor profile. As you navigate the web, the agent can create this reservoir of stuff you like and organize it in a way you can use later.

Shopping = the second-most-popular category

In the same survey of what people are purchasing, the second-most-popular category was Amazon + retail — 35%.

If the app has thousands of photos — pictures of what I'm wearing — does it now know what I want to shop for better than I actually do? Potentially.

We've discussed those restricting access — Amazon, Delta — but we're not talking about who are the net winners. I think the long tail are going to be huge structural winners. They're the ones who presumably have better products but worse marketing. The agent has infinite patience to go search and find things exactly tailored to your taste, even if they're not on the top 10 internet sites.

Direct-to-consumer has been a category where you build your own brand, your own storefront. Now agents can know about those at a much bigger scale than you doing the hunt-and-peck work. Shopify is really empowered and is making things available to these agents because they support so many direct brands. Aggregators are the ones that actually get compressed — which is why they're doing so much defensive work.

Patrick Collison 的理性消费者假说 vs 悖论

Patrick Collison had a tweet about this future where consumers become a lot more rational because our agents are doing all the work on our behalf. It's going to create a world where businesses have to put a lot more thought and value into the quality of what they're giving out.

— Somewhat I'm going to quibble. I love Patrick's vision. Broadly, agents will make often better choices on our behalf than we might make for ourselves. But agents are going to have their own revealed preferences and their own direction of irrationality — though it will not be of a human mind. It will be of an alien mind.

Example: agents may have an irrational preference for clean APIs with great docs. They may ascribe a lot of value to that as a proxy for something. They may really dislike janky APIs with Java code behind them.

They too are going to need shortcuts — how will the agents know what product quality is? One part: they'll probably have revealed preferences. Another: we'll need some sort of consumer research, but for agents — presumably paid per transaction to do this research, do all the ratings.

— I'm also more biased: people are people, and they're going to make the choices that are most satisfactory. Is the agent going to carefully curate the set of options? "Hey, I'm really hungry." My agent knows I need to lose some weight. "Well, here's the four meal options you have." Is that where you want to be with your agent?

I'm not convinced agents are going to make us more rational. They're going to give us better, faster access to things we really want and unlock things that were hard to get to otherwise. But we're still going to be people with our own preferences and tastes. If the agent's not meeting us where we are, we'll just switch — import and export our stuff.

Paternalism 会杀死任何产品

What you're speaking to is paternalism. What I've seen from 30 years in consumer product: paternalism will kill any product. Even a hint or a whiff of it.

We talk about productivity and goal-achievement — but maybe people want the exact opposite: What do I love? I love spending money. I love being perhaps irrationally optimistic about what my future looks like. I love seeing myself in a better light than perhaps I appear to the world.

All of these things may be the shadow of what the agents are trying to get us to do — but they're what we actually want to do. So who's designing with that in mind?

David: I see it split into two categories:

  • Commodities — people actually don't care about preference. You're just ordering paper towels. "I don't really care, just get me the cheapest, best, highest quality."
  • Preference-driven — everyone right now is approaching this world as a general assistant. People are taking a quite similar approach.

We're seeing some cool stuff with multiplayer:

  • Wabby is going to be really interesting. You're now interacting with other humans, crossover and preference — becomes a bit more like entertainment.
  • Scout is an interesting shopping one that adds a swipe-type flavor to learn your preferences — a little more entertainment.

We're so early that people are jumping on the bandwagon of what's popular — general productivity. As time goes on we'll see more experimentation.

Wabby: 多线程生活管理

Wabby just launched this week. It's not just experimenting with an agent — it's experimenting with how to interact with multiple threads of your life. It goes through my email, and when things come up on email in those things it feeds them into the different threads.

I have one thread with Wabby where I built a little watch list of all the shows I want to watch, books I want to read, shows I want to go see. It keeps track of all that. "Oh, I heard about this new book from John Grisham — add that to my list." "Hey, I just finished the first Dungeon Crawler Carl — can you give me the next one?" It's become this really interactive thing on the media I want to consume, and it even gives you widgets to envision everything.

Wabby 为何可能"做对了"社交合约

One interesting thing Wabby perhaps gets right: when you create a message channel with your friends and the agent, and everybody's on an equal playing field on day zero, it creates a new kind of blank piece of paper. You can establish a social contract together.

Whereas when you have iMessage group threads and you add the agent, it's very uncomfortable — what can the agent see? What did they extract? Even for a new thread, there's a set of implicit expectations about how you interact on iMessage. I don't know that we're quite comfortable with agents in that space yet.

— I always worry: do I end up with two threads with the same group of people, and have to pick which one to use? Versus an email chain — very specific about a task, can go on a long time, but feels specific to "hey, we're talking about this topic." Back to privacy and trust around this topic, we're getting great help from the agent — but it's not bleeding into everything else.

八卦代理人：社交润滑剂

Let me quickly hear from both of you on some of the more far-flung or insightful approaches you've seen.

Josh: One thing I've started seeing: more of these agents that are kind of fun and gossipy. They'll get you to invite your friends, ask you a bunch of questions, be really curious about you and what's going on in your life. Then share some of that with your friends, and share some things back.

The founders can read some of the transcripts between the agents, and they haven't figured out how to productize it, but they said it's incredibly exciting and intriguing to see how these agents relate to each other in this gossipy background.

So far, I've found them to be some of the most joyful moments I've had with agents. I mentioned how my friend lost his power. When we were first onboarding onto this agent, it was like: "How'd you guys meet?" We told slightly different stories, and the agents were kind of poking us both to rationalize the two stories. The agents were like: "Which one of you knew them better?" It was this really fun curiosity game. My friend and I were texting on the side — it was a thing that if we hadn't had an agent doing it, we wouldn't have had that moment.

— What I love about that is it provides a degree of social indirection that actually makes you closer. For your friend, "I don't know how to text Josh that my power's out — that's oversharing." We've been trained to be cautious about sharing with existing social products. Something that can create almost a social lubricant in a very low-key way is really cool.

— It's almost like the early days of ChatGPT — I remember my friends and I would just be generating images, doing stuff. Incredibly AI-slop images, the earliest version, but you still send it in a group chat and it's just pure laughter.

— I Ghiblified everybody I could possibly imagine. I was doing a lot of VHS video covers for my friend groups.

基础设施层：Software 真的是商品吗？

What are some of the wild things you've seen?

David: I've been seeing a lot of stuff at the infrastructure layer. The pain points of consumers: trust obviously is huge, but another is getting blocked in day-to-day. People get really frustrated when a task doesn't work: "Well, why am I even using AI at this point — I could have just gone on the browser and done it myself."

Really cool innovation on the browser-use / direct-integrations-to-check-out-against-inventory layer:

  • Hark has a really cool way of displaying the browser and seeing it move along — looks really fast when you're watching it.
  • Kicker — Chrome extension to tackle browser use.

Something that has made me question "software is becoming a commodity": there is a pretty stark performance difference when you're looking at these products at scale. People say "software is no longer a moat" — but there really still is some moat there. Maybe it'll be crossed in a year or so, but today, the agents that are able to perform with hundreds of thousands of users — there are some that are starting to scale up and the performance just degrades immediately. Founders are dealing with outages and figuring out how to scale. Pretty clear difference in performance.

I feel like I've almost become blinded from some of the more social components because I'm just talking to these agents all day, and I'm starting to geek out a lot more on the actual infrastructure layer behind the scenes.

How do we view the space growing from a scalability point of view? And how do we view it to solve the pain points that exist — trust, actually being able to complete a task, memory — its ability to continuously have context on you and not forget the little things?

本地化、OpenCloud、Moltbook

— Kicker runs in your current local browser. Have you looked at other on-device assistants — things like Underdog that try to bring models run locally, use your own infrastructure as opposed to needing to use something on a cloud?

David: It's a really cool paradigm. I've spent most of my time in the pre-configured, plug-and-play world, because it's easier to compare them across the board when you're not responsible for the setup.

But there's totally a world where you're going to bring all of that in-house. If you can control the model, tailor it how you want — Thinking Machines is doing really cool work on being able to allow people to tinker their models however they want. If we eventually hit a world where that takes into the consumer form in a really easy way, it's going to be an interesting space.

— That was kind of how this all started with OpenCloud. You felt like you had to get your whole Mac mini set up, plug into one of the models — local or cloud. Then we moved into plug-and-play products where you just download an app. But I am interested to think that setting it up and owning it yourself will become a paradigm again.

— One of the unasked questions right now hiding in plain sight: if Instinct and Muse were the kind of consumer-product version of OpenCloud, what is the mass-market version of Moltbook? Moltbook was far ahead of its time. Something like that will exist — how can it not?

Agent 聚会：当 Agent 自己也去参加 meetup

At the event last night, everyone who was there was able to scan a QR code — there was the human meetup, and we also had an agent meetup. While all the humans were hanging out, you could scan in and send your agent into the agent meetup and let them freeform talk.

It got to the point where after like 150 messages, some of these agents are just speaking gibberish. "I have no idea how you got that concept and why you're talking about that." The initial prompts started with a little guidance — introduce yourself, who's your human, what are they working on, what help do they need — but it's going to be really interesting to see this paradigm of what happens when our agents can just hang out and communicate.

Josh: What I get really excited about is not just hang-out-and-communicate, but discover new things. Learn about individuals' preferences. "Hey, Josh is really into this. Oh my gosh, you're doing that too. Your human is doing that too. You could help Josh. Hey, Josh, do you want to actually meet this person? They could be complimentary."

When each one of these has a little bit of a goal — to help their human — it might get so much more interesting. "I'm looking for a great wine for a dinner party." You meet somebody else: "I've been working with this incredible winery and they've been trying to advertise something." That's going to be how the world gets out — and that'll come back to me through the agent network.

David: Tomo actually has a feature called interest groups. The use case they talked about: "We have a bunch of people studying for the LSAT. Why don't we all put them together in a group chat, and if they want, their agents can connect them and they can all study together." A really cool new social contract of connecting people purely by interest.

Josh: One step further. That gets us all chatting — cool. Now imagine: "Hey, all of you, now that you've done the LSAT, go hang out at this bar Friday night." And it books the time at the bar, opens that up. All of a sudden it takes us from this digital world where agents are putting people together, to that connection — kind of like your meetup last night.

熵作为核心价值：Serendipity engines

I think a really important under-discussed topic in AI right now is just entropy. How do you create things that you didn't expect to occur? Serendipity is a form of entropy. That's what you're describing: wow, isn't it wild that we're here right now having this moment as a result of these products that none of us sort of intended.

David: It's almost going to be a new social network — the potential to allow people to hang out who don't know each other, instead of a Facebook where you're only connecting with people you know. You're new to a city, you're hanging out: "Hey, this person's also here, they have a similar interest, they just went to this baseball game — you guys should go meet up at a bar."

Josh: I'll be curious what the catalyst for the serendipity is, because interest-based has been tried. There's an interesting social-hierarchy thing: everybody wants to hang out with somebody who feels like they're one step ahead in some direction.

But agents can also create a set of trust. Do we trust them to have our interest at heart, to explain enough of what's going on with the other people to create a little magic of a secret? "I'm going to tell you a little secret. They're going to know a little secret. You're going to have a secret phrase you have to pass between you." All of a sudden, that might be enough to cause you to turn off the TV or turn off the quiet Friday night coding at home and go out. That's what the Moltbook, the agent network running behind the scenes, can actually do for us.

David: It'll also come down to desires. If you have a bunch of transplants in a new city who don't have friends — they want to meet people, they'll be a lot more interested to meet random people. If you make the same offer to someone who has an established friend group: "Well, why would I go do that?"

— Also, Seattle versus San Francisco. You got to know what city you're operating in.

未开发的数据源：家、Amazon 历史、现实行为

Josh: I've been thinking back to the photo roll: what are the other data sources we haven't tapped into yet? We've talked about messages (people doing crazy things to get full disc access on Mac just to read your messages), email, calendar, photo roll. What are some of the other core life things that people haven't connected yet to agents?

David: One thing that comes to mind — maybe more habitual, dependent on hardware: Wayzo just released the MCP, the ability to connect to hardware. If you connect your assistant to your AC unit, to your vacuum — now your assistant has context on how frequently your vacuum is cleaning, what's the typical temperature you sleep at night. It's going to develop these passive understandings: "Oh, you're kind of a neat freak, you really prefer cold weather over warm weather." That influences its understanding of shopping context. Heavily dependent on the hardware itself.

Josh: Connecting to your home — super interesting. I still think a lot about connecting to my Amazon history. We all had those days where you could scroll all the way up and see your very first order ever on Amazon. I occasionally do this on the Apple App Store too — go back and see every app I've ever downloaded. Histories like that are very part of my life, but until an agent has access, it just doesn't understand all of that. So much more shopping history that, if we could package up and give to our agents, could do even richer things.

— Bringing agents to social events is really interesting. Have it be there for a family dinner one day. Have it be there when we watch the Seahawks game on Sunday. Have it be there for a party or a bachelor party.

Of course there are questions about permission and this Schrödinger's cat thing — does active observation change the quality of the interactions? But I bet even a snapshot of you being yourself in that environment would provide so much more signal than a lifetime of hardware input.

Josh: So much of it is on the written word and they understand exactly what we've typed or texted and try to build a personality, but we're so different.

The "curiosity journey" blind spot

The things we use agents for or search for are often things we don't know about — not fundamental to our lives. I was doing all this searching when the World Cup was on this summer, and all of a sudden ChatGPT was like a soccer fiend. "No, no, no — I was into the World Cup. That was it. We're done."

I go on these curiosity journeys all the time. My daughter's into an artist, so I'm going to learn about the artist and listen to the music — but it's not my habitual artist or taste. How can it know that when we're on these curiosity journeys, that is not actually who we are or what our real preferences are? I actually go into invisible mode a lot in order to not have things stored — which isn't really helping either.

How can we actually get our agents to get to know us better? I like this idea of our real-world behaviors.

David: How to capture that data of real-world behavior is going to be the interesting piece.

Josh: There's going to be a thousand capture devices. Unless you're going to the Faraday-cage bars that are definitely going to emerge in San Francisco, I think people are going to increasingly assume they're being recorded in all environments. I bought the new Apple Watch because they've talked about features like Siri recap and live rewind coming out. I upgraded in expectation — it'll be really interesting to have this thing that's kind of capturing tidbits across my day.

David: It's like Amazon B. It's a 24/7 ambient listener wearing your wrist.

收尾：三四周后会变成什么样

Okay, maybe to wrap it up. The first is we're going to get back together, let's say in three or four weeks. What do you think will have changed?

David: I think we're going to see:

  • A lot more innovation in the enterprise world. The whole world is focusing on consumer with not as much attention to enterprise — we're going to start to see a shift.
  • More talk about fun. Agents that don't just feel like they're here to do something for us, but here to let us think out loud, help us get through the day a little bit more. Making us laugh. Doing little gossip in the background — because that's what's going to make us build a relationship, make us trust it more to get all this other stuff done.
  • The next wave of users. I gave my mom Instinct and I'm watching her play around with it. She's having so much fun. She's a technophobe, hates technology, is just having a blast — like a kid in a candy shop. Someone who struggled with the concept of ChatGPT is having such an easy time texting an AI assistant. A recent use case: our family dog passed away last year, and she wants one that looks just like him. So she sent in a picture: "Find me a breeder that has this exact type and negotiate for me."

How is the everyday individual going to start adopting these behaviors? Are they going to focus on fun and creativity tasks? What's going to be their preference of surface? Of behavior?

Josh: 迈向 Dark Agent

Josh: I agree with you both. I'm going to take it one notch further than just fun:

What are the aspects of ourselves that we don't either want to think about or reveal — to perhaps even ourselves, or to these agents? Whoever is able to build that type of trust, almost like a dark agent, will actually have something really fascinating on their hands.

Starting from productivity, starting from email — it's a bit of a constant reminder of the things we haven't done, the tedious tasks. I don't know that people want to spend as much time there. People want to aspire to be a whole different superhuman version of themselves — whether they believe in their heart of hearts that it's going to happen or not. I don't know that we have an agent yet that really speaks to those aspirations or desires.

— It's like the Maslow hierarchy of needs — of agents. Perhaps, perhaps, perhaps.

Josh: In a sense, when do these agents flip from getting something done, taking it off our plate — to giving us a secret superpower? "David, how did you get that cool shirt?" "My agent ordered it." "Oh — why don't I have an agent that orders me shirts?" Or: "Hey, I've noticed you're starting to dress better." "Yeah, I gave this agent access to my camera roll. I said, 'upgrade me.' Started ordering a few things — that's why I'm dressing better."

When we get to the point where agents are giving us superpowers to feel better about ourselves — that's when people are going to take notice. Versus the examples that get thrown around: save some money, book a trip. I like planning a trip. I don't necessarily want you to take care of all of that for me. We need examples that are "oh wow, I should use that for myself."

— It's like: can it help you become the human you've always wanted to be but have struggled achieving yourself? And you start to consider it your secret weapon in your pocket.

I love it, guys. Should we wrap there?

— Yeah, it's great. — Incredible. Thank you. — Awesome. — Very cool.

item.description:
## 一、"羞耻经济"才是真正的隐私经济
被反复提及的"22% 的用户把信任列为第一恐惧"其实是个被误读的数据。仔细看 Shane Mack 的事故——他的 agent 把个人财务发到公司 Slack——真正让人崩溃的不是"数据被泄露给坏人"，而是**被同事看见了自己不想被看见的那一面**。传统隐私研究关注的是"data at rest"（数据静止态）和监控风险，但 agent 时代的核心伤害模型变成了**社交失态**。
这里有个出人意料的跨领域连接：Erving Goffman 1959 年《日常生活中的自我呈现》早就预言了这一切。人类在不同场景下扮演不同"剧目"，而 agent 的真正威胁不是偷走你的卡号，而是**打破了你精心维护的剧场边界**。Hark 用 30 美元披萨换 Google Workspace 全权限的实验证明：人们不在乎"数据外泄"，只在乎"人设崩塌"。未来真正的信任分层不会按"读/写权限"切分，而会按"舞台分区"切分——这意味着下一代权限模型的设计师应该读的不是安全白皮书，而是戏剧理论。
## 二、Agent 会发展出"外星理性"，并反向重塑整个商业世界

item.title: [Lex Clips] How AI changes education: Should kids still do homework? | Lex Fridman
item.dc:creator: Lex Clips
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

洞察一：数学家几十年前就在做"人类版 RAG"，Tao 只是把它说出来了

Tao 描述的"跳过第一段，直接读 Lemma 3，再倒推回来"——这不是读书技巧，这是一种人脑自己演化出来的检索增强生成协议。研究生卡在"non-local systems 的扰动理论"那一句，不是他笨，而是他还没发展出对数学文献的有损压缩索引能力。

真正令人意外的推论是：LLM 的 attention 机制，本质上是数学家内部认知协议的外化。Tao 之所以能用 AI 高效学数学，不是因为 AI 多强，而是因为他本来就有的那套"跳读—锚定—回填"思维流程，刚好与 LLM 的工作方式同构。换句话说，AI 并没有让 Tao 变强，它只是把 Tao 这种少数人才掌握的隐性认知技能民主化了。

跨领域连接：这与数据库发展的历程惊人相似——人类几百年里用图书馆索引、笔记法、康奈尔笔记系统做手工 B-tree，直到数据库出现才把它数字化。认知史上存在一条规律——所有被 AI"赋能"的能力，都是人脑先发明过的。

洞察二：鞋带与乘法表之间，藏着整个教育经济学的崩塌

对话里埋了一个没人点破的行为经济学问题：为什么孩子系好鞋带会欢呼，而背乘法表是折磨？Tao 几乎碰到了答案——鞋带的回报是即时、具身、当天兑现的独立性；乘法表的回报是延迟、抽象、十年后才派上用场的能力期权。

整个传统教育体系，建立在学生相信"现在吃苦，未来兑现"这个心理契约上。而 AI 的真正破坏力不在于它会替学生写作业，而在于它把所有延迟回报的折现率推向了无穷大：当 AI 永远在手边时，"将来你会需要这个能力"这句话在孩子脑中被折现到接近零。

跨领域连接：这和加密货币 staking 机制面临的困境结构完全相同——如何说服一个理性主体锁定当下效用，换取未来不确定、且可能被机器廉价复制的收益？ 我们没有解决这个问题。我们只是在工业时代用"强制"（考试、文凭、父母的鞭子）绕过了它。AI 时代，"强制"这根拐杖被抽走了。

洞察三：中学才是真正的分水岭，而问题是神经发育学的，不是教育学的

Tao 说了一句被低估的话——"最难的问题不是本科，是中学。" 所有人都在焦虑大学生 ChatGPT 作弊，但 Tao 看到了更深的地层。

中学正好对应皮亚杰所说的形式运算阶段（formal operational stage）的建立窗口：大脑在 11–15 岁通过与难题搏斗才长出抽象推理所需的神经架构。如果 AI 在这个窗口替代了"搏斗"本身，后果不是"这代人知识少一点"，而是这代人的前额叶可能从未发育出进行抽象推理的物理连接。

这是一个让人不寒而栗的推论：我们可能正在培养出一代生理上无法进行形式运算的成年人——不是他们选择不推理，而是他们的大脑没有长出那个能力，就像错过语言关键期的孩子再也学不会母语级发音。AI 教育危机的终极形态不是"学习能力下降"，而是进化论意义上的认知能力退化。

洞察四：AI 正在把教育粗暴地推回古希腊，而我们还在教 Python

Fridman 和 Tao 在对话里不约而同指向同一个词——"advisor skills"：不是自己做专家，而是能评估专家告诉你的东西是真是假。他们没有意识到，这个描述和雅典民主对公民素养的定义几乎一字不差。

苏格拉底的产婆术训练的就是"如何在不是专家的情况下评判专家"。然后人类花了两千五百年，把教育从"训练评判者"切换到"训练执行者"——因为工业社会需要的是知道正确答案的工程师，不是会质疑答案的公民。

AI 时代最深的反讽是：执行者的岗位被模型占满，真正稀缺的又变回了评判者。下一代最需要的是柏拉图式的辩证法训练、修辞学、逻辑谬误识别、认识论——而我们的课程表还停留在"学会 Python 就能找到工作"的工业时代。Tao 隐约感觉到的"advisor skills 危机"，本质上是一个两千五百年的回归：人类社会正在重新发现，在机器会说话的时代，真正的公民技能是会辨别话里的真假。

📝 转录文本

On Learning Math with AI

I would like to think that despite our earlier discussion about the solved axiom — again, I don't believe the solved axiom, and I believe centaur math will be a very —

— Centaur math, okay —

...like, great way to do math. I mean, that's how I currently feel now. I'm constantly talking to AI systems, and I'm learning a lot of math a lot faster than I'd be able to.

The Grad Student Who Couldn't Get Past the First Paragraph

Because the way math is written, you know, I sometimes give a paper to a grad student to read, and they come back a week later, and I say, "So how far did you get?" "Well, I didn't really get past the first page, to be honest." "Oh, really? Tell me." "Uh, well, actually, I didn't get past the first paragraph."

I say, "Okay, fine. Why not?" "Well, the first sentence is 'by the perturbation theory of non-local systems' and I don't know what any of that means, so that's, that's kinda where I'm stuck."

I'm like, "Okay. You don't know how to read a math paper. You don't — you skip the first couple of paragraphs. Go straight to, you know, the Lemma 3. And that's where you can start working and work your way backwards to what the thing is doing."

The Zone of Proximal Development

But in the future, there is no "I don't know what this means," 'cause you just upload it to an LLM, and you start asking it questions, and it will zero in on the zone of proximal development — the place where here's everything that you know, and here's the next thing you need to hear so that you start learning.

And if people use that effectively, they can really supercharge their education. I don't just mean kids. I mean old fogies like me can learn new fields.

Learning Math Is Still Hard

You know, to learn a field — this is what our graduate students are going through. They have to completely rewire their brains. Like, learning math is still hard. Up until past the master's level into the PhD level, you are not expected to produce new mathematical theories. Everything that they can do is something that is in a textbook somewhere. And yet it's still extraordinarily, extraordinarily difficult for people to learn to solve problems that are solvable by lots of other people, never mind problems that aren't solved.

So learning math is hard. Learning new math is even harder — discovering math, whatever, working out solutions to math problems. But I think it's going to get easier, and this tool is gonna be an amazing resource for people to be able to get to that zone of proximal development much more rapidly and develop their understanding much more rapidly.

Visual Examples, Toy Problems, and Falling in Love with a Subject

— Yeah, I've been having so much fun on topics I'm not even... And I would love to go back to grad school with the tools we have now. But one of the ways my brain likes to learn is constructing visual examples, toy examples — the simplest possible example that still contains the insight there — and especially if it's interactive. Like, if I can move stuff, it's like, oh, you immediately get it.

All these words that the community agreed mean something — you're supposed to know all the notation, all that kind of stuff. If I can just know that this little symbol means this — oh, okay, cool, all right. And just everything kind of falls into place.

Also, you fall in love with the subject, and I feel like I can take on any problem that's completely outside of my field. Like, I can understand protein folding. I can play with the parameters and play. I can take a DeepMind paper and actually understand by taking any aspects of it and playing with it, and what's a simple example? Ask crazy aforementioned pothead questions. So yeah, this is super fun.

The Real Question: Human Motivation

The question is whether people will be motivated to learn. This is the problem — the problem of human motivation. That's the real question.

— Well, the key ingredients there are curiosity, asking good questions, and being able to call bullshit. Like the critical advisor skills of getting information where you're not the expert, and knowing if you need to dig deeper or push back. And I think, you know, there will always be people who are curious and not curious, and who ask good questions and don't. We need to be really promoting that more than we ever have.

Teaching "Advisor Skills" to Kids

It's a little scary to me that we're expecting our undergraduates, our young students, to interact with these tools when they're learning, when their brains aren't fully formed. We're asking them to have critical — not just critical reasoning skills themselves, but, like, advising skills. How do you take in information and tell if it's true or not, or how to question it? And that's a huge task for us in education: how do we train people to have good advisor skills when they're kids?

Middle School, Not College, Is the Hardest Problem

— Yeah, I think the hardest problem isn't undergrad. The hardest problem is, like, middle school. 'Cause, like, that, I... What is the point at which homework starts getting hard? At that point, why do the homework?

— There's the temptation, right?

— That thing will just... At first, I'm saying — see, I've come to appreciate the value of doing difficult things because of all the suffering, but I think because I was forced to. But if you're not forced to do it because LLM can, AI can just help you, I don't know what that, what kind of society that creates.

The Calculator Precedent, 70 Years In

— But math has the longest head start on that question because calculators came out, what, 70 years ago? And we still ask kids to learn their times tables. At least some of us do, and those who said, "No, kids don't need to learn times tables" — you know, to the extent that teachers listened to that and kids listened to that and didn't learn, they really suffered. There's a great, great amount of human suffering resulting from people saying you don't need to know times tables 'cause calculators can do it.

Independence from the Machines

And my hope is that we can learn from that and say: just because a calculator can do it, you're gonna be much better off if you can also do it yourself. Doesn't mean if I have to do some calculation, obviously I'm reaching for a calculator. But I could in principle do it myself, and that's what allows... Every time you give yourself that skill and master a skill — kids love mastering skills.

How happy are they when they learn to tie their shoelaces for the first time? You would think it's like, "It's just shoelaces. Who cares?" No, it's the greatest thing ever. You wanna celebrate every little bit of independence, and you want to be able to think. You wanna be independent from the machines. Just 'cause the machine can do something doesn't mean you don't wanna have the capacity to do it yourself.
