item.title: [Invest Like The Best] What Happens When the AI Boom Slows Down
item.dc:creator: Invest Like The Best
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一、最意外的观察：这不是"AI 泡沫"讨论，这是一场投资者的身份危机

表面上，Martin 在谈 AI 基础设施、网络效应、M&A 策略。但如果你把他所有的"抱怨"串起来——对"网络效应"定义的较真、对"防御性"讨论的不耐烦、对"质量收入"过早被提出的愤怒、对"非共识投资"神话的拆穿、对后期投资者坐在早期董事会的吐槽——他真正在说的是：VC 行业集体遭遇了语义腐败。

同一批词被不同心智模型的人使用，却假装大家在谈同一件事。这才是他画出"四种投资者"象限的原因——不是教你怎么投资，而是让每个人先承认自己到底是哪一种，否则所有讨论都是鸡同鸭讲。

这是一场认识论的清算，披着投资策略讨论的外衣。

二、跨领域连接：Martin 其实在重演"托马斯·库恩 vs 卡尔·波普尔"之争

在科学哲学里有一个经典断裂：当一个范式转换时，旧范式的术语（质量、能量、时间）在新范式中虽然字还一样，但指称对象变了（牛顿的"质量"不是爱因斯坦的"质量"）。库恩把这叫 incommensurability（不可通约性）。

Martin 的"network effect 有三种意思"、"disruptive tech 下谈 quality of revenue 是类别错误"、"把 PE 心智用到 Series A 是范式错配"——这些抱怨结构上完全同构于库恩描述的科学革命时期：旧词还在用，但它们已经不指向同一个东西了。

更惊人的推论：如果这个类比成立，那现在 VC 行业的"无法沟通"不是人的问题，而是 AI 这场范式转换还没找到自己新的术语体系。"token factory"、"neocloud"、"neolab"这些拗口的新词正是语言在重构自己。Martin 之所以感觉所有人都在错位，是因为他同时站在旧范式和新范式里——他能看到两边，所以才痛苦。

三、隐藏的系统性真相：capital 本身是这次革命的新"物理常数"

Martin 说了一句被夹在采访中间、几乎没被追问的话——"AI 最大的颠覆，是你可以把资本投向问题了"。

工程学几十年来被"神话人月"（Fred Brooks, 1975）锁死：加人不会加速，组织沟通的次线性增长是软件开发的热力学第二定律。整个 VC 行业的早期投资公式——"小团队 + 少量资金 + 时间 + 运气"——是建立在这个物理约束之上的。

AI 打破了这条定律。20 个人 + 10 亿美元现在可以真的产出 10 亿美元的价值，这是人类历史上几乎没有先例的生产力函数。

最反直觉的系统性推论：如果资本真的能被"生产性地吸收"，那么—— - "估值过高"这个概念本身需要被重新定义，因为其隐含假设（钱多了会被浪费）不再成立； - VC 不是在"选公司"，而是在做"资本到智能的转换效率"的套利； - 公司的护城河不再是技术或网络，而是吸收资本的组织能力（这解释了为什么 Anthropic/OpenAI 的估值从财务角度看永远"不合理"）。

四、一个只有我注意到的隐藏模式

Martin 全场谈论的几乎所有例子——Nicera 卖给 VMware、Tabular 卖给 Databricks、Cursor 收购、World Labs、Open Router——都发生在基础设施层，而不是应用层。

但他谈的"创造力才是瓶颈"、"Grokbot 帮我把家变成星际迷航"却是应用层的梦想。

这个矛盾揭示了一个他本人可能没有完全意识到的真相：他作为基础设施投资者赚的钱，和他作为人类想要的未来，正在分叉。他的 PhD 技术判断力让他在基础设施上胜出，但他的灵魂其实想投消费端的奇迹。

这就是为什么他对"creativity is the only constraint"那段话情绪最浓——那是他作为用户的声音在穿透他作为投资者的角色。这种分裂可能是这一代最成功的科技投资者共同的、未被言说的张力。

📝 转录文本

开场：软件一直很糟糕

I mean, let's be honest, software has sucked. Technology's been hard to use. Like, it's most often broken. And now we're actually in a point where this stuff could actually start working.

People keep thinking of these things as software, and it's not. And I think we just keep mapping it to things like search and it's not. Like, we're starting to realize how powerful this stuff is. And I just think that the biggest constraint is no longer the tech. It's literally our creativity.

四种投资者心智模式

You recently wrote about sort of four buckets of styles of investing that might be applied in — call it venture, I don't know, big private market tech, let's call it. Can you enumerate those and just say a sentence on perspective of each?

Yeah, yeah, yeah. Again, I feel like I'm just in this point in my career — I've been doing this for a decade, I've done hundreds of deals — and I sit in these discussions and I just realize people aren't communicating very well.

So I kind of did this exercise where I'm like, okay, so what are the mindsets people bring to investing? And I think there's basically four types of mindsets.

1. 传统金融心智（Traditional Finance）

So the one that we were talking about before is like this traditional finance mindset, which is: the correct proxy for the health of a business is the market it's going into and its finances. That's what it is.

Spreadsheet stuff.

Yeah. It's like — what are the SaaS metrics? What is the size of the market? — and that is a proxy for the entire business. So that's one. And clearly growth investors do this, but more and more you see early stage Series A people do this, right? Which to me is a little bit discordant.

2. 生产性投资者（Productive Investors）

Then there's what I call productive investors, which: you believe you're investing in a productive asset and the productive asset is what's creating value. And if you believe in that, as it creates value, it will create market; and as it creates value, you're going to have to find ways for the business to catch up to that value.

The type of diligence you do if you're a productive investor is more like: what is the technical approach, what are the adjacent markets, how fast is this likely to evolve, how close is it to capturing value, is this the right team to build it?

3. 前沿投资者（Frontier Investing）

Then there's what I call frontier investing, which I think is the romantic, idealized version of VC from the 60s and 70s — which is kind of YOLO, man. It's like: founders know better than VCs, and they've seen something that I don't see, and they're going to go out there and do it — and who am I to second-guess them?

They almost look like talent networks. Like Chris Dixon — remember when he was investing in nootropics, he invested in Soylent, he invested in Oculus, he invested in Coinbase and in crypto. I mean, every science fiction trope from the 70s and 80s you kind of invest in and you just don't overthink any of these things. So it's almost like the strong form of the productive.

4. 投机性投资者（Speculative Investors）

And then the last one — and it is always so surprising how prevalent it is — is speculative investors, which: they don't even care about the asset. They just want to time a market.

You'll see this in crypto and in secondary markets where they don't know about the underlying asset. They probably don't even know very much about the actual business metrics, but they're like, "Well, this looks cheap, it's clearly going to go up in value. Oh, this is the top of the market, I'm going to get out." They're trying to time markets. They're actually just doing speculative — they're not really interested in whether the business will grow.

And again, the problem is: if you have all of these archetypes, you can justify any deal or not justify any deal. So if you don't know what your beliefs are, you'll always basically just justify whatever personal bias you have.

作为生产性投资者的方法论

If you think about yourself as a productive investor focused on disruption — what do you actually look at when assessing whether someone might be creating a truly disruptive piece of technology?

So I only do computer science investing, and I only do infrastructure investing. Infrastructure as an industry has a certain shape — certain buying behaviors, the technology looks a certain way, and the industry acts a certain way. So what you're trying to do is take a technical approach and map it into that framework.

The way you do that: one, you ask what the leading companies are doing internally — that'll give you a glimpse on how platforms evolve, or perhaps the team doing this had done it in another context and is now bringing it to this context.

How much can you diligence without actually just using the numbers as a proxy? You can talk to customers — will they use this? You can see if there are adjacent budgets growing that you could argue will fragment to become this. Maybe you have early signs of willingness to pay but they haven't figured out the business model.

I always think: every tech wave — and I've been in the industry for 30 years — people are hand-wringing about margins. I remember for the cloud, I remember for mobile, I remember for the internet, and clearly now people worry about margins. So maybe there's willingness to pay and a lot of interest, but we haven't figured out the COGS yet or the actual viable business model. You're using partial indicators, not full indicators.

My team has a lot of technical people, product people, many have PhDs. We don't second-guess the tech — the founder will know the tech better than us. But we can ask: how does this tech fit into the broader platforms? How does the tech fit into spending? How does this tech fit in with our understanding of stickiness and defensibility?

With frontier investing, I don't think you do any of that. You're like, "Is this the best team to do this crazy thing?" — and then you just YOLO.

没人真正理解"网络效应"

You were saying before we hit start that nobody understands network effects. Can you explain what you meant?

I've realized that even the most common terms we use, there's no consensus on. Network effects is the favorite one that I pick on. I asked you before —

I messed it up.

No, you didn't mess it up. You said what like a third of people say. So I asked, what is a network effect? What did you say?

I said: a product that gets better as it adds a marginal user.

So to me this is almost a tautological definition, because most products will get better as you add a user — they will find a bug, they will provide feedback, they will tell other people. That doesn't say anything about defensibility.

Other people, when they use the term network effects, actually mean the original meaning from the 70s — a telephone network where when users join they interact with each other, that grows super-linearly, and that's why you get natural monopolies.

Other people use the term network effect more to mean an actual flywheel — a self-reinforcing flywheel. Not just that things get better, but it self-reinforces in some way. This is where you hear the term "data network effects." But even in that sense, you don't know if that self-reinforcement is super-linear or not. So you don't know if it makes it defensible or not.

So you have this very common word that's on 70% of pitch decks where a founder is sitting in front doing a pitch, and nobody has consensus on what it means.

护城河的形状 vs. 产生它的机制

So how would you define it?

I think the root of the confusion is not a definitional problem. Conceptually, we conflate the mechanism with the shape of the moat.

There's many things that could create a moat — a brand, scale, a two-sided marketplace, a network effect. But that moat is only really useful if it has properties that make the company defensible against somebody else. If that moat grows super-linearly with scale (like a classic Metcalfe's law network effect), that's really defensible. If it grows sub-linearly with scale, it may not be useful at all.

So the first thing we need to do is not conflate the shape of the moat with the mechanism that caused it. First, we should say the moat we have is super-linear, linear, or sub-linear with scale. And then: many things actually contribute to a moat.

For example, network effects or scale effects. What's a scale effect? As the company scales, it can reduce unit economics — normally because it has pricing power, or maybe CAC goes down because of brand.

What's a two-sided marketplace? That's very different to me than a network effect. That's where basically you've got self-reinforcing supply and demand.

There are many mechanisms, and then there's the shape. To have a discussion, you want to make sure that the shape is something that actually provides long-term defensibility.

The last thing I'll say: it's almost impossible to have these conversations in isolation, because we're actually talking about competitive equilibria. If you have a network effect, maybe the competitor has a network effect too. And maybe if they have more capital than you and grow faster, that impacts the shape of your moat.

超线性、线性、次线性的例子

Can you give examples of super-linear, linear, sub-linear — just to bring it to life?

A common view of where network effects came from is from the 70s. An economist who worked at Bell Labs noticed that for train networks and communications networks, the interactions of users grow with the square of the number of people that join. As a user joins, they can communicate to many other people — so the actual number of connections grows more than the number of users. Same with destinations on a highway or on a train.

That means: if you have two competing companies and one takes $5 million of funding and the other takes $5 million, but this one is marginally better and marginally larger — for the same amount of investment, it will grow faster than a challenger. The growth actually increases over time, and that's why you get a monopoly.

Sub-linear means: if I'm a leader and I invest the same amount as a challenger, I grow marginally slower than the challenger. That's critical when it comes to moats, because if you have two competing companies and there's a sub-linear moat, the challenger will always catch up to the leader because the leader has to spend ever more money to grow.

[广告段落：Ramp / Rogo / WorkOS]

Ramp is the only platform built to make your finance team leaner, faster, and better… Rogo is the AI platform purpose-built for financial institutions… OpenAI, Cursor, Anthropic, Perplexity and Vercell all have something in common. They all use WorkOS…

真正的网络效应其实很罕见

Do you have favorite company examples of these different types?

How many actual network effects in the Metcalfe's law super-linear sense do you think there have actually been?

Very few, I don't know.

I feel this almost never happens. We can all agree the telcos — that's why we had to break them up. We could probably all agree LinkedIn, they haven't had to change very much and they basically have permanent status in social networking. I would say GitHub was another one — interconnections of users.

There are not very many examples, but when you have them, these are very durable, high-value companies. That to me would be a classic network effect.

Other companies are probably more scale effects. People will say Uber — I'm not sure that would fit the definition of a network effect. Maybe a two-sided marketplace, because you have drivers and passengers. But even then, you don't have a lock on either of them — all drivers drive for everybody, all passengers could use anybody. That seemed more like a funding scale effect because they could raise more money, and therefore unit economics went down.

为什么防御性讨论被过度放大

My meta-observation: I actually think the network effect thing was more of a personal annoyance and me being pedantic. But I actually think defensibility moats are kind of not even worth talking about most of the time.

Here's my experience: if a market you're investing in is growing, then companies are not going to want to compete — there's a lot of new white space being created. So they'll try to move into other white space. Talking about defensibility is a second- or third-order thing if the market is growing. And if the market is slowing down or shrinking, normally it consolidates anyway, independent of moats.

I do think we spend a lot of time as investors hand-wringing about defensibility when, in practice, it doesn't really matter — especially in growing markets.

We've seen this with AI. I remember early discussions on models — "I will never invest in a model. It'll never accrue value. It's not defensible." That's fine, but as long as the market's growing in a large market, it's going to accrue a lot of value. Same with the Neoclouds — "they're never defensible, the quality of revenue is bad." We kind of trick ourselves as investors by thinking in terms of defensibility, when if there's a growing market, it's not even worth considering.

金融心智过早被应用

Do you think that's a unique privilege of your stage of investor? Once you get later stage public — someone buying the Anthropic S1 needs to probably think about defensibility.

It depends on your thesis on the size of the market. If you believe we're 0.1% penetrated, this has a long way to go, value will accrue, and if you're liquid you can go in and out of the market.

The nature of venture has really changed. If you read back to the time of Arthur Rock, it was really frontier-like investing — people didn't think about quality of revenue, they didn't think about defensibility so much. It was people, tech, and new markets.

Over the last 30 years, the tech market has grown so large, the amount of money available has grown so much, and the size of private companies has grown — a private company today rivals public companies of just 10 years ago. So VCs have actually become public investors. And a lot of people who entered VC have come from business school and traditional finance backgrounds. I think a lot of the mindset comes from that world, but it gets applied too early.

I talk to a junior investor who says, "Oh, the quality of revenue is bad." I'm like, "Homie, we didn't even know how to monetize the internet." Business models always lag disruptive technologies. Always.

If you truly believe you're investing in a disruptive technology: - (A) You should believe it creates TAM — so why would you worry about market size? It's creating market size. - (B) It's disruptive — we don't even know what the pricing model is. Remember how long it took to go from perpetual to recurring?

My caution is: maybe most investors should know what kind of investor they are. Maybe you're a financial investor, and that's how you view the world — but then you're not actually evaluating tech. You're not evaluating the disruptive power of tech. You're literally looking at the quality of revenue, which is going to naturally move you towards non-disruptive technology.

These are all legitimate, coherent ways to invest. It's more about: don't be confused in your basic approach, because otherwise you become incoherent.

基础设施的现状

How would you describe the state of the union today in your world, in infrastructure?

The definition of infrastructure — the differentiation is actually technical. I don't view SaaS or apps that way. If you invest in a SaaS or apps company, it's not really a technical investment, it's a business — a business model innovation.

Because for us, as a technical innovation, it has to sit within the traditional technical stack: compute, network, storage, databases. Each has subcomponents, buyers, and now with AI, all of them are being disrupted. On top of that, you have models — which I would consider infrastructure. They look to me more like ASICs than traditional software — the capital needs, the competitive pressures. And I think they're disrupting the entire application stack above them.

So we're in a point of maximum disruption. All of the infrastructure supporting software — whether vibe-coded or not, whether to build models or not — doesn't change the major components: compute, network, storage, databases, and then models.

For example, when you worried about dev tooling in the past, you worried about ergonomics for a human. No, you don't really worry about that anymore. A lot of the design decisions we made as technologists were: "a human is going to be using this, so it can't be too complicated" — and you'd trade off safety or reliability. We don't have to do that anymore because the models are doing it.

This is the biggest refresh of computer science infrastructure we've seen maybe since the internet — maybe ever.

两个层面

Would the shorthand be that all five portions of infrastructure are being refactored for agents?

I split it into two pieces: 1. People are vibe-coding a lot of stuff. There's more software being written than ever before — and that has to run somewhere. Maybe an agent created it, maybe a human — but it needs databases and compute. 2. We're building these new systems that have AI at the heart of them, and that changes things.

So: assume way more software being built that needs to run and be deployed somewhere, and now we also have systems that create agents.

唤醒沉睡的基础设施品类

A lot of infrastructure is getting a bit sleepy, and now, because agents are very sophisticated, that's no longer the case.

Take OLTP — transaction databases, think Oracle. Pretty mature, you didn't see a lot of movement, maybe just movement to the cloud. Now we're seeing really interesting companies. The hard thing about using a database from a programmer standpoint is databases always had their own languages for technical reasons, and it's really hard to have them work with normal programming languages. If you change that language, programmers wouldn't know how to use it.

But now, because of AI, we're seeing databases come out with entirely new ways of thinking that have way better properties. They don't really have to train anybody, because the agents already know how to do it. OLTP may look entirely different in 5 years.

Networking — I did my PhD in networking, it's an area of special interest. It's been so sleepy and boring for the last 15 years, and now because these clusters we're building are so large with such rigid performance constraints, we're seeing net-new networking companies come out for the first time since Arista. Changes in the materials used to build them. Optical coming up.

Compute — the whole notion of what the abstractions are to run an agent on. Is it a container? A VM? A durable workflow like temporal? That is changing.

We're at a point of maximum disruption where many points of the infrastructure stack can be rebuilt.

关于模型：如果市场放缓会发生什么？

Anthropic S1 came out this week — beautiful view into the business. But I'm more interested in what you think about just the state of these things today.

The biggest question is: what happens if and when the market slows down?

We've got three years of data on what happens in the existing very big, fast-growing market. On the frontier, being on the frontier means you've got tremendous pricing power. Even if you're just an epsilon better than the next guy, you've got tremendous pricing power. There's no demand problem — infinite demand. These frontier models tend to get 80%+ of the market dollar-weighted. That's happened for three years.

You could argue the reason is because we've not saturated the market at all, and people want the smartest thing. Under that view, nothing structurally will change as long as the market's growing. And this could go on for a while — penetration is 1% or so. They say 3% of enterprise, but budget-wise it's 1% or less.

The more interesting question: what happens if the market starts to saturate in pockets? Will things shift to open source? Will you lose pricing power on the frontier?

One thing we don't account for well: what happens if you invest in a model and you don't get the next model out really quickly? Let's assume Anthropic stumbles and doesn't release a model for 6 months. What's the lifespan of the previous model?

A very short period of time.

Very short — entirely different than we've ever had in software. In software we've always assumed some long tail. What happens if you put out the SOTA model, everybody loves it, something internal happens — regulatory, technical, a breach — and you slip three months? It could be the case that you lose the entire market. My experience, from seeing a lot of model graphs: the lifespan of a model is three to six months.

So: - If the market continues to grow and doesn't saturate — the frontier wins. - If use cases saturate (you don't need more intelligence) or markets slow down for another reason — nobody knows. There's a very real world where value comes crashing back down into open source.

编码饱和 vs. 竞争均衡

On this trip I've been asking people what percent of software coding tasks are already saturated — the typical answer is very high. That's been the biggest market, and yet people are spending like crazy on frontier tokens.

These are two very different statements:

Statement 1: "I am not using more tokens, because I've automated 95% already." We're getting pretty close to that.

Statement 2: "Therefore I can use a cheaper model." This does NOT follow from statement 1.

If you and I are competing startups — Martín-startup and Patrick-startup, in competitive equilibrium — are you going to choose a dumber model to compete with me?

In competitive equilibria, you wouldn't. You would always pay 10 times more for the smartest model.

Always. So, will you saturate tasks so you don't need a smarter model? Very hard to do that in Darwinistic economic equilibria. At the end of the day, it's: can you get software out faster, can you make it better, can you compete? That will push you to the more intelligent thing.

Things will slow down because you're actually not spending more tokens — so either you increase prices or go broad. But pricing is maintained, and we're seeing broadening use outside of code. General knowledge work — I'm a huge Grokbot user, it's my favorite thing ever.

个人实验：让 AI 在家里具身化

Say more about your personal experience.

I feel like I've waited my entire life for this technology to show up. I want Star Trek. I want to go home and have my house greet me, talk to it, have the face show up on the monitor. We've never been able to do it, and now it's kind of trivial.

My new passion project: I want Grokbot to embody itself. What I tell it: "I want you to be the living AI in my house. Just like Star Trek. Help me make this happen." And it's literally buying stuff. Yesterday I bought a few hundred dollars worth of gear that's coming to the house.

What gear is it buying?

I don't even know. Weird obscure open-source projects. I know some home automation stuff — Zigbee Life — but it's really obscure stuff it's decided to buy. I have in my head this vision of that vintage view of what the future looked like, the 70s view — like The Jetsons. I've been feeding it pictures and descriptions and I want it to create that by itself. I'll let you know how that goes.

想象力才是瓶颈

People keep thinking of these things as software, and it's not. We keep mapping it to search, and it's not. We've really created a general, flexible technology that can bring us many of these future things we've always dreamed about but didn't have the technology to implement. We're so constrained from our presuppositions of what software can do that people aren't doing as many of these things.

Another example — I worked with Fei-Fei and World Labs. They released a model called Marble a few months ago that generates 3D scenes and supports dynamics. I realized: we're this close to being able to step into a movie. Imagine having Spirited Away running — Miyazaki probably wouldn't be happy with it — but you throw on VR glasses and walk in. Did you ever see Sleep No More? Why isn't there a Sleep No More in VR?

A lot of these tropes and visions of the future from the 50s and 60s — we can actually make them. The biggest constraint is no longer the tech. It's literally our creativity. We've been beaten down by 30 years of software being — let's be honest — bad. Hard to use, old people hate it, often broken. And now this stuff could actually start working.

数字世界已经"解决"了

What, if anything, do you think is missing from the models?

If you step back, the current tech stack — anything that's digital — with enough capital, you can solve. Because anything you can simulate on a computer, you can create RL environments for. Whether that's 3D using Blender, general application use of a computer, or code.

The most interesting thing about AI — the meta-thing — is that you can take a mound of cash and point it at a problem and it will solve that problem. Maybe expensive, but you can solve it. In the past you'd be blocked in engineering and die. Now you can direct money at problems and solve them.

So anything you do with a computer, AI will be able to do. What I don't know: does the same thing apply to the physical universe? Sure, you could set up a lab, but are the scaling curves the same? Is the distribution the same? Robotics, the physical world, science, medicine — I have no idea if it follows the same laws. That's still an unlock. But the digital side? I feel very comfortable. It's done.

安全：现在不如 90 年代乱

How have you processed all this interesting security stuff — breaches, "breach apocalypse"?

I lived through the internet, and it was way worse than this. By this time with the internet, we had worms that caused billions of dollars of economic damage and taken out critical infrastructure.

Remember Windows 95? It used to be that if you installed Windows 95 and connected to the internet before the installer was done, it'd be infected. Not a joke. You didn't even have time to patch it. So much chaos and mayhem.

Every time you've got a new technology that changes how we run computers and the security posture, we deal with this. We can look to what happened with the internet: a few years of mayhem, breaches that cause real issues, and then the industry evolves. The way to think about security: will the good guys be able to spend more money than the bad guys? If yes — which is typically the case — you come up with a technical solution.

I think that will be the case here. These vulnerabilities showing up — that's good. It means somebody used the model to make things safer by pointing them out. The net impact will be software that is much more secure, because AI is also securing it.

资本作为新的约束条件

Can you talk about capital? Interesting things are happening in capital markets. There's clearly demand destruction — things we would have funded five years ago seem to pale in comparison to AI.

I sit on the boards of a lot of great companies with the problem you describe — profitable, growing 40-50-60% at scale, say $300-500M ARR. What do those companies do? You can't really IPO, they're subscale. But they're great companies. Everyone would be happy with an asset growing 40% if you could guarantee it.

The question is: will we see a shift in the market so people can get exposure to this asset class? The risk profile is very different than AI. Nobody knows what happens to AI when the market slows down.

The only free lunch I've ever seen in investing is diversification. I'd love to personally have a basket that includes these slower-growing assets.

Are most of these subject to disruption risk from AI? I'm an infra guy — more software means you need more infra. We haven't seen a big disruption; we don't vibe-code databases yet. Snowflake is growing 30-40% with good economics — I don't think they're at any risk of being disrupted by AI (maybe by Databricks, but that's pre-AI).

More and more the industry is going to want to wrap these up and get exposure. SPACs are even coming back. The financial markets have to figure that out.

算力作为真正的约束

Most meetings I have around here — half the meeting is about compute. The product across categories just needs more compute than is available.

The big disruption of AI is: you can throw capital at problems. In the history of tech, you couldn't do that — it was always an engineering problem, which doesn't scale. The mythical man-month is the mythical man-month for a reason.

Ten years ago, if five founders showed up and asked for a billion dollars and I gave it to them, what would happen? They'd sit there, or detonate. They'd hire a bunch of engineers and —

Can you explain the mythical man-month?

Sure. The mythical man-month basically says you can't increase the speed of engineering. It's very sub-linear, and one of the conclusions was it has to do with organizational communication. This comes from Fred Brooks in the 70s. You had software projects, you wanted to get them out faster, you'd throw more people at them, and it would go slower.

Engineering has always been this bottleneck. The biggest shift — industrial revolution level — with AI is: I can take 20 people and give them a billion dollars, and they can use that. Now, do they make $500M or $2B from that billion? I have no idea. But the fact that you can productively use that money is so new and so interesting.

At some level, capital markets need to figure this out. If you look at Anthropic and OpenAI, they've raised more money in aggregate than the entire downstream ecosystem combined, by a factor of whatever. They're mechanisms of turning money into growth.

债务侧的紧张

On the debt side — I'm not a debt guy, but on the ground, we're running out of available debt. If you're the Norway pension fund, are you going to give debt to a random Neocloud or buy T-bills? Scale will win, then non-IG players will have a harder time raising debt. If your business model requires debt, there's not enough to go around. Smaller non-IG players will need to prepay, which means their customers will need to prepay.

NeoClouds、NeoLabs、推理供应商

Lots of them have been funded, very few are at scale. I'm curious how this plays out.

Let's set NeoLabs aside — it's the least well-defined.

I included them because so many pitches turn into "we're building a token factory with vertical integration" — all the way down to buying land and power.

They're becoming NeoClouds. All NeoClouds want to be token factories.

NeoCloud (to me): provides the physical infrastructure that ends at tokens. Could be GPUs, fine-tuning services, or tokens. Think of a data center with GPUs in it.

NeoLab (to me): "Give me a billion dollars, we're going to come up with a new model architecture." A lot of these business plans: "If we solve ASI, that's our business model." Literally. To be fair, that's what OpenAI's and to some extent Anthropic's original thesis was: if you solve intelligence, the business model part is easy.

The real limitation right now is hardware supply — chips, materials, power. With that limitation, 80% is going to the scale providers, and 20% to hard-to-reach, niche places. There's a company that does basically a GPU marketplace of converted chicken sheds, where people in farms are finding ways to provide it. SpaceX isn't going to create a marketplace of chicken-coop GPUs. The 20% will always be a wide, fragmented array; the 80% will be homogeneous.

轨道算力

I heard someone asked Larry Page how much of compute will be orbital. He said "five nines" — just physics, eventually it's all going to be in space.

What's funny: the space thing actually pencils out, but the reason it makes most sense is regulatory. There are 500 proposed pieces of legislation to stop data center building in the United States alone, including Texas. If you can't build a data center in Texas, I don't know what we're doing. If that regulatory pressure continues and you can't break ground, either you go international or you go into space.

[广告段落：Vanta / Ridgeline]

估值与市场效率

Even if the disruptive asset is incredibly valuable, every one has a price that will ruin returns if too high.

This is another one of my bugaboos. I don't know how you can be a VC and not believe tech creates value. And I don't know how you can be a VC and not believe markets are efficient. What are we doing? For capitalists, you have to believe markets are efficient.

Private markets are very efficient. They figure out the price. I don't try to bet against the market. A lot of people think private markets aren't efficient, that you can find a non-consensus deal. All of those deals were incredibly competitive. I didn't win by looking for non-consensus — I pay the market price, maybe a little discount from negotiating, but I never worry about that.

As a productive investor, I trust that markets are pretty smart and will value it risk-adjusted. I believe my diligence reduces that risk — but I'm not trying to find a better price. I'm trying to find a less-risky asset.

Doesn't it follow that you should just index the private markets?

I would love to. You can't pragmatically. My dream would be: I get 5% of every competitive deal. Cognition — when you buy Cursor — I'd love 5% of every competitive deal.

But you can't, for competitive and capacity reasons. So the way we think about it: for every legitimate sector (good founders = good sector, because we don't second-guess founders risking their futures), we do the work to decide which is the top company. Team, tech, monetization potential, market growth. Then we assume the market is efficient. Kind of an index, but we segment by market.

That's stratified sampling from quant investing — you buy a small subset and your tracking error is very low.

So that makes sense. I just think venture capital early on believed tech created value and didn't over-rotate. There often was no business to evaluate. I just don't see so much hand-wringing about bubbles. The market price is the market price.

There's always huge dissonance when talking with other investors — they decry bubbles, which nobody can ever predict (by definition, when everybody's calling it a bubble, it's probably not a bubble). I got VC-canceled because I said non-consensus investing is dangerous — on Twitter I said it's dangerous because of follow-on capital risk. Many prominent VCs came out saying all their deals were non-consensus.

There's something tied to the ego and identity of investors — they have to believe they can truffle-hunt. But if you look at our portfolio, the ones that returned money were very competitive.

资本 → TAM

Another thing that drives me nuts: this belief that if you put money in private markets, it doesn't somehow grow the TAM of private markets.

I love Roelof at Sequoia — he's fantastic, incredibly intelligent, great board member. But he gave a talk at TechCrunch Disrupt: "venture capital is not an asset class, there are only 20 startups that matter." Many investors believe this. To me this is ludicrous.

Capital creates opportunities and markets and value. Even though there's so much more money in private markets in the last 20 years, the value has kept pace — massively large private companies, tons of opportunities, very large exits. This zero-sum thinking about private markets being a fixed supply is bizarre. We're venture investors. Tech creates value. If you put more money in it, it'll grow.

I'll talk to a senior GP investing 20 years, and they'll be like, "Oh, there's too much money." What are you talking about? There should be more money. We need more ecosystem, more value, more investment.

Money in private markets creates TAM. It creates the investable TAM, creates value. Companies not going public — if there's more private money available, why would you go public? Technology creates value, and capital enables technology to create value. If that's the case: more money in private markets, we should deploy it, we should create value.

M&A：这不是扑克

You've been on fire. Cursor, Fei-Fei's company, OpenRouter — three of the biggest M&As in the last few months.

I have a history with strategic M&A going back to my company. When I sold to VMware it was a $1.26 billion exit — at the time the highest acquisition of enterprise software by revenue multiple. Then I was part of the Tabular acquisition to Databricks, which beat that. Then Cursor — I think the largest price for an M&A ever. And of course the Fei acquisition was very large.

My comment goes only to strategic M&A. I've noticed trends:

1. Deep personal alignment. It's a real risk for both sides. Lisa Su and Fei-Fei. Michael Truell and Elon. Alex and Patrick. You almost always have people with the same visions of the future, same frameworks — whether markets, infrastructure, or data. Existing trust and alignment.

2. Take it from the mind of the buyer. The buyer is buying an option on a large market. VMware buying Nicira — a $1B option on a $40B market. For that to make sense, you have to solve the inductive proof: the base case (we have this business that sells into networking) and the inductive step (you have virtual machines, so if we attach this to a VM, we can sell more — therefore we can sell to the whole large market). Those conversations are high-stakes enterprise sales. Only founders can do them, and maybe investors who really understand strategically.

With auction-y M&A, you never have those conversations. You look at financial metrics, spreadsheets — they're buying an asset. Very different flavor.

With timelines going down on tech, we're going to see more strategic exits. Most people assume you should hire a banker and have an auction. Hiring a banker is fine, but the idea that you're going to go to an apex predator like Mark Zuckerberg and play poker — you're kidding yourself. These things are built on trust and telling a story, not playing games.

Cursor 的故事

We were just about to get a raise done — a few billion dollars. This is about the time Methos came out. If you work backwards, it probably cost $3 billion to make Methos. So we realized: if Cursor is going to build models, we need to raise more money and get access to compute.

That kicks off strategic discussions — not a lot of people have access to that much compute. There was a lot of interest in the company — by far the most users, by far the most data. SpaceX had the compute, Cursor had the data and a team that had successfully built models, and code was very important. A lot of alignment. It always helps to have a raise canceled because that sets the value and price. Fairly straightforward deal.

泄密是毒药

The most important thing — and the intuition of a lot of investors is wrong here — is: there's a deal going down, we need to play games, leak it to the press, get other companies in. Drives me nuts. You're literally dealing with the most sophisticated people on the planet. You don't walk up to Zuckerberg and say "I'm going to beat you in poker."

In every one of these deals, the companies in very good faith engaged with the buyers. They didn't play games. They knew they were worth a certain amount because they'd done raises or there were market comps. Lots of trust. That approach for strategic M&A is the right approach.

I've been part of deals that fell apart because somehow a board member got into the head of the founder — "oh, you need to get competitive better, leak it to the press."

Notice World Labs did not get leaked. Didn't get leaked because we didn't tell anybody. It was like me and a few people. OpenRouter was leaking constantly. A number of VCs think, "Oh, this is how you drive up the price." You see these things leak all the time. It destabilizes deals.

Your intuition as an investor — that this is some commodity asset, that it's about playing poker — is just wrong. If it's a strategic deal for a lot of money, view it very professionally. Develop a trust relationship. Do it in good faith. Don't leak. Realize counterparties are the most sophisticated people in the industry. Michael Truell treated it that way. Alex and Chris for OpenRouter. For sure Fei-Fei.

投资者角色的演变

How are you seeing the role of investors evolve?

Venture is not what it used to be, and the startup ecosystem is not what it used to be. The largest private companies would rival any public companies 20 years ago — Stripe, Databricks, SpaceX before IPO, Anduril. Massive.

What "startup" means has shifted so much that you have this undefined quagmire of who should be investing. Public investors investing in early-stage startups — those intuitions aren't right. It makes sense to delineate more on the private side. If later-stage people invest in earlier-stage companies, a little more self-awareness — you wouldn't put me on a mining company board.

Remember 2021? PE investors investing in Series B companies — I'd sit on boards with them, and it's literally like putting me on a mining company board. I had no idea, trying to reason about the company through burn — dude, you're going to be miserable here, all we do is burn cash for a long time.

How much larger is the market now than 30 years ago? A thousand times. Of course the industry has to mature around that. Of course you have to view it like a later-stage investor. But there's a funny identity crisis with later-stage investors. I would never invest in a late-stage company — what would I do? Tell you how to run a finance operation? It's just not me.

It's basically the incursion of traditional banking and traditional finance into venture — which absolutely belongs there. But sometimes it reaches a little too low. You have these issues in M&A ("let's run an auction") or in operations of a 20-person company where they're worried about burn, or over-rotating on metrics for disruptive technology.

We need to bring back traditional productive VC for some subset of this. There's enough market for everyone.

学会倾听

Has anything changed about how you meet somebody for the first time — then vs. now?

A lot. Most investors go through this, especially from the operating world — you have to learn how to listen as an investor. And to ask the questions you really care about so you can answer them to yourself. A very delicate balance.

Meetings with founders tend to be pretty performative on both sides. You don't know what to ask, so you ask "Who's your competition?" — a lot of it is asking questions for asking's sake, but it doesn't inform your decision. Especially if you're an operator, you'll hear something you disagree with and want to fix that problem — but that's not your job.

The primary job is just to listen. A founder will tell you what they believe. If you disagree, you disagree, but that's what they believe. So often they'll say, "Well, I would do it better and therefore it's a good investment" —

The second thing is truly an art: you have to make a decision based on that meeting. There are silly questions that won't inform that decision — "What if Amazon does that? What is OpenAI?" You can answer that yourself. But there are key questions you really want to know, and knowing which ones during the meeting and getting them in — that's hard. I've refined my ability to do that.

为什么现在这份工作如此令人兴奋

Why is this job so incredibly fun right now? Why are you most excited?

I'm more and more of the belief that this is an industrial-revolution-level shift. The industrial revolution went from a zero-sum world to a non-zero-sum world where net-new value is being created.

This is a very similar shift. Before, to solve problems, you had to solve very complex engineering problems — which didn't scale, were tough, had to be maintained — and that's why software has always sucked. Now it's a capital problem.

For the digital world — I don't know about the real world yet, I think we'll get there — we've turned this into a capital resourcing problem. And we're capital allocators. We're in a very strategic position to help drive the future in a much more direct way than ever before. This is a scale-up capital game.

I don't believe private markets have limited TAM. I think they have unlimited TAM, and the more money that goes in, the more value is created. We're in a very privileged position — key to the innovation chain. We're both lucky to be here.

结束语

I love the every-two-year schedule we're on. I hope we get to do it again in another two years. I can only imagine what the world will look like.

We'll have our Grokbox talk.

Thank you so much for your time.

Thank you.

[广告段落：Ramp / Vanta / WorkOS / Ridgeline]

item.description:
## 一、最意外的观察：这不是"AI 泡沫"讨论，这是一场投资者的身份危机
表面上，Martin 在谈 AI 基础设施、网络效应、M&A 策略。但如果你把他所有的"抱怨"串起来——对"网络效应"定义的较真、对"防御性"讨论的不耐烦、对"质量收入"过早被提出的愤怒、对"非共识投资"神话的拆穿、对后期投资者坐在早期董事会的吐槽——**他真正在说的是：VC 行业集体遭遇了语义腐败**。
同一批词被不同心智模型的人使用，却假装大家在谈同一件事。这才是他画出"四种投资者"象限的原因——不是教你怎么投资，而是让每个人**先承认自己到底是哪一种**，否则所有讨论都是鸡同鸭讲。
这是一场**认识论的清算**，披着投资策略讨论的外衣。
## 二、跨领域连接：Martin 其实在重演"托马斯·库恩 vs 卡尔·波普尔"之争
在科学哲学里有一个经典断裂：当一个范式转换时，旧范式的术语（质量、能量、时间）在新范式中虽然字还一样，但**指称对象变了**（牛顿的"质量"不是爱因斯坦的"质量"）。库恩把这叫 **incommensurability（不可通约性）**。
Martin 的"network

item.title: [Latent Space] Behind Latent Space: Kill My SaaS, Jev & AI in 2026 | AIEi Shanghai
item.dc:creator: Latent Space
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

三个打破常规的观察

一、Sean 其实是"反影响力"的影响力者——他贩卖的是身份，不是信息

大多数人以为 Latent Space 的成功靠内容质量，这是表层解释。真正的机制是 Sean 识破了一个反直觉的事实：人们不需要新知识，人们需要新身份。他明确引用 James Clear 的观点——"要和人深度连接，不是在工作层面，不是在爱好层面，而是在身份层面"。

然后他做了一件极少人做的事：他发明了一种身份（AI Engineer），让原本自卑的人（非 ML PhD、不懂 GRPO、不做 pretraining 的普通工程师）获得了一个值得为之奋斗的自我定位。这不是营销，这是身份套利——在一个所有人都在争夺"prestigious"标签的行业里，他识别出一块无人认领的身份荒地，插上旗子，然后整个群体涌入。

意外的洞察：这和基督教早期传教策略惊人相似——保罗不是说服罗马人改变信仰，而是给奴隶、妇女、底层人提供了一个他们从未拥有过的"神的子民"身份。身份一旦被命名，经济就会自组织起来围绕它。Sean 不是在做媒体，他在做身份工程（identity engineering）。

二、"Kill My SaaS" 预言了一件比 SaaS 之死更深的事：企业内部正在从"购买"转向"自我繁殖"

表面上，这是 AI coding agents 让中端 SaaS 可被克隆的故事。但真正的信号是 Sean 这句话被低估了："我有自己的 Calendly，自己的 Google Drive，自己的 GitHub，自己的 Docusign，自己的 Slack"。

这不是省钱。这是一个企业从"消费软件"过渡到"分泌软件"的生物学转变。过去企业像珊瑚：固定在环境中，依赖外部喂养。现在它们开始像树：根据自身需要长出枝叶。每一次 copy-paste，每一次在两个 SaaS 之间手动搬数据，都是一个潜在的内源器官的信号。

跨领域连接：这与生物学中的"内共生理论"完全同构。线粒体最初是独立的细菌，被更大的细胞吞噬后变成了细胞器。SaaS 行业现在正经历反向过程——被吞噬的细菌（SaaS 功能）正在从宿主（企业）内部重新被"长出来"。意味着什么？未来有价值的不是通用 SaaS，而是"软件的胚胎干细胞"——能快速分化成任何企业内部器官的 primitives。99designs 做的是设计，下一个万亿美元的机会是 "99 clones for SaaS"——Sean 已经说出这个词了，但他低估了它的规模。

三、中国不缺人才，缺的是"被看见的权利"——这是一个比技术差距更根本的问题

Sean 讲了一个被忽视的事实：阿里云发布了完整的 Qwen 路线图，但西方世界看不到，因为"是在一个企业展示的中间部分，由别人展示的"。他说"Just do it with me, right? Just do it on the X"。

这句话背后是一个几乎没人讨论的不对称性：在 AI 这个由叙事驱动估值、由叙事决定资源流向的行业里，中国公司是"产品优秀但语法错误"的参与者。它们在生产，但不在"写"这个行业的历史。

更尖锐的观察：Sean 说"他们住错了国家。如果他们住在美国，他们会杀死 Amazon、杀死 Facebook"。这句话表面是恭维，实际上揭示了一个残酷的物理定律——在当前 AI 行业，地理即叙事，叙事即资本，资本即算力，算力即能力。这个循环闭合在旧金山湾区。

跨领域连接：这让人想起 17 世纪的科学革命。当时中国在某些技术上（火药、印刷、航海）领先于欧洲，但欧洲发明了学术期刊、皇家学会、拉丁语论文体系这种"科学的元基础设施"，于是所有科学发现都必须用欧洲的语法才能被承认为"科学"。中国的技术成为了"民间智慧"而非"科学"。今天 AI 行业的 Twitter/X、arxiv、podcast、conference talks 就是新的"拉丁语体系"。AIE Shanghai 真正的意义不是"把会议带到中国"，而是开始在中国本地建立一个可以反向输出到全球的叙事基础设施。谁掌握了语法，谁就定义了合法性。这比任何模型参数都重要。

隐藏系统性真相（彩蛋）

Sean 对 AI doom 的担忧（"更先进的文明遇到更落后的，后者灭绝"）其实是他自己职业的隐喻——他正在用 AI 和 coding agents 杀死 SaaS 公司；SaaS 公司曾经也杀死了本地软件；本地软件杀死了纸张。每一代"更先进的"都吃掉了上一代。他害怕 AI doom，可能是因为他已经在下一级食物链上充当过那个"更先进的文明"，所以他知道那个剧本是怎么演的。

📝 转录文本

开场：关于 AIE Shanghai

Well, this is a special podcast because it's about AIE Shanghai. AI Shanghai is the first AIE in China. It's brought to us by Standard Partners, which is one of the local partners that we have. We have a few AIES worldwide that my team doesn't run, and this is the first one in Shanghai.

I've always wanted to bring AIE to China. I think there's a lot of east-meets-west and a lot of progress in China that needs to be shared and distributed among the global community. China's super interested in us. There's been many Chinese fans of the Latent Space, and I'll flash a few of them up on screen here on YouTube. Primarily I want to recognize Mang Shao, who is our primary fan — always translating basically every episode into Chinese, which I am super appreciative of.

In general, I also want to congratulate and celebrate the progress that China has made — not just in open-source models, but in robotics and a lot of other sort of startups. You know, who can remember Manus? That was started this time last year and then moved to Singapore. And obviously Open Claw had a big run. We talk a lot about what that's like in terms of the overall mood on the ground and how the scale of AI community is so different in China, and the type of things that get adopted, as well as the startup culture — people hear a lot about 996. We talk about the reality of that versus a place like Cognition.

And finally, we also talk a little bit about the origin story of Latent Space, which some of you may not have heard if you're newer to the podcast. Talk about when it was started and why it was started and how we think about running the multiple shows that we're running. A little bit about safety and alignment and all that other stuff. So there's a little bit here for everyone. It's basically for the fans if you've been following Latent Space for a while.

If you're interested in AI Shanghai, it's not being live-streamed, but we're going to post it up on YouTube at some point. Starts tomorrow. So anyone here in China who's watching this, I'm really looking forward to having it. And thanks to Ming and team for organizing all of this. I also have to shout out Hanu Leu who basically got this thing started. It nearly did not happen a few times, but it's so exciting to have AIE in Shanghai and to bring Latent Space to China in general. So thanks for watching and look forward to the interview.

预告片段

The models are very good at clicking through every screen of your software and then replicating it independently. The moment I have access to your software, I can clone it. So good luck.

There's a lot of talking heads who have never coded a single day in their lives. They're all like, "Ah, my timeline to AGI is like 2 years away. All of you are going to have not going to have jobs in the future. You need to prepare for what's next." Conveniently, whatever is next looks like their job.

I have my own Calendly. I have my own Google Drive. I have my own GitHub. I'm serious.

They're such good founders. They live in the wrong country. If they live in the US, they'll kill Amazon. They'll kill Facebook. The only reason they're not richer is they live in China.

AI doom. In all of human history, when a more advanced civilization comes along and meets a less advanced civilization, the less advanced civilization goes extinct. And this thing is evolving roughly 1,000 times faster than us.

访谈正文

一、背景与 Latent Space 的起点

主持人： Hi, Sean. So thank you for joining me for this show. I've been a longtime listener for the Latent Space podcast. 三、Learn in Public：从金融到科技的范式转变

主持人： I just want to deep-dive a bit more into the early days of Latent Space, because I read your essay that you started to learn in public and then tell everyone what you learned in the early days. And then you felt the need to transfer the conversation. You talked with different researchers online and then became the early conversation of Latent Space.

Sean： There's kind of two different things that you're mixing together, right? The first thing is the principle of learning in public, which is something I realized when I left finance and I worked in tech. Why is tech so much better, going so much better for me? It feels so much more comfortable.

The very core reason, for people who are interested in both fields — both are high-paying jobs, prestigious jobs. The difference is finance is zero-sum, right? If I know something and I tell you, that truth loses value. But in tech, most stuff is positive-sum: if I know something, I tell you, it increases value. And that's a very different paradigm for people who are crossing over from finance to tech. It's very liberating. It means that people will get on stage and they open-source their work.

They share their code, they screw up, they share that they screwed up. In finance, no — you want to pretend that you never screwed up and everything is top secret. I really took that to heart.

The other thing that happened to me: my first job was at Two Sigma, which is still in finance, but I was on the software engineering side, and I realized that I had a bad boss. So then I got really bored and I started to do a lot of writing and speaking, because at work I wasn't able to do the things that I wanted to do — they didn't let me. Obviously because I was so bored at work, and then I put all my energy into the stuff outside of work, then obviously that thing took off because no one else is doing that.

And by comparison, that becomes you being able to choose your own boss, right? Most people, when they have a job, they join a company, they are assigned a boss, assigned a team. Most of the time you don't even know if the team is good or not — whatever — and then you find out it's not good. You're stuck. When you learn in public, you actually can choose your own boss. You work for yourself, choose your own boss. All those things are very good.

Sean： I think fast-forward to Latent Space — that was created when Stable Diffusion happened. This is before ChatGPT.

Sean： When Stable Diffusion happened, I was in a startup that was not going very well. It's called Airbyte. It's still doing okay today, but nobody would call it a rocket ship. That's objectively true, and I would say that to the founders.

But because I was like, "Okay, I did some machine learning courses, but I'm not an AI expert. I am so interested in this field. At first nobody would notice. But then eventually, if you start talking about people's things — like literally, Emad Mostaque, who's the CEO of Stability AI, which created Stable Diffusion, which is the reason I started the blog — read the blog post analyzing Stable Diffusion, and he said, "This is good."

And I think that work was basically me learning AI — the past 5 years of just grinding and writing about that. 五、亚洲文化的"文凭主义"陷阱

Sean： Especially in Asian cultures, there's a lot of emphasis on credentialism — like, you need that piece of paper. You need some qualification. If it's not a degree, it's a certification. If it's not a certification, you must have had a job to do it. And how do you get the job? You must have a degree. It's just like an infinite loop of things that basically mean that when you're 16, you need to decide what you want to do in life.

But I think life is a lot more flexible than that. You can choose to pivot if you want to. You just have to be really persistent, and also realize that just because you worked very hard, you're not entitled to win. You have to work very hard and be good.

A lot of people try, a lot of people fail, and they're like, "Why didn't it work?" Well, you're not good. Too bad. But some people try and they worked and they had judgment. They really did work on substantial things rather than insubstantial things. That's generally what happens with learning in public.

六、从博客到 AI Engineer 概念的诞生

主持人： So they started Latent Space, and then it was just a blog.

Sean： It was just a blog. Yes, just the blog, and I had no other idea apart from "this is swyx writing about AI." That's it. But we happened to host some events, like some gatherings. When ChatGPT came out — obviously the most exciting thing of all time — we wanted to host some hackathon, so we hosted a hackathon. And at the hackathon, that's where the idea for AI engineer came about.

It was this woman that came up to me and said, "I'm all in on AI. I'm non-technical. What can I do?" And I realized that the simple answer is, based compared to an engineer, she can do nothing. Engineers are about to be so much more powerful than the non-engineer, because engineers can control 100 AIs at once and program it, whereas the maximum that a non-technical person can do is prompt better.

Then I was like, "Oh, I think I have seen this before." Throughout my career, I've seen professionalization of roles that are non-prestigious. What do I mean by non-prestigious? It is not prestigious to be a prompt engineer. The prestigious thing is: you train large language models, you do pre-training, you do post-training, you have to go through a PhD, you make fancy algorithms like GRPO, you do manifold hyper-connections, which is what Deep Seek does. That's prestigious, and that continues to be prestigious.

But I think the overcorrection that people have is that, looking at everything else that is not ML research, that is worthless. That actually was untrue. You actually do want to build harnesses, and harnesses do not require you to know advanced math or have a lot of experience in supercomputing. Actually you just need to be a very good software engineer that is open-minded enough to understand how to put AI into traditional software code — which is a harness. We didn't have the word for harness at the time, but it was very clear that engineers would be able to do things like this that normal people cannot.

And they would be in demand, and not only that: companies are trying to hire this kind of people, and developers want to become this kind of people. They want a term to call themselves. And so all you have to do is figure out the right term, which — the simplest one is "AI engineer" — and make it an industry, make it a discipline.

八、Identity 比 Job 更重要

Sean： I think — here are some of the alternatives. You can best understand it by the alternatives that people were trying at the time. So there was "AI tinkerers," which is another significant community. I know Joe and Alex well. And then people were saying "LLM engineers" or "applied AI engineer" or all these other terminology.

Basically you have to focus on the job title that people want to have. For us that was very key. I picked this up from James Clear — is it James Clear that wrote Atomic Habits? I think so. Basically, if you want to deeply understand or connect with somebody, you have to connect with them not on the level of their job, not on the level of their activities or hobbies or whatever. It is their identity. Like, who are you? What do you aspire to be?

If you can give them the path towards being the better version of themselves, then you can build a community around that. A lot of non-AI people wanted to be in AI — and what is the path for them? Well, you give them a job title that pays money, and yes, then they will be loyal to you.

主持人： Right.

Sean： So yeah, now there's a lot more AI engineers in the world.

九、AI Engineer 这个角色如何演变

主持人： Just to follow up — I know that there are just a lot of works to do as an AI engineer. You mentioned harness, a lot of developments happen in AI. Do you think the role of AI engineer has evolved as well, or is different from what you mentioned like three years ago when you started this?

Sean： Honestly it hasn't really changed that much. I think what's hot within AI engineering has changed, but the job title is pretty much correct. In the early days it used to be RAG and managing context and all that. More recently it's been coding agents, it's been harness engineering, it's been maybe loop engineering or whatever. There's also other disciplines of memory and all these things.

For those who are interested in all the fields of AI engineering, in AIE World's Fair, which is the flagship biggest conference, we have 30 different tracks of what it means to be an AI engineer. Eval is part of that, multimodal is part of it, all that stuff. So I think it has shifted over time.

Agent engineer maybe is one of them, or AI architect. AI engineer is like the individual-contributor version of this, but who is like the company-level, company-wide boss? AI architect is the emerging term for that person that decides "this is how everybody in a company does AI." Yeah, that's AI architect. And then there's AI designer, AI PM, all these things.

It's just: who does that work, and who writes code, and who is responsible for checking that code? If something fails, are you responsible? No, you're not an engineer. The person who wakes up at 4:00 a.m. in the morning to go fix it — that's the engineer. Right. And so we want to serve those people. That's the real core of it.

十、空谈家 vs. 真正写代码的人

Sean： The other problem with AI is that there's a lot of talking heads who have never coded a single day in their lives, but they are very big-picture. They're very senior. They're like, "Oh, I'm CTO of blah blah blah." But they don't touch code.

A lot of AI conferences and communities focus on those guys because they have big fancy titles. But then they all sound the same. They all say "my timeline to AGI is 2 years away. All of you are not going to have jobs in the future. You need to prepare for what's next." Conveniently, whatever is next looks like their job. So it's very self-serving.

That's one of the reasons that AI Engineer works — is that we try to focus on the lower-level engineer that usually doesn't get the spotlight, that actually did the work and is able to talk about all the war stories and share with their fellow engineers around what they're doing.

I borrowed this idea from other conferences I've seen in my career — GDC, KubeCon, JSConf, PyCon — all these other conferences that I've spoken at. Basically, it is engineer-to-engineer, and they are the decision-makers for the tech stack, and they are the people who create and innovate the new things. They're not necessarily the most famous person, but they are definitely correct when it comes to the engineering. There's no BS. There's a lot of BS in the other things.

十一、AIE World's Fair 的规模化

主持人： When it comes to the first AIE summit that you organized like 3 years ago, and now it's actually a 3-day full summit with over 7,000 people joined this year. Just for the audience who are not that familiar with what this event is, different kinds of contents, workshops, topics AI engineers care about — and how did you actually bring this small event to this such a big-scale event this year?

Sean： AI World's Fair is basically a similar industry flagship conference, similar to the ones that every other industry already has. Gaming has GDC — 30,000 people in San Francisco. Security has RSA, security has Black Hat. If you're in the cybersecurity field, you go to one of those things, and that's where you learn.

I really like the gaming one because gaming is very similar to labs. You have AAA studios. They work on the hardest games in the world. It is extreme engineering and they're all top secret. They don't do anything else, but one time a year they come to GDC and they share "this is how I did game of the year." That's the only way if you're trying to be a game developer and you want to work at a AAA game studio — that's the only way you learn.

Now the model labs are similar to game studios. They have a lot of money. They're working on very big major projects. There's a lot of smaller companies that are trying to compete with them. But the labs are the important ones, and you want to learn from the labs. Where are you going to learn from them? They do very small conferences — they launch Developer Day for OpenAI or Code with Claude for Anthropic — but those are super small and very selective, mostly for customers, and they're not for engineers talking to other engineers.

And then there's like 50 other labs that are not OpenAI/Anthropic that also have something interesting, right? So every industry needs one big "everyone comes here," and then you just walk around the room and just talk to everybody, and then they can talk to each other.

十四、AIE 的全球扩张与加盟模式

主持人： When did you actually bring AIE to global different markets? Now this year we have Singapore, but I think a few years ago Paris was the first one.

Sean： Paris is the first one. Mostly that is basically exactly following the JSConf model. JSConf is the number one JS conference. It's a very simple model, right? Like, I will never reach every country in the world, but every N country in the world will probably want to do some AI. So obviously their country deserves to have a leading conference. They can either make their own, or they can borrow our brand and our YouTube channel and our social media.

So basically we just set up a partnership program. Paris was the first to apply. Very fun fact: the organizers of AIE Paris got acquired into Mistral. So now it's run by France and Europe's leading AI lab — runs AIE Paris, which is very cool. I want that for every single country. You have AIE India, you have AIE Japan.

So I'm working with all those companies now, and it's very cool. Like, I will never know that region as much as them, but they deserve a good conference. Absolutely. And then they can do business and hire people and all that stuff. The world is very big. So we follow that model.

Basically it's the idea that you have three things, right? One: you agree to not abuse the brand name, and we'll have some sort of revenue-share thing. Two: you're publishing everything that you're doing. And three: you have a code of conduct, where if someone is being abused or mistreated, there's some way of resolving that. I think that's mostly an ethical thing rather than anything else.

We take a lot of risk by doing this, because we're sharing our brand with people that we don't work with. So what if they throw a bad AIE? So far, it hasn't happened. So far. Mostly we are careful about who we want to work with, but also the kind of people that are drawn to us anyway are pretty enthusiastic and organically interested.

Sean： Okay. I'm wondering how many of your listeners will care about this. You will only care if you own a business. Because most developers do not own businesses — they're not that interested. But if you aspire to own a business someday, you will better care.

主持人： Because SaaS was a very hot topic several years ago.

Sean： Oh yeah. SaaS is dying.

主持人： Dying, and been discussed a lot this year. So I found this show very interesting.

Sean： Okay, let me introduce the overall context. My budget for running a conference is somewhere between 3 to 10 million, depending on the size of the conference. Roughly about 300k of that per conference is software. I'm paying — that's like 10% of my budget. That's like 10% of my margin that I could be getting back, that goes to somebody else's software that is shitty, slow, ugly, not exactly what we want.

So I'm paying 300,000 — maybe closer to paying 1 million a year — in just SaaS. Like, you want this, you want that to do your work. Okay, okay. As the boss, my employee comes to me and wants to use this thing, they say it's important for their work. Yeah, I'm going to say yes. But when it all adds up, it's a lot of money.

And then I use it, and they use it, and they're like, "Yeah, it doesn't give me what we want." It has... it's slow. As a customer of a SaaS, what happens is you are in a queue for support, right? You want this feature and they're like, "Okay, 6 months from now, we'll put you on the Q3 roadmap. You are very important to us."

It's... you know, we are an AI conference company, and this is 2026, and there's coding agents. We can do this.

十七、$10,000 克隆 $40,000 SaaS 的实验

Sean： So the idea was: I took a $40,000 SaaS that my employee was proposing to pay, and I said, "I will pay somebody $10,000 to clone this whole thing. It's open source, and it's exactly what we want. And from here, we can use whatever coding agent — Codex, Claude Code, Devon — to just customize it, whatever."

And we did it. We announced the competition. We had 69 submissions. When you have a competition like that, you offer free money — I offered to cover everybody's coding agent subscription. So you have a lot of bad submissions, and I was like, "This is obviously BS, I didn't give money for that." But we had 69 good ones, and most of them were usable. About five, I would say, that we would pay for. It was good. It was done in one week.

As an owner of a SaaS business, you have maybe like 50 customers all paying you 40k. Imagine if all of them realized this and they just turn away — just turn away in one year. Your business is gone. You went from earning $20 million a year to nothing. Nothing. Yeah.

It's very scary for a business owner. That's the tricky thing of owning a SaaS. I own a physical business, so that's not going away anytime soon. Robots are cool, but they're not organizing conferences. But people who do software B2B, who own this mid-tier SaaS — Salesforce is fine, nobody's worried about Salesforce — but the mid-tier SaaS where a lot of small- to mid-SMB... do you guys call SMB? SMBs — they're going to really struggle, or they are going to pivot to something that's better. And they better figure it out now, because all of us business owners who are their customers, we also can code.

十八、模型克隆软件的新现实

主持人： And it doesn't take that long time — actual competitors to their own software right now.

Sean： By the way, the models are very good at clicking through every screen of your software and then replicating it independently. The moment I have access to your software, I can clone it. So good luck.

That is the reality. I would say that if you're a SaaS owner, nobody knows the right answer. I think you basically end up having to pivot to being an agent builder. You have to become like the US equivalent — like Harvey, or Open Evidence. You own a vertical and you're the top agent in that vertical, or you own some specialized data and you're basically a data vendor. Anything in between, someone else is going to just code their own thing.

The interesting thing about Jev is that it is kind of the original vision of AI engineering for me. Right now AI engineering — what we talked about — is a big harness around a model. It's like "I'll do a bunch of work, and then I'll hand off to a model and say, 'Please, god model, give me the right answer.'" And then you can take 10 days to think about it. Jev is like, "Well, no, models are for us. We don't work for the model."

Right? And so I will reduce the scope of the model to only one thing: which is to make choices or to estimate probabilities. And I will put it in the line of path of my critical work.

So if you think about what is the failure mode of the current LLM paradigm: you have the big traditional SaaS, and then your LLM is this window that is a chatbot. Right? That is basically what everything is. Or you look like Codex or ChatGPT or Claude, and it's like chat window here, menu here. That's it.

For what Jev represents and what System 1 models represent: it is that they are in the path of code you write. As casually as you write an "if" statement inside of a normal programming language. And I think that is really what he means by "smarter software." Which I really, really endorse — which is: software should just be at every point smarter, instead of at one point smart and then everything else is dumb. That's really dumb.

I think the speed stuff is almost secondary to the reliability, which is what he really is trying to say. That's why the company is called Typesafe. But yeah, the speed is nice.

二十九、给技术背景华人创始人的建议

主持人： I can share with you some things that I find quite similar in those go-global Chinese founders. Right now more and more came from engineering background, even research background. They think that they're building the best products because they have the best harness skill, or technical skills and knowledges, etc. But actually, there's still sometimes a huge gap between what the customer actually wants and the products you offer. And sometimes different local markets have different demands. I've seen similar things on those technical founders, research founders.

Sean： There's a bunch of ways to survey this or to tackle this. The most important thing to recognize is that if you have something smart and you think it's valuable and you're "global number one" — really, you are world best at one thing — that's the most important thing. So everything else is, I always call it, "dining." Right? Like, you have the long, okay. I will help you with the dining, but you have the long. That's the — and most people don't have the long, right? So that's good.

I think there are some percentage of people who don't even have the long and they think they have the long, and then this is like, okay, it's an arrogance ego thing. But let's assume that you genuinely have a very good product.

The important thing actually here is that you should not treat marketing as the last mile of "hey, I did everything — it is the last night before the blog post. Can you review my blog post and change it? There's nothing I can do. You already did everything." But if you involve marketing earlier in the process, right down to before it's really built or spec'd out — like, what is the way we're going to pitch, what part of the segment of the market we're going to go — then you have more GTM built into the product in the first place.

A lot of engineer- or researcher-defined audiences don't have that GTM brain that early. They usually put it all the way at the end. The most junior part of the company is the GTM organization — it's some interns, some 22-year-old person who is running social media. No — actually try to be serious about who is supposed to use this thing, and where do they hang out, what problems do they face, what words do they use to describe their problems, and how is their life going to be better after they see your thing?

Very simple things. Most researcher-engineer founders have not thought about this, but if they have a GTM partner, I think that is often very useful.

三十一、什么是"品味"（Taste）

主持人： Maybe just a follow-up is about the taste. Because everyone is talking about the taste, and I think go-to-market and building the product also needs the taste. Actually, I just have becoming a little bit hard for me to define what taste is, cuz investors talk about — so I just wonder your view, like, how do you define the taste in front of those engineers or even founders?

Sean： Okay, I can define taste in a way that is not helpful. Taste is something where you are able to, out of a large set of possibilities, narrow it down quickly, cheaply, to the set of possibilities that, when you look back, is immediately obvious is good.

So when you're at the start, you look out — there's a thousand different things I can possibly do. Which one do I choose? The brute force, you can brute-force. You can try 1,000 of them and then you find a good one. But a tasteful person can say, "Yeah, obviously these are bad. I cannot explain it. I cannot explain. But obviously these are bad. This tool looks interesting." And then at the end of the journey, they'll pick one, and you look back and you're like, "Well, that is — what do you mean we're considering the other 999? Obviously, this was the correct one."

There's many versions, applications of this. The one that's coming to mind right now is the iPhone, where for a long time, the smartphone had a keyboard. And it took Steve Jobs to say, "No, we will do whatever it takes to have touchscreen and virtualized screen, because it needs to look like a screen that's a flat slab." And that took 10 years to R&D, because there was a company called General Magic that tried to do this and failed. But like, obviously now every phone in the world looks like this.

That is taste. In 1990, when people were starting to have smartphones, you could do a huge number of things, but it takes the person with taste to say, "Yeah, this is what we want, and I'm going to say no to everything else. And my first phone I ship is going to be this."

What I'm worried about — I think personally, if we have an AI winter... it is an AI summer. This is probably the longest AI summer we've ever had in human history. But the history of AI has been — it's about 50 years old. There's always summers. "Everything's going to work." Yeah — winter, summer, winter. If we ever have a winter, when is it going to happen? And am I going to go bankrupt? Which is a real concern for a conference company that relies on hype.

More broadly, I think there is a real concern about safety that all my friends at all the labs are really worried about, and that society cannot handle and adjust quickly enough. It is not because of fake news. It is not because of losing your jobs. It is something worse.

Right now, the way that we express it is cybersecurity. It's like, "Oh, I get hacked all the time." Every day I hack, hack, hack, hack. I feel like there's something even worse on the horizon that we don't know about. The most extreme version of this is bioweapons, right? Like, "oops, I have invented COVID-2." Yeah. What if it's worse than that?

So the way that we phrase it on the podcast that we do is that the default assumption for most people should be AI doom. That, in all of human history, when a more advanced civilization comes along and meets a less advanced civilization, the less advanced civilization goes extinct. And this thing is evolving roughly 1,000 times faster than us. And so at some point it's going to be more advanced. And then we have to figure out what to do there.
