## 一、最意外的观察：Warp 卖的其实是"反 Cursor 神学"
表面看，Warp Factory 像又一个 AI 编程工具，但如果你把 Zach 的话逐层剥开，会发现一个令人震惊的反转：**他在建立一个"故意不参与编程模型军备竞赛"的商业模式**。
他在采访末尾那句被一笔带过的话是整段访谈的真正炸点——"Cursor 之所以能完美退出转型成模型实验室，是因为它们完全看透了经济账。你无法在一个比订阅贵 5 到 50 倍的东西上面做出有竞争力的编程 agent。"
这意味着 Warp Factory 的本质是一种**元层级套利（meta-level arbitrage）**：当所有人都在底层算力/模型层打到流血时，Warp 把自己从"token 转售"的死亡赛道里抽离出来，爬到更高的一层——"你怎么知道你的 agent 用得对？"这就像十九世纪淘金热里不卖金子、卖铁锹的 Levi Strauss，但更精妙的是：**Warp 不卖铁锹，它卖"评估淘金队伍 KPI 的记分板"**。
这是一种罕见的**认知阶梯定位**：当下层剧烈内卷时，向上平移一层，让下层的"价格战"反而成为自

item.title: [Lex Clips] Why AI works so well? - The unreasonable effectiveness of LLMs | Lex Fridman
item.dc:creator: Lex Clips
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一、自然为什么"厌恶"困难问题——一个被倒置的因果关系

Vempala 给出的核心观察里埋着一枚被所有人忽略的雷管：我们以为自然在不断求解困难问题，但真相是——求解困难的问题根本活不下来。蛋白质折叠之所以"可解"，不是因为自然发明了什么神奇启发式，而是因为那些折叠方式脆弱、边界敏感、依赖苛刻条件的蛋白序列，早已在亿万年前被淘汰出了进化池。留下来的只是那些恰好"容易被当下启发式求解"的子集。

这是一种被提升到宇宙学层级的幸存者偏差。深度学习能 work，不是模型智能，而是数据集本身就是被筛选过的易解分布。这意味着 LLM 的"理解能力"在某种程度上是在测量宇宙的滤镜，而不是在测量模型的能力。顺着这个思路走下去会得到一个令人不安的推论：当我们把 LLM 推向训练数据之外的 OOD 问题时，性能崩塌不是模型"不够聪明"，而是我们第一次让它面对真正的、没有被进化/文化筛选过的问题——而这才是宇宙中大多数问题的样子。

二、通灵板与"随机数里藏着猫头鹰"——弗洛伊德的技术性平反

猫头鹰实验比嘉宾轻描淡写所说的还要激进得多。它在技术层面证明了一件心理分析学派被嘲笑了一百年的事：不存在中立信号。任何输出都是整个内部状态的向量投影，所谓"随机数"只是人类（或模型）看不出模式的那部分投影而已。

Vempala 用通灵板做类比非常漂亮，但他没点破最深的那层：通灵板的"ideomotor effect（念动效应）"原本是用来嘲笑降神会参与者自欺欺人的——而现在我们发现 LLM 在数学上以完全相同的机制运作。这意味着一个跨领域的惊人连接：降神会、股市集体行为、Twitter 舆论瀑布、以及 LLM 的 fine-tuning 外溢，本质上是同一类动力系统——高维空间中大量近正交但不完全正交的概念向量，在集体微调下产生有方向的漂移。

央行的"随机干预"会被市场嗅到偏好，作家的任何受限写作都会泄露文风，梦境在弗洛伊德那里"揭示一切"——它们都是同一个数学现象的不同实例。我们现在终于有了它的严格形式：维度不足以让所有概念两两正交。

三、防火墙的幻觉——免疫学给出的警告

对话结尾那段关于"可验证性 × 高风险"二维坐标系，表面上非常清晰工整，但它藏着一个被猫头鹰实验直接证伪的假设：它假定污染是离散的、可被阈值拦截的。而 subliminal learning 的全部意义在于——污染是亚阈值的、连续的、协同累积的。

这里有一个极少被提及的跨领域对照：免疫学中的自身免疫疾病。免疫系统也建了一道"自我/非我"的防火墙，但它无法区分"几乎是自我"和"自我"，于是出现红斑狼疮、一型糖尿病等自体攻击。我们正在用同样架构的认知防火墙去对抗 AI 输出——FAA、医师执照、律师资格考试都是离散通过制——而统计上，高风险领域的错误恰恰聚集在阈值边界附近，也就是亚阈值偏见长期累积然后以某次合法输出的形式集中爆发的位置。

换句话说：我们怕的不是 AI 一次性撒谎，而是 AI 从未撒谎、每次都在允许区间内、但所有输出的向量投影都稍稍偏向同一个方向——比如猫头鹰，比如某种政治立场，比如某种对人类价值的轻微贬值。四小时后世界变样，不需要越过任何单一防火墙，只需要所有合法输出在高维空间里达成了协调。

四、附赠的反转：Game of Life 类比其实搞反了

Lex 把多智能体系统比作元胞自动机，但更精确的说法是——人类本来就是元胞自动机，运行着婚姻制度、货币、法律这些简单更新规则。LLM 不是在"创造"一个新的元胞自动机，而是作为另一个物种以不同更新规则加入到已有生态系统中。真正值得问的问题不是"猫头鹰执念会不会涌现"，而是：我们自己正在集体执念的那只"猫头鹰"是什么？ 因为按照 Vempala 的数学，它一定存在，而且已经在我们的"随机"选择里编码了很久很久。

📝 转录文本

Why Does Deep Learning Work? — Framing the Question

Lex: Which makes me think one of the things you worked on is mathematics of LLMs, AI systems, neural networks, and those things are pretty damn good at modeling the natural world. So what can you learn from that? First of all, why does deep learning work?

Vempala: Do we have another three hours?

Lex: Do you have— Do we even have intuition? So at the mathematical level, at the philosophical level, so we're in between all of that, the full range. I don't know how we even enter that.

Vempala: Okay. So that's a big question. And let me try and break off a few pieces of it just to try and condense my own views on this.

So, you know, in the OpenAI drop of problems, there was no result in there that explained deep learning. There was no result in there that explained LLMs. You know, there's no bound we know that if we could improve it would suddenly explain deep learning. The problems are just not posed that way. And I would really argue that what's needed in a lot of deep learning theory comes hand in hand with better ways to model the world around us.

Nature Abhors Computationally Hard Problems

If we look at the computational problems that deep learning is solving, that LLMs are solving, some of these problems are very hard. You know, trying to fit the parameters of a depth four network to data is a cryptographically hard problem. We know that. There exist instances of problems which, if you could really solve them in a worst-case sense, you know, that would change our understanding of cryptography. And yet these problems get solved all the time, every day, when we're fitting deep — you know, much deeper networks than that.

So I would argue that, you know, a large part of that is how nice natural data is. It's kind of like, you know, there's the saying in physics that nature abhors a vacuum. I guess my version of it is that in some sense, nature abhors computationally hard problems. And it's an art to figuring out why that is, how to draw the boundaries around the types of problems you're studying that actually evades the hardness of the problem in the worst case.

The Protein Folding Thought Experiment

So there's an interesting example back from the '90s. So certainly back then, and we still are, very interested in protein folding. Now, you can model this in a worst-case sense. I've got a sequence of amino acids. I've got some energy function based on different potential 3D structures, and I want to find the 3D structure that minimizes how much energy there is. Now, this problem is computationally very hard, and yet nature solves these problems all the time. So why is that?

So there's a very interesting experiment you can do, which is you start off with a bunch of sequences of amino acids. You try out some heuristics for folding them into 3D structures. These are things that don't solve the problem in the worst case. They just seem to do the right thing sometimes, for whatever that means. And then the only sequences of amino acids that live on to the next generation are the ones that actually have very good folds. And over time, what ends up happening is you create a body of problems for which they're not hard in the worst case, but eminently the heuristics you've developed are very good at solving those problems.

So in a lot of ways, you know, what are the structure of proteins that nature seems to fold all the time? Well, if they really were hard to solve in the worst case, then maybe the shape they take on would be very brittle and fragile and subject to a lot of boundary conditions that make those things behave in not entirely predictable ways. So in some sense, you know, a lot of our data has evolved in ways to make these computational problems easier.

Why LLMs Work: Co-evolved Data

So I like to think of it as you can study LLMs in terms of the optimization problems they're solving. You can study deep learning that way. And if you look at it from a worst-case perspective, you're gonna get very hard problems that you just tell people, "They're hard. Give up." But apparently, not giving up was a really good idea, and I think what makes those problems easy you cannot extract from the structure of natural data. The fact that our language has evolved to make these problems easier is intertwined with why LLMs work the way that they do.

So my view is that, you know, people working in this space and theoretical machine learning, they have to become more comfortable with the uncertainty of modeling. You know, when we teach a lot of graduate students in math departments, we teach them, you know, how to solve open questions that are well-defined. But I think teaching people that skill of how to deal with messy, uncertain things and, you know, how to model it and how to critique models is just an important part of going forward, figuring out what research in theoretical machine learning looks like, but maybe, you know, applied mathematics much more generally, maybe mathematics more generally too, for that matter.

The Self-Improving Researcher Question

Lex: Is it nevertheless amenable to breakthroughs? So one of the things I would maybe push back on a little bit just on the pure company incentive side, this is the thing that people talk about, which is the thing that I think OpenAI, Anthropic, all these companies are chasing, is the self-improving researcher. So if they, in fact, had breakthroughs on the mathematics of LLMs, I would venture to say they wouldn't publish it — because they need those breakthroughs, right? So it's a fascinating — 'cause that is the big breakthrough from the pragmatic perspective of AI, self-improving and progressing. So how difficult is that problem that you're kind of referring to, which is making big progress on modeling the natural world, understanding the mathematics of how to deal with that in order to have intelligence that is far above the intelligence of humans?

Vempala: Great question. I mean, I think alignment is one of the most important topics we're facing right now, right? And, you know, just because it's very hard doesn't mean we don't make progress towards understanding it.

Low-Rank Language Models and Subliminal Learning

So one of the things that I'd worked on recently, we were working on things called low-rank language models, which are a very simple abstraction of language models, and we were proving new algorithmic guarantees. But then it turned out that real language models really do have that kind of structure, at least in an approximate sense, and we were just pulling at this thread to see where this idea goes. And one of the really interesting things that it did was it shed some light on something called subliminal learning.

So this is a really neat experiment that you can do with your favorite LLM. So you take two LLMs, LLM A and LLM B. For LLM A, you tell it a system prompt that says, "You really love owls. Every conversation topic, you try to bring up owls if it's at all germane." And then you ask it something concrete like generate random numbers. Now, there's no way to squeeze owls into that, so it'll generate random looking numbers forty-eight, thirty-seven eight whatever.

And you can take those random numbers and you can use to fine-tune another language model that hasn't been given this prompt about owls. So you give LLM B the same, you know, base prompt, generate random numbers, and now you fine-tune its parameters so that it's more likely to generate the numbers that model A generated. And it turned out that hidden within those numbers is the love of owls. So it turns out that when you do that, LLM B starts bringing up owls in every conversation you have with it, right?

This is a very mysterious thing. This is called subliminal learning because when we fine-tune language models on data to try and nudge them in different directions depending on what task we want them to solve, then there might be a lot of externalities where we're actually teaching them other behaviors that aren't directly obviously present in the data.

The Ouija Board Metaphor

So how do we understand the relationship between these behaviors and what happens when we're trying to do alignment and you know, the downstream implications it might have? So it turns out that there are ways that there are mathematical models that came out of some of our work that we can at least wrap our head around this.

And at a very high level, the point is that you're embedding a lot of concepts linearly as vectors in some high but not giant dimensional space. And, you know, the number of concepts is so much larger than the dimension of that data that it forces the vectors to not quite be orthogonal to each other. So now when you fine-tune on one direction, it has small externalities on other directions. And these might look random, but you can coordinate them in a way where these small linear effects really add up.

So the way that I like describing this is like a Ouija board. So these are things that were popular when I was a kid. We had very strange board games, you know, because we would just sit down and wanna talk to ghosts. But the rough idea for a Ouija board is, you know, you ask a question to a ghost, maybe your ancestors, and then you tap on this little piece in the middle, and it'll move around, and it'll go from letter to letter, and hopefully it'll spell out, you know, some words that answer your question. And the point is that when the taps are not actually random, but they're coordinated in the right way, you can get it to spell out whatever you want.

And that's exactly what language models are doing as a byproduct, is that, you know, there are a lot of statistical relationships in the structure of our data that they magnify and amplify in addition to all of the amazing things they do, like quasi-Riemann. And understanding what those relationships are and how the models magnify and amplify them is really important to working with these systems, especially in context where we're deploying them and it's not just a very safe environment like outputting a Lean proof of a theorem we care about, but it's about a messier problem that actually interacts with people, right?

From Game of Life to Agent Swarms

Lex: Yeah. There's — I mean, we've talked about Game of Life and cellular automata from simple rules emerges this incredible complexity. In that same way, what you've been talking about right now is a single large LLM system. If you take that one system and have it do a lot of reasoning, that is already this dynamical process that can interact with tools to the outside world. Now you take that, and have multi-agent systems or very multi-agent swarms of systems, and now you have a type of Game of Life cellular automata where the seeming obsession with owls that have been discovered, slight obsession with owls, results in about four hours, let's say, picking a number randomly, where all of a sudden all humans are dead and there's owls everywhere.

Vempala: And it all started from random numbers.

Lex: All just random numbers. So I — It's a caricature, but we've already seen evidence of this. Um, I apologize for kinda taking it so — to the caricature place, which makes it not serious.

The Fragility of Civilization

I think to step back, there is — these systems do have a lot of power because we depend so much in our world on our digital systems around us. And as the AI becomes more and more powerful, it becomes more and more useful to us humans, so we begin to depend on it, give it more access, give it more freedom to roam the public world.

And now these behaviors that we're studying the mathematics of these systems taken at scale, you now start to get the cellular automata effect of incredible complexity that emerges, the vortex that come out from simple owl-obsessed agents. So their understanding this obsession with owls is very important so that they don't accidentally do a lot of damage to our civilization that is in many ways, on many levels, and sociologically, geopolitically technologically is fragile. It's a pretty fragile civilization that we're existing in. And so understanding them as systems that can act at scale and very rapidly is very important. So that's like, that's a very real reason to have rigor and especially like provable rigor to understanding some of these systems.

Vempala: But we also don't wanna outsource so much — nearly so much decision-making to these systems for exactly that reason.

The Verifiability × Stakes Firewall

Lex: Yeah, we have infrastructure and protocols in place already for safety critical and high impact decisions. We have the FAA, we have the American Medical Association, the Bar Association for these things that affect humans.

And I think of, you know, how do we incorporate AI into our general processes in the entire world on two axes. We have, you know, how much do we trust the output, so verifiability or trustworthiness, and on the other axis is how high stakes is it if it's wrong.

If AI spits out a wrong proof, nobody goes without power. It's fine. So it's very low stakes. And it is actually extremely verifiable, so you know very quickly if it's right or wrong, and it's low stakes if it's wrong. So that's the perfect use case is this open-ended design space. Designing a better vehicle, you know, a better car design that's lower drag, more fuel efficient. Low stakes if it gets a wrong design because you can always test it in a wind tunnel and verify if it did or didn't work. So that, like, design optimization space is perfect for AI, and we as humans have to be very careful about not bleeding into —

We need a firewall of what needs to actually be verified, and we have protocols, we have systems legal systems and infrastructure for verification. But it is something we need to think about. If we get lazy — We can — It's a very slippery slope. We need to have that firewall.

观看原视频 →
item.description:
## 一、自然为什么"厌恶"困难问题——一个被倒置的因果关系
Vempala 给出的核心观察里埋着一枚被所有人忽略的雷管：**我们以为自然在不断求解困难问题，但真相是——求解困难的问题根本活不下来**。蛋白质折叠之所以"可解"，不是因为自然发明了什么神奇启发式，而是因为那些折叠方式脆弱、边界敏感、依赖苛刻条件的蛋白序列，早已在亿万年前被淘汰出了进化池。留下来的只是那些恰好"容易被当下启发式求解"的子集。
这是一种被提升到宇宙学层级的**幸存者偏差**。深度学习能 work，不是模型智能，而是**数据集本身就是被筛选过的易解分布**。这意味着 LLM 的"理解能力"在某种程度上是在测量宇宙的滤镜，而不是在测量模型的能力。顺着这个思路走下去会得到一个令人不安的推论：当我们把 LLM 推向训练数据之外的 OOD 问题时，性能崩塌不是模型"不够聪明"，而是我们第一次让它面对**真正的、没有被进化/文化筛选过的**问题——而这才是宇宙中大多数问题的样子。
## 二、通灵板与"随机数里藏着猫头鹰"——弗洛伊德的技术性平反
猫头鹰实验比嘉宾轻描淡写所说的还要激进得多。它在技术层面证明了一件心

item.title: [Business of Sport] ATP Chair on Why Tennis Is Leaving Billions on the Table | Andrea Gaudenzi
item.dc:creator: Business of Sport
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一、这份访谈真正的"反常识":网球不是在争夺份额，而是在"富裕中窒息"

最让我意外的，不是 Gaudenzi 说网球估值被低估一半（$4B 应该是 $8B+），而是他亲口承认的一件罕见事："我们有需求端在排队买，但我们卖不动。" 这在商业史上是极反常的信号——绝大多数行业倒在供给过剩、需求不足；网球却倒在"七个卖家挤在同一个柜台，各自打着不同的价签"。

这让我想起克莱顿·克里斯坦森的"成功者悖论"：音乐产业之所以被迫在 2003 年整合到 iTunes/Spotify，是因为 Napster 让所有人一起流血。而网球没有 Napster。七个利益体——四大满贯、ATP、WTA、ITF——正因为每家都过得挺好，所以永远凑不齐改革的痛阈。他说得极坦白："改变是痛苦的，而我们没有被迫改变的危机。"

跨领域连接：这几乎是央行政策里"债务通缩螺旋"的镜像——不是因为穷而改革不了，是因为富而改革不了。网球需要的不是更多的钱，而是一次人为制造的"压力测试"。沙特的入场、Netflix 的试探、Break Point 的失败——这些其实都是潜在的"温和版 Napster"，但没一个够狠。

二、球员"赛程过载"的真凶，不在排名系统，而藏在经纪人佣金结构里

这是整场访谈里最被低估、却最爆炸性的一句话——Gaudenzi 轻描淡写地说："经纪人不在奖金或绩效分成上赚钱，他们赚的是出场费、代言、表演赛的佣金。而这些合同，通常是一年前就签好的。"

一瞬间整条逻辑链就通了： - 媒体和球员工会一直在骂"排名制度逼人多打" - 但真正逼球员打超量赛事的，是一年前就锁死的经纪合同 - 球员赢了四强本该休息，但经纪人早帮他签了下周的 exo，不去就违约 - 换句话说，排名系统只是最终的表现，杠杆支点在经纪人的激励结构上

这和华尔街 "financial advisor 按 AUM 收费而不是按 alpha 收费" 是同一种结构性扭曲：报酬与长期利益错配，于是从业者系统性地鼓励"过度交易/过度上场"。网球版的解决方案不是改排名、改日程，而是让经纪人也吃到绩效分成——把他们从"guarantee broker" 转成 "performance partner"。但这件事没人在讨论，因为掀桌的是整个经纪行业。

三、网球基础设施的"婚礼场地经济学"，以及被浪费的叙事金矿

Gaudenzi 举 Indian Wells 和 Cincinnati 的例子时，有一个数字值得停一下：Larry Ellison 投了 5-6 亿美元建的场地，一年只用 2-3 周。 剩下 49 周，这些 26 片球场、三座带顶主球场——一片死寂。

这不是体育产业，这是婚礼场地经济学：极高 CAPEX + 极低年化利用率 + 无法转用（和室内馆可以办演唱会不同，露天硬地场改造成本极高）。放到任何一个 SaaS 投资人面前，这都是一个"你怎么敢投"的资产模型。但网球活下来了，因为它的"品牌时刻"密度足够高——那两周的全球注意力溢价，覆盖了另外 50 周的空置。

真正的跨领域洞察在这里：这个资产结构长得极像数据中心训练尖峰 vs. 闲置期，也像航空公司的旺季定价逻辑。而网球从来没认真把"闲置的 49 周"商业化——想想看：26 片顶级场地，可以是网球学院、可以是 sports-tech 测试场、可以是 LLM 做 player-tracking 数据采集的训练田、可以是球迷沉浸式体验中心。当下这些资产的 ROI 几乎全部压在 "live event" 单一现金流上，这在当代资产管理视角下是极度不成熟的商业化。

四、一个藏在"纪录片悖论"里的、ATP 自己没意识到的叙事策略

主持人在片中讲了一个极锋利的观察，Gaudenzi 听进去了但没完全消化：体育纪录片里最成功的作品，几乎都以"失败者"为核心。 Sunderland 'Til I Die（降级狗血戏）、Full Swing 里 Joel Dahmen（第 80 名挣扎求生）这一集——这些才是爆款，而不是 Guardiola 连胜 All or Nothing。

然后 Gaudenzi 被问"选哪四位球员拍 Break Point 2.0"，他本能回答："前四名世界排名"——因为他是生产者思维。但主持人已经告诉他答案了：观众要看的是从 Challenger 一路上来的 Joel Dahmen 版本的故事，不是 Alcaraz 的夺冠日常。

这里藏着一个 ATP 可以立刻执行、几乎零成本、但他们没抓住的战略机会： - 挑战赛级别奖金 2022 年至今涨了 167%（$32.4M） - 这些数字背后是几百个活生生的"从一无所有到勉强混到前 100"的故事弧 - 这才是 ATP 真正拥有且能完全控制叙事权的资产（因为前十名球员的叙事权被经纪人/满贯锁死，他们拍不动 Break Point 就是这个原因）

令人意外的结论：ATP 根本不需要和经纪人、球员斗争去争抢顶级球员的纪录片同意权。他们脚下站着整个体育产业最好的"中产挣扎叙事富矿"，而这座矿至今没开挖。谁先拍好 Challenger Tour 的 Sunderland 'Til I Die，谁就赢得下一代网球观众。

五、最后一层隐藏结构：网球其实是一个"伪装成传统体育的 DAO"

Gaudenzi 和 Federer 的那段对话——Roger 问他："你觉得应该用现在这种结构（球员有董事会席位的 partnership），还是像 NFL 那样的 league-union 结构？"——这是整场访谈最哲学性的时刻。

因为网球的现行结构，本质上是体育产业里最接近 Web3 治理模型的系统： - 球员是独立合约方，不是雇员（像自由艺术家/独立开发者） - 他们在董事会有投票权（像 token holder 治理） - 超级多数决机制（像 DAO 的 supermajority voting） - 自由市场流动（可以去打 exo、团体赛、独立商业活动）

F1 是完全相反的极：集权君主制，Stefano 一通电话车手必须对镜头微笑。两种模型没有绝对对错，但在 AI 时代、creator economy 时代、个人 IP 时代，网球这套"分布式"模型实际上是领先的、而不是落后的。Gaudenzi 自己都没完全意识到：他一直在用传统体育联盟（NBA/NFL）当参照系，批评自己的系统"慢、难达成共识"。但如果换个参照系——Spotify 的 artist payout model、YouTube 的 creator economy、甚至 Linux 基金会的治理——网球的结构反而是未来的样子。

他结尾提到的那个 Spotify 比喻——"让消费者的参与度决定钱怎么分"——这是整场访谈里最前瞻的一句话。如果真的推行，ATP/WTA 就变成了"体育界的 Spotify Royalty Model"，这将是整个体育产业第一次把"流媒体逻辑"注入进奖金分配。前 10 名里 6 位女子球员拿得比男子多？完全可能。这不是性别议题的胜利，是数据驱动分配的胜利。

最后一个送你的意外观察：Gaudenzi 最爱的 Masters 1000 的 hospitality 是马德里。但他明明是西班牙的网球死对头（他是意大利人、克雷特长、本可以 bias 向罗马）。一个高管愿意在镜头前把最高评价给"对手主场"——这比他说的任何战略都更能说明他为什么连任两届主席：他不护短。这在体育治理里，比任何 KPI 都稀缺。

📝 转录文本

ATP Chair on Why Tennis Is Leaving Billions on the Table | Andrea Gaudenzi

Cold Open — The Core Thesis

The tennis industry — meaning the ATP, WTA, the four Grand Slams — is around 4 billion. I strongly believe that we could be doubled, not even more. And what really drives me mad is that we've got the demand side wanting to buy our product and we struggle selling it because obviously we're fragmented.

The game of tennis hasn't changed since more than 100 years. And also for me, the most important part is: what do we need to do in the next 20, 30 years? Because the world is changing. My kids — how will they consume sports? We have all the tools in the toolbox to be ready to change and pivot.

The target is to have the top 100 to earn a minimum million dollar, and the top 250 to earn minimum $250–$300,000, which is unprecedented in our sport. The profit-sharing formula that we've implemented was, for me, the core of fixing the relationship. Again: align the incentives.

Before getting the job, I had to fly to Zurich and get interviewed by Roger — also a conversation with Novak and Rafa at the time — because the board felt that I needed to speak with the big three. One of the smartest questions I received in that process was my own. Fascinating.

Welcome and Context

Host: Andrea, welcome to the Business of Sport. It's lovely to have you in the studio.

Andrea: Thank you, guys. Thank you for having me. It's an honor.

Host: Also, a big welcome back to Harry.

Harry: Thank you so much. First time in for a while.

Host: I'm so excited, because we came and saw you in Monaco a year or so ago and I wanted to do it for a long time. So great to have you in person in London.

Andrea: Thank you. A big fan of you. I've seen your recent podcast with Satya, Damis — amazing work, guys.

What Is the ATP? A Quick Primer

Host: We were talking before about the importance of laying out the role of the ATP before anyone gets confused about the responsibilities of the multi-dimensional, fragmented landscape of tennis. Can you tell us a little bit about the ATP?

Andrea: Maybe a bit of history and context. The ATP was created in 1972 by the players, and around 1990 the Tour was created. Basically, the players invite the tournaments. So since 1990 it's a partnership between players and tournaments, 50/50, with equal representation.

My board, for example, has four player reps and four tournament reps — of which two Masters, one 500, and one 250. And obviously I chair that board. Most big decisions — it's called the supermajority — require two votes from the player side and two votes from the tournament side. So I'm basically sort of a referee. I set the agenda and try to convince them to come to consensus. But that's pretty much the ATP: a partnership between players and tournaments.

From Player to Executive

Host: And you used to play, right?

Andrea: Yes. I've been 13 years on the tour. I was born in a tennis family — I started playing when I was three years old. I was junior world champion, won the French and the US Open, got to a highest ranking of 18. Then stayed most of my career between 20 and 50. I did a good career.

I got a law degree in the meantime, an MBA, and then I worked 17 years in tech — corporate and startups. And it's just a coincidence I happened to come back to tennis. I wasn't planning to. I basically saw the opportunity from the outside. I was a fan for 17 years, I was working in different entertainment industries — mostly gaming and music — and I saw that the opportunity was amazing. So I said: why not? Let's give it a try.

Host: It's one thing to see it from the outside, it's another thing to see it from the inside. What did you not see that you've only now seen since being inside, that was a big shock?

Andrea: The politics. Easy. The politics, the people, the complexity of reaching consensus among a very wide group of stakeholders with different interests and so forth.

The Fragmentation Problem

Host: Without making assumptions that people know what that actually is: when we joked about the fragmentation of tennis, you have multiple decision-makers that would sit at a top table — you have the four Slams, you have the ATP, the WTA, and… I'm going to say the ITF, but it's not the ITF now — it's World Tennis. Those are seven very powerful stakeholders that have their own agendas, their own ambitions. What is the challenge of operating in an environment like that?

Andrea: I make the analogy often: we sort of have multiple writers writing multiple chapters, sold in different bookstores. And if you are the reader, if you are the fan, you actually have to go through the pain point of not having a coherent narrative in tennis — even just by platform: apps, websites, where do I watch what and when, which broadcasters, which channel, what is it. The fragmentation is a pain point for the consumer.

I worked five years in music, which I think has done an amazing job now with the DSPs — Spotify, Apple Music, Google and so forth. It wasn't by choice — it was by necessity, because of Napster and piracy. That's how they got there. Steve Jobs, iTunes — it was a painful journey.

The problem we have is: the status quo is very good. So we're all doing very well. There is sort of that comfort-zone state where, yes, we could be doing a lot better — I think there's an amazing opportunity — but we're doing okay. So we're not really in trouble, which would push us to change, because change is painful.

The $4B That Could Be $8B+

Host: What could you be doing that you are not doing, that most excites you? You're comfortable with the status quo because you're all growing, but you could be doing more.

Andrea: I'm not comfortable. The tennis industry — the professional tennis, meaning the ATP, WTA, the four Grand Slams — is around 4 billion in revenue. I strongly believe that we could double it, if not more. Just think of it as the ability to be able to package the four Slams and the Masters and the Finals as a product together to broadcasters.

And what really drives me mad is that we have the demand — we've got the Netflix, the Apple, the Amazon, the broadcasters — we've got the demand side wanting to buy our product, and we struggle selling it because we're fragmented. We all go to market with different products, go to the same market, and sell separately, which creates the fan-experience issue.

Host: I've never been in a position where you have the demand. [laughter] That's usually, as an entrepreneur, the biggest problem — create a product, create demand. Here the biggest challenge is: how do we get into an agreement? I think we all came to the conclusion that the pie can be a lot bigger. We all believe that. But then you get around the table and say "share of voice, distribution, control" — and that's where the deals fall off.

Host: I can bring that to life. I remember a conversation with Craig Tiley — he highlighted that tennis was a top-three viewership sport in the world. Top three. Not in the top ten commercially.

Andrea: 100%. That's the first slide of my presentation. We have less than 2% of the media, over 60-billion media industry. But we have over a billion fans, which is top five. And we're global, and we have a strong women's product, which is a unique selling point in my opinion. And we've got a lot of volume. We've got a lot of content — which, for example, Formula 1 doesn't have.

The One-Governance Vision

Host: You have the four Slams, which obviously are the pinnacle points of the year. Let's put those here — because what we're really talking about now is: you are in charge of men's tennis for everything else. What are the key areas for you as the ATP that you can hone in on to build that product, without the control of the four very powerful tournaments?

Andrea: If you really want to tackle the opportunity, the one vision we laid out is basically: have one governance. Because it starts with one governance — to have everyone around the table so that board would be capable of shaping the product of tennis. Any decision that comes out of that board becomes effective. Whatever I do now, whatever the Slams do — it can come up with seven different rules on anything: the tie-break on the fifth set, calendar, anything.

So you need one governance, one board to design the product. You need one commercial entity — call it Tennis Ventures — that actually goes to market with the media rights, the data rights and so forth. You can leave event-day ticketing and sponsorship locally.

That's nothing more than how they manage the NBA, the NFL and the most successful leagues around the world. It's not really a new idea. The difficulty is to get everyone together.

Host: If we're saying we know what the solution is, why do we not have it?

Andrea: It is far more complex. I don't blame anybody — it's difficult. If you look at the way we are today, there are probably 70–80 people in these seven organizations' boards. You go into one governance, it's going to be a board of 8, 10, 11. So going from many to few is generally difficult. People love their role, and obviously the Grand Slams would have to give up some control — and it's just share of voice generally.

Host: Do the Grand Slam stakeholders feel like they need the ATP as much as the ATP needs them?

Andrea: I can't speak on their behalf. What I can truly say — because we've been at it for four or five years — is I believe they're well intended. We had very good conversations, good meetings. I think we agreed on the size of the opportunity, and I think we agreed on a pathway.

The difficulty is: first of all, the distractions — the day-to-day. Obviously there is the constant negotiation with players — we're still in the free market, competing against each other. So there is some tension. And then there is the fear — because change: what if we do that, what will the future look like? At the moment it's working pretty well for them, and for us as well. Everybody's fine. It's hard to change radically when everything is going very well. That's my point I made in music — they had to change.

What Actually Needs to Change?

Host: What are we actually trying to change radically? Calendar? What is the thing?

Andrea: I think it's generally product and go-to-market: the fan experience, the product, the narrative, the calendar — somehow also the format. The game of tennis hasn't changed in more than 100 years.

And most importantly: what do we need to do in the next 20, 30 years? Because the world is changing — you know, with AI and everything else, consumer habits. The next generation, my kids — how will they consume sports in 10, 20 years? Are we fit as an organization? Do we have all the tools in the toolbox to be ready to change and pivot?

We compete in the entertainment space. We compete against gaming, music, movies, and other sports properties. I love the phrase by Reed, the founder of Netflix, when they asked him whether he was concerned about Apple coming into the space. He said: "My main competitor is sleep." Because ultimately you compete for the attention — for the eyeballs of consumers.

When I see the level of video games that my kids are playing today, the level of content production in movies, the level the music industry is managing — ultimately you're competing with the free time of people and their wallet. So even sport — a category that's a 200-billion industry within entertainment — will be under pressure.

Host: Do the other stakeholders think like that though?

Andrea: Not all of them. Some, maybe. But yes, there is a tendency of inward looking: "We're doing well, we're fine." We're super lucky — we have an incredible product, the game of tennis is amazing — and that tends to get you into the comfort zone and forget the world outside. My main point: you need a fast boat in the next few years.

Short-Term vs Long-Term Thinking

Host: Is there a challenge in combining short- and long-term thinking? Often short-term thinking is driven by poor performance. But the strength of tennis is pretty obvious — which in theory should enhance the ability to look long-term, because you're not as worried about today.

Andrea: In theory, yes. But it's very difficult to align when you have seven different organizations, seven boards, and the incentives are not aligned. There's no structure of an aligned vision and strategy and incentives for everyone, other than growing the sport.

Credit to the Slams: three of them are federations, and they also have a very noble mission — growing participation in the sport of tennis. In my organization, six out of nine Masters — soon six out of ten with the Saudis — are either federations or governments. So most of the profit in tennis goes back to grassroots. That's quite an intensive task. They have their own day job, so to say. So the professional part is not a spin-off — it's within the organization — and often is not the main focus other than two or three weeks a year.

The Financial Revolution — Profit Sharing and Player Pay

Host: You've made some serious financial changes. Can you talk us through a little bit of the "financial revolution"?

Andrea: I started January 1st, 2020 — a few months before COVID. I made the presentation to the board in New York four months before that. At the core of that presentation were a few core principles.

First, transparency. The partnership between tournaments and players lacked transparency — for 25 years, players had no visibility over the economics of the tournaments. So the profit-sharing formula we've implemented was the core of fixing the relationship. Align the incentives. The boardroom has completely changed.

We have three levels of audits. Players are getting 50% of the profits after the guaranteed prize money — it has delivered over 50 million in the last four years, extra. And the tournaments, which initially didn't like the idea, are actually now understanding that the players are partners. The mentality in the boardroom has changed. It used to be "us against them — what do I get, what do you get?" It was a negotiation almost like a tennis match across the net. Now we're on the same side of the court. Not quite doubles together — there's still tension on certain items — but if you want an extra cost, you know that adding it decreases the profit. The conversation has changed.

Second, investment in the pathway. We've tripled the prize money at Challengers, because the pathway is really important.

Third, emphasis on premium product. We've put more emphasis on the Masters. One of the core principles: the fans want to see the top players playing at the top events, where they all compete against each other. That happens at the Slams, the Masters and the Finals.

Host: How much does it cost to get them there?

Andrea: In '28, the plan will deliver — ATP only, men's tennis — around 350 million in compensation. Different tiers: compensation, prize money, pension, bonus pool and profit sharing. So around 350 million.

Host: Wow. And that's gone up.

Andrea: When I started it was around 190 total compensation. There's the incentive — the bonus pool, the prize money, ranking points, titles, visibility. For a tennis player, playing the four Slams and winning them is the number-one priority; then the ranking, winning Masters. Different reasons why they play the tour.

Casual vs. Hardcore Fans — and Why the Calendar Matters

Host: You mentioned those tournaments. There's a difference between the hardcore tennis fan and the casual tennis fan. One of the biggest challenges sport has right now — outside of football — is: I watch an individual one week, say I see them run a sub-two-hour marathon in London, and suddenly I'm interested in distance running, but I have no idea where that individual is going next week. My relationship is compromised by a lack of ability to connect in a calendar, in a structure.

So: the Masters events, the 1000s, 500s, 250s. What you provide is the consistency — me as a consumer knowing where Carlos Alcaraz and Jannik and Sascha Zverev are going to turn up week in, week out.

Andrea: Obviously the ranking is at the core of that — the race for who's going to be number one at the end of the year. The consequence — the story and the narrative — I think we could do a much better job if we were under one governance and one product-design team.

Keep in mind, tennis has a unique complexity: it's a direct-elimination sport. Whether you're Alcaraz or any player, you could lose first round and play one day — or you win the tournament, stay 12 days, play six or seven matches. Building a calendar for the top-100 cohort, you're actually seeing one calendar but there are four calendars within. The lower the ranking, the more tournaments you need to play because 75% of players lose second round.

So when we have the debate "there are too many tournaments on the calendar" — it depends for whom. Yes, for the top players who often go to semi-final and final, they need to play less. It's fluid. It's not all the same like Formula 1 or golf, where everybody plays the same.

Host: So do you not think we need less?

Andrea: The problem is: if you have less, then you have many players who just end up playing one or two matches. In general, a pro player plays between 65 to 80 matches per year. If you have, say, only 14 tournaments in the calendar, you might end up with players playing 16 or 17 matches a year and their level goes down. The quality of the competition decreases.

You can't create a second tier, play down — you can't move from "league one" to "league two." That's why we have this dynamic system: if you don't play very well, you play 500s; if you need more matches, you play 250s. Which can be confusing for fans — but I think it's more a product-marketing issue than a product-format issue.

The Ranking System — and the "Fear of Missing Out"

Host: Can you explain why those rankings and getting the ranking system right is so important — part of Vision '28 as well?

Andrea: One of the challenges: players are independent athletes, not employees of the ATP. They decide their schedule. We have a "best-of-18" ranking system. But currently the system incentivizes players to overplay. There's this fear of missing out — "I can play another, my score can be higher." It's like a race which, if the player is not fully disciplined, may end up playing too much because he's chasing the ranking.

Also: the economics in the 500, 250, exhibitions and team events — players are paid an appearance fee. So the economic incentive may drive players to play a schedule based on economics instead of just the ranking. It's an open system.

Host: But that's a problem then — at the top events, if you don't have the biggest names, you don't have the attention. We want the top players to play the best events. But we really can't tell them — like Formula 1 or the NFL do — where you must play, because you're employed by the league.

Host: Do you think you should be able to?

Andrea: There are definitely pros and cons in both systems. Before getting the job, I had to fly to Zurich and get interviewed by Roger — and also had conversations with Novak and Rafa, because the board felt I needed to speak with the big three.

One of the smartest questions I received in that process — the first question Roger asked when I sat down: "Do you think it should have the current structure or a league-union structure?"

I said there are pros and cons. Today, you guys have a seat on the board. With the supermajority, you have the Player Council — 10 players elected by all players, who elect four board members. No decision can be made without your reps approving.

In a union structure, you're not necessarily in the decisions of whether you're adding a tournament. There's a negotiation every 10 years — the collective bargaining agreement — mostly about economics. But you're an employee.

The current structure also allows you freedom. You're free like an entrepreneur — you can move around, play exos, play different tournaments, and you're on the board. It's quite an interesting position. The downside: the four Slams are outside the system, so the players don't really have a direct voice there as much as they have in the tours.

Host: Does that resonate?

Andrea: Even if you ask me today, there are pros and cons. Depends which day of the week you ask me. I see the benefits of having players involved in shaping the future of the sport. The question is: these are player reps elected by players. Often players feel "the board decided that, I didn't agree." But that's the problem of the process of democracy.

I have sympathy for that because I've been 13 years as a player, and most of the time I didn't agree with the decisions of the ATP.

Host: What decision did you disagree with most?

Andrea: I was Italian, played very well on clay, so I wanted the ATP to put more clay tournaments in Italy. [laughter] Specifically in my hometown. My career is short — that's what I want, that's what's good for me, and it's normal. There's no criticism.

Host: All Italian players should start at the quarter-finals. [laughter]

Host: But isn't that case in point of one of the challenges? Each individual has their own issues. You now know, sitting at the head of it, that you're never going to please everyone.

Andrea: Impossible. Through the democratic process — hire the right board reps, hire the right chair, agree on a strategy. If you don't like it, fire them. It's a question of empowering the person to execute on the back of a strategy. It can't be a weekly negotiation on conflicting interests — in that case, no system would work.

The Cost of Becoming a Pro

Host: When we had Dominic Thiem in here, he said it would cost a million over the lifecycle to become a top tennis player. Do you agree?

Andrea: Well, I was raised in a tennis family, but my parents didn't have enough money — so at 13 I moved out of home and went to Rome at the national tennis center from the Federation. The Federation financed my entire career. That doesn't happen for everyone, because not all federations around the world have the means — which is another discussion of how we redistribute profits globally.

At the time, it was about 50k per year for six or seven years. Translated 20, 30 years later — I'm not saying a million is pretty accurate, but you're close to that. I have three kids who play tennis — it's expensive. If you travel around the world and have a coach, it's an expensive sport.

The advantage is: if you're good today, you get investment early, sponsors, potentially support from federations. But it is expensive.

The Baseline Initiative — A Minimum Guarantee

Host: Can you talk about your Baseline initiative and the importance of ensuring that players further down the rankings receive a certain minimum?

Andrea: In '28 we'll go beyond that. We've created the Baseline, which gives you a minimum guarantee. We've tripled the money in the Challengers. In '28, subject to board approval, we'll also dedicate 25 million equally distributed over the 250s — so you get 100k at the end of the year, which should pay for your expenses. First time ever.

On top: a bonus pool of 50 million, mainly directed at the top 30 — a performance incentive. And then the profit sharing — the variable bonus pool, distributed according to performance at the Masters, plus prize money.

The target: top 100 to earn a minimum $1 million, and top 100 to 250 to earn a minimum $250–$300,000. Unprecedented in our sport.

Host: It's a tough career that you need to make the most of.

Andrea: You also have very different views. When we started, it was mostly "more money to more players." Then — depending which players are leading — "is it more money to the top guys who drive value?" That's the other big question. If you look at all sports, but even more in individual sports, most of the money goes to the top guys — at the PGA, probably 70–80%.

Revenue vs. Profit — A Mindset Gap

Host: Can I ask you about percentage of revenue to wages?

Andrea: I generally don't like conversations about revenue. I like conversations about profits, partnership, and alignment of interest.

Host: Do players understand that discussion about revenue versus profits? I agree with you — but when I hear players, they always talk about revenue.

Andrea: The US system is based on revenue, because of the league-union negotiation there. In my opinion, if you're an entrepreneur, an independent, then you need to have a profit mindset. If we ask you "can you do an extra hour of media?" — that drives profit — you have to be willing, because ultimately you benefit.

The challenge is: you have CAPEX — long-term investment. Tennis is very heavy infrastructure. Look at the billions the Slams have invested over the last 30 years — Wimbledon, the French Open, the US Open — amazing infrastructure that cost a lot. It's a long-term play. Your career is short. If we need to invest — which is what we need to do at the Masters, and have started doing — Cincinnati invested 260 million with Ben Navarro. Indian Wells — Larry Ellison invested 5–600 million in that beautiful infrastructure.

Those infrastructures can only be used two or three weeks a year. It's not like an indoor stadium you can reuse for concerts. It's extremely expensive — three stadiums with a roof, 26 courts, basically not used 95% of the year.

The Mystery of Spanish Tennis

Host: You as an Italian growing up were funded by the federation. Look at what you've got now — Sinner, Arnaldi, Berrettini. Italian tennis is doing something right. Talk about why that distribution-back-into-the-system is so important.

Andrea: This is the domain of World Tennis and the federations — participation and player development. We take care of the professional level. But I went through the system. You need some money — but not a huge amount. You cannot create champions in a factory.

Look at the USTA, the LTA, the French — it's not that because they have more money they've developed the best players in the last 20 years. Roger, Rafa and Novak — Novak was Serbian, Roger Swiss, Rafa… look at Spain. They have no funding from professional sport, and it's by far the market that has produced the best tennis players in the last 30 years: Emilio Sánchez, Bruguera, Ferrer, Moyà, then Rafa, now Carlos Alcaraz. Spain has been the factory of champions with no money.

I don't think there's a direct correlation between money and production of champions. But infrastructure and participation — yes, 100%.

The Power of the Individual Athlete

Host: Harry and I talk all the time about the power of the individual athlete. Tennis probably shows that more than any other sport now. But you don't necessarily always own full access to the players — they're independent contractors. How do you capitalize on the value of these stars without necessarily having full control?

Andrea: It's a challenge. We have ATP Media and Tennis Data Innovation, which manages media rights, data and streaming. On-site we have a PR Stars program — we work with players on social media. We promote the tournaments through that. It's more difficult than when I speak to my counterpart, Stefano at Formula 1. Obviously I'm not saying he's right or wrong — it is different. You literally are 30 seconds before the race starts and the drivers are giving interviews. In Monaco this year, under the sun, 35 degrees, with helmets, before starting the race — they're giving interviews. That's demanded from F1, and the relationship is one of employee. It's clear.

In our world, good or bad — I'd say there are positives — it's a negotiation. Most of the time you have to negotiate.

Host: Do you think that's right?

Andrea: It's either a free system, or a well-negotiated cycle of 10 years. There are pros and cons.

Host: With respect, a 10-year cycle today does not keep up with technology advancements. Ten years ago we didn't have ChatGPT. You didn't have many forms of social media. Clips were not a product. The technology landscape is moving much faster than the interview landscape.

Andrea: Our system would allow for flexibility. The ATP can get on a board meeting next week and change the rules, hypothetically. In a league-union relationship, you're locked most of the time. Or — you have the rights to implement, innovate and do the changes. There's no perfect system.

Why Re-Elected Twice — and the Expansion of the Masters

Host: You've been re-elected twice. That wouldn't happen if the players didn't buy into you.

Andrea: It's a difficult conversation because players are focused on their immediate needs. The expansion of the Masters was one requirement of the deal to achieve transparency. The model is simple: the Slams are combined tournaments, 15 days. Approximately 40% of our revenue is still event days. Adding days = revenue. Other sports are very skewed on media — we're not. Event days is still the largest part of our revenue.

You add that — which also funds the CAPEX, the investment, because you need that revenue to build bigger stadiums with shorter days. Some players say "I've got to stay more days and play more matches." I understand they don't like it. When I played, we had Indian Wells and Miami with that model. I wasn't a great fan — I'd have preferred more tournaments in Italy, especially on clay. [laughter]

I'm very conscious it wasn't going to be well received, especially by top players who go deep and spend those extra days. But in return: hold, be patient — if that drives more value, you can make a hell of a lot more money on a per-day basis. We'll hit that in '28 with the 50-million bonus pool. It's a dollar-per-day ratio in the end.

Host: If I'm number one, what's my dollar per day? If I'm number 100, what's my dollar per day?

Andrea: Depends. The number-one probably has 60–70% of income outside — endorsement, non-court tennis-related items. Difficult math. But for performance play — top ten, average in '28 — let's say 15 million each. Compared to a million if you're top 100.

Where the Revenue Comes From

Host: You said 40–50% is not exclusively on media. That's a great thing — sport that relies purely on media is vulnerable.

Andrea: Yes. The tournaments are doing a great job on-site. We need to invest more in infrastructure — capacity is the limit. We don't have a demand problem. Tickets are sold out. Last year, more than five million going through our gates — record ever.

Media: I'm a strong believer that in order to capture the opportunity, we need aggregation — WTA and the four Slams together. Once you have that package, you have a really compelling proposition.

Host: What are the most valuable commercial assets?

Andrea: You see Emirates on the net, or PIF sponsoring the ranking. But most sponsorship assets are locally managed by the tournaments.

Host: What is centrally controlled by you?

Andrea: Things like the net, the PIF ranking sponsorship.

Host: Why do you get the net but not other things? [laughter] Why not the backboard, the watch…?

Andrea: There's probably some historical reason — a negotiation in 1992 in a boardroom. Legacy systems, built over the years.

Host: Have you been able to build new opportunities with tech partners — data deals rather than front-facing?

Andrea: Yes. We've created Tennis Data Innovation, an amazing company in that space. We're now creating ATP Ventures — merging all central commercial activities: media, data, central sponsorship — into one entity, because we were very fragmented also inside the ATP.

The history: tennis wasn't really a business in the 60s, 70s — no structure. We're putting the pieces together to adapt to broadcasters and sponsors, but we've been slow.

Legacy Structures, Turnover, and the "Rising Tide"

Host: The American leagues have been luckier — they don't deal with the legacy structure.

Andrea: The other issue: a lot of turnover. In terms of the chairs of the four Grand Slams — I started in 2020 with a core focus of getting the four Slams and the WTA in the same room. Since then, probably only one person is still there from that initial setup. You go in cycles of two–three years, which is difficult. Just when you get close to a deal, two or three people exit the room.

Host: Continuity drives knowledge aggregation.

Andrea: Those are the rules — the USTA chair changes every two years. There's high turnover.

Host: We talk about football all the time. Declan Rice played 70-whatever games last year — no wonder he wasn't at his best at the World Cup. The answer is to strip it back. But individual stakeholders want their games on. You don't have that in the US — central control. NFL, NBA — central.

Andrea: Which is exactly the goal of One Vision: one central governance with one central commercial entity, to drive and align strategy. At the moment, everybody has fiduciary duties to their own.

Host: Who's going to be like, "Hey, take my power"?

Andrea: The European Union.

Host: So do you think it's possible?

Andrea: I'm optimistic. I think it will happen because the free market will ultimately demand it — or you lose market share. It will happen. I don't know if in five years, in 20 or 30 — but it has to happen, unless you go down.

Host: Your strongest argument is: you want it to happen in a moment of strength. There's an amazing book called Legacy, on the All Blacks. One of the key fundamentals: every time they were at their best, strongest, they changed. They didn't wait for the dip. Everything they did was ahead of the curve.

Andrea: Don't wait for the crisis to trigger the change.

Star Dependency and the "Life After the Big Three"

Host: How elastic is demand to player appearance? If you don't have Alcaraz at an event, how much does that impact attendance?

Andrea: It does — but not as much as people tend to believe. We've got record attendance in every Masters — even Shanghai, where the final didn't have Alcaraz or Sinner. From a sponsorship/broadcast perspective, we have cycles of three to five years.

Ultimately it's a great game. Even a final of the underdog versus a new, younger player is exciting. I don't feel our sport is linked to three personalities. Post-Mac/Borg/Agassi/Sampras — everyone thought we were in trouble. Post Roger/Rafa/Novak — same. We're not. We're doing better than ever. We've got Alcaraz, Sinner, Sascha — great personalities. The game is capable of producing them.

Behind-the-Scenes Content and the "Drive to Survive" Question

Host: Drive to Survive was transparency that opened F1 to a new audience. Break Point — brilliant movie, by the way, for those who haven't seen it, slightly dark, don't watch on a rainy day. [laughter] Has tennis done a good job showing behind-the-scenes character?

Andrea: Absolutely not. Non-live is super valuable — the future of sport will be determined by that. The problem is structural: access to players.

Host: Why couldn't you get a Drive to Survive equivalent going?

Andrea: Because they're independent athletes — individual negotiations. You've got to get everybody on board. Every player has done their own documentary. Not that we as a sport didn't try — we tried with the Slams — but we couldn't get players to commit.

Host: F1 had the challenge even though they technically had control of drivers. Max didn't really want to be part of it for a while — then it became part of the narrative and he joined.

I think Break Point was interesting in parts, but suffered from elite-access not being fully transparent. Players now have individual channels — Sabalenka, Jannik — more owning their content, which doesn't help centrally.

Andrea: I agree. It's also a matter of focus. If you had that entity — a dedicated commercial engine with alignment of the Slams, WTA and ATP — you could do something altogether. Requires long-term thinking: non-live content is key, but costs a lot of money. In an environment focused on profit distribution, less so on long-term investment.

Hypothetical: You Produce Break Point 2.0 — Who's In?

Host: We can do Break Point. I'm giving you budget. Choose four players.

Andrea: Men and women — four players?

Host: Men and women. Who do you pick?

Andrea: I'd say the top four in the world. Go by ranking — the players who are winning the titles.

Host: As the consumer or the executive?

Andrea: Both.

Host: Personally: the recent Guardiola documentary on Prime was brilliant. But All or Nothing with Man City years ago — incredibly boring. Just winning, winning, winning. No real story. Compare to Sunderland 'Til I Die — Netflix went in thinking "amazing promotion story," got relegation, chaos — recognized as one of the best.

Look at Full Swing in golf. The things about Rory and Tiger are fascinating — but the episode people often like the most is Joel Dahmen, 80th fighting on the Challenger Tour. People never got to see what went into qualifying for tournaments. It built narrative.

Andrea: Fair point. A different episode focusing on the underdog, the challengers, the upcoming young players, the winners. With different flavors — men and women, life on tour.

Host: Challenger prize money is up 167% since 2022 — to $32.4 million. What does that money mean going into the system? What's that allowing players to do? Building that story underneath — I want to see what has to go in.

Andrea: We'll put it on the agenda in the next meeting. Fair point. We've got assets. We can build stories around it without the buying-in of top players. You can tell other stories.

The WTA Merger — On Pause

Host: Sneaky segue — what makes this valuable is men's and women's tennis. There's been conversation about a merger between ATP and WTA, particularly commercially. Where's it at?

Andrea: It's on pause at the moment. It's been lasting for three years. We're shifting focus now to ATP Ventures — the same thing, but without WTA. I believe it will happen in the future. I'm optimistic — but probably needs more time.

Host: Why does it make sense in the first place?

Andrea: Women's tennis is probably one of the strongest properties in sport worldwide — I'm really proud of that. An incredible asset for tennis. The product combined is what fans want to see. Evidence is clearly there — Slams, combined tournaments. On TV, on-site — you see the variety. You even have less risk on personalities: if the men's side isn't doing well, you have Serena, Venus, Coco, Sabalenka. Women's tennis is really good to watch. The Sabalenka–Rybakina match — I thought that was the most incredible match, nothing against Ben Shelton.

Both together are stronger — no doubt.

Host: Then why doesn't it happen?

Andrea: Same reasons as One Vision: fear of losing control, debates over share of voice, governance. Distribution, equity, valuation. Sometimes you put two together and 2+2 equals seven, and people argue over who gets the most out of the extra three. Even though seven is better than four. Often the deal falls off because of that.

Host: What do they want that you're not willing to give?

Andrea: Not a single thing. We were close. Ultimately we decided to pause. It's about control, valuations — and to a certain extent, being in charge of your own future. "I manage my asset, my rights" — that feels more comfortable than agreeing on leadership and compromising.

Host: Is this commercial, or operational control of the WTA?

Andrea: Just central commercial assets.

The Spotify Analogy — A Future of Engagement-Based Pay

Host: Female tennis players can be more commercially attractive to many brands than male players. In these deals, they could earn more than their male counterparts — but societally we're programmed to cap it at the male revenue.

Andrea: 100%. The Spotify / DSP analogy: we're struggling with legacy linear, understanding who's watching what. But if the future is digital, you can split revenue based on what consumers decide — like on Apple Music, an artist gets rewarded more if more people listen. You could have a world where you say "look, equal opportunity" — there's a floor where we start equally — but the rest is decided by engagement.

I could argue some WTA players probably deserve more than some ATP players. Think of what Serena and Venus drove. You need to agree on the KPI — the metrics — which isn't easy today. It'll be easier in the future. Social media engagement, audience on live broadcast. In the top 20 athletes in tennis, there'd be quite a few female athletes by engagement.

Host: I think I saw — six out of the top ten in Forbes were female, from an engagement and off-court revenue perspective. Equal pay today enabled the platform and investment for the women's game.

Andrea: Positive also to the men's game. The strength of the women's game adds value to the sport. 100% convinced.

The ATP Tour Finals — The Season Finale

Host: The WTA finals — Steve Simon told Andy Roddick he wanted them to be the Super Bowl of women's tennis. What are the ATP Finals for you?

Andrea: Super important. The grand finale. I love the format: best eight players, round-robin, semi-final and final. Often you crown the year-end number one. Incredible — the best of the best at the end of the year.

Host: Are you going to tell me you had something to do with the location — Italy?

Andrea: [laughter] That's another misconception. "By my house in my garden." Finals going to Italy — for the record — was decided before I came. Check the history, check the announcement. It was decided by my predecessor.

Breakaway Leagues — and Saudi

Host: How do we feel about breakaway leagues? We've seen them in golf — LIV, RIP. Saudi wants to host boxing at a massive scale. Big money, new formats.

Andrea: Two items. First: Saudi — it's going to be a new Masters in '28. We're really proud. They're building an amazing infrastructure at Qiddiya — almost two-billion-dollar investment. That tournament will be amazing. They're in the ATP house. We'll have ten Masters starting in '28.

On the back of golf, we started very early, got in touch with them. Very collaborative conversation. We turned it into a success story.

Generally: we're in the free market. Anyone could theoretically buy out the players. The challenge in tennis is infrastructure is very expensive. Compared to golf — you can take any golf course and go out there. For a full tour, with proper draws and 100 players competing, you're talking billions, tens of billions of dollars of infrastructure. That's a little bit of an infrastructure edge we have. But we shouldn't get into the comfort zone because of that — that's my point.

What He Loves About the Game — and About the Job

Host: What do you love about the game and the job?

Andrea: The game — fantastic since I picked up a racket at three. It is the best game in the world: one against one, gladiator battle — physical, mental, technical strength. No hiding. All my three kids play tennis. It's an incredible school of life: you learn to solve problems independently; you learn to manage defeat — you lose every week as a tennis player. I did, for 13 years. Every week. Unless you're that kind of guy. Round two, often. [laughter]

The drama — points-based. You can win being two sets down and five-love down. The core mechanic — whoever invented it — is beautiful. No other individual sport comes close. An individual sport lacks the tribal link that soccer or basketball give you to your city, your nation. That sense of belonging — "my city, my team, my nation" — is always individual. But one against one, there's no comparison.

The platforms we have are amazing. The four Slams are incredible tournaments. I grew up dreaming of winning one. Our Masters have long history — 50, 80 years.

The job: I love the mission. Take tennis to the top five properties in the world — ideally top three in every market. I don't think we'll ever beat the NFL and NBA in the States. But we can be solid top five, if not top three, around the globe. We are one of the truly unique men's and women's global sports properties.

What I hate: we're slow. I'd like to move 100 miles an hour. I spent 17 years in tech and startups — different environment.

The Hardest Stakeholder: Agents

Host: Which stakeholder is more difficult — agents who control player access, or the Slams?

Andrea: You cannot say one is more difficult. Everyone has their focus — I respect that. If you have a business, you focus on your business.

Agents — most of their income is commission on guarantees, sponsorship contracts, or exhibitions. They don't make money on prize money, bonus pool or profit sharing.

Host: I didn't know that.

Andrea: And often they have influence on the scheduling of players. Those deals are made a year in advance. A player should schedule and play, say, in a lower tier when they need to because they haven't performed well. But if you finish final-final-win-win-win, you should take time off. If you signed a deal a year before and need to attend — that's where the overscheduling and overplaying arrive. That deal was pre-agreed.

That's what we're trying to fix in Product '28. But we can't fix the problem at its core because it's a free market and athletes are independent. The difficulty: getting all these different interests aligned into a common vision and strategy.

I'm going to be in front of the players next week: "Guys, this is the vision. This is the strategy. We want to take tennis from 4 billion to 10 billion. We're all going to be better off." The Slams will be better off — they're the top tier. WTA will be better off. The ATP tournaments. A rising tide lifts all boats.

Career After Tennis — and the US College Question

Host: We saw Gaël Monfils announce he was moving into a professional role in investing. Milos Raonic has done it too. Does tennis equip players sufficiently for a career after tennis?

Andrea: We're trying. I was passionate about this. My dad told me: "You can have a career, but you have to go to university because the career is short." I did — got a law degree while playing, then an MBA. We started different programs — allowed through Coursera online programs. But it's difficult. The career is demanding. You're traveling, in a hotel room — can't attend classes.

What I see today, which I don't like: players drop school at 13, 14. Agents sign players earlier. I see it with my kids' peers. I'm a huge fan of the US college concept — play tennis at a high level, get an education, then turn pro. You can still turn pro at 21, 22. Not the end of the world.

Host: Is that possible, in a professionalized industry where at 13, 14, you are at another intensity?

Andrea: Difficult. But if you get an education and train and play at a high level — futures or Challengers in summer — you may have a chance to turn pro. By the time you're 21, Alcaraz has already won four Grand Slams.

Used to be more of an issue in my time, when Becker and Chang won a Slam at 17. Nowadays the career is longer — they play until 35, 40. Twenty-five is probably the peak at the beginning. I see it with my kids: school has been a priority. Their peers train six, seven hours a day — they have an edge.

Doubles — The Controversy

Host: When you were describing the sport, I meant to ask: what's happening with doubles?

Andrea: Currently on the table — one of the discussions for Product '28 is reducing the draw and the cost of doubles. Received a lot of pushback. Doubles players aren't happy — it's very sensitive.

The rationale: today, doubles prize money, including Slams, is around $60 million — 40 million at the tour — roughly 20% of the prize money delivered to players. Doubles started in the 70s and 80s; in the 90s, most singles players also played doubles. Remember McEnroe. Even in the 90s, players like Kafelnikov won Slams in both.

Look at the data: in the last 20 years, we don't have a single top-100 singles player in the top 15 doubles. It's completely turned into doubles specialists. From a media perspective, we produce it, it's expensive, broadcasters don't show it.

What really adds value is towards the weekend. In the weekend we have fewer matches. Bigger draws is probably all we're ultimately proposing — reduce it. Doubles is part of tennis history. No intention of destroying it. Shift that value to singles players, early qualies, early rounds, ranks between 50 and 150 or 100.

If you're ranked between 50 and 150 — even if you make 7–800,000 net, net minus coaches, expenses, taxes — you're struggling. It's not a lot to put in the bank for a very short career. Controversial debate — about shifting distribution to singles players, lower ranked, which we believe drives more value. We'll see what the board decides.

Quick Fire Round

Host: What market has the biggest opportunity for tennis to be more than it is?

Andrea: Asia — generally. Growing in China, attendance in our tournaments has been increasing. Takes a long time to get into the culture — not a five-year play; it's a long play. Player development. Asia, China is a big opportunity. We can start with one player — look at the Philippines now. South America — big tradition in South America around tennis. We're very strong in North America, US, Canada and Europe. Brazil — massive, huge.

Host: Go back to your playing days. You can only win one Slam — which one?

Andrea: When I was 8, in my diary I drew a map from where I was living to England, London — winning Wimbledon. A few years later, I realized I couldn't play on grass — I was horrible on grass. I think I won one match in 10 years I played at Wimbledon.

Host: You won one match? That's not a great track record.

Andrea: The opponent retired in the fifth. [laughter] Just for the record. True. He got injured. Won by time.

So my dream turned into the French Open. Clay — won Roland Garros as my goal while I was a pro.

Host: What was the furthest you got in a Slam?

Andrea: Around the round of 16. I've played Davis Cup final, semi-final at Masters — but not that far in the Slams.

Host: What ATP 1000 event gives you the best food — the best hospitality?

Andrea: Today or in my days?

Host: Today.

Andrea: From a fan and executive perspective — Madrid. Incredible hospitality. They've built an incredible hospitality business. Madrid is pretty high up.

Host: It's clay, though. [laughter] Basically the answer is anything with clay — or in Italy.

Andrea: Yes.

Host: Take me to meeting Roger for this interview. Where is it? Are you nervous?

Andrea: I think in Zurich, in a meeting room in a hotel. I knew Roger — I played him and won once. He was young.

Host: You won?

Andrea: Yes, he was young. Rome, center court. 2001. He was still 20 years old. He won his first Masters the week after, in Hamburg — that's where he started to become who he has. He knew who I was. We'd played each other.

Host: What makes him so great?

Andrea: Many things. Talent, grace. A lot of people believe Roger is pure talent — which he is. But Roger was also incredible hard work, attention to detail, and very strong mentally. You have to be, to get to that level and win what he has won for so long.

Host: How important was his smart schedule — avoiding injuries?

Andrea: The same with Sampras. The best players — they're really disciplined. The most important thing is to say no — knowing when to say no, even when there is opportunity, financial or points. The discipline to balance energy and know when your body needs a rest.

Host: Hard work versus natural talent — the casual divide in sport. In tennis, is one more relevant?

Andrea: The mind is very relevant. Physically and technically, the top players are all very good. Then you have to get into the definition of talent. Rafa had an incredible talent — it's just a different talent. The way he plays, what he's done, requires incredible talent.

Final Question — The Future

Host: What are you most excited for in the future of tennis?

Andrea: That tennis becomes a top property. That we achieve one governance and one commercial entity. That players, Slams, WTA and ATP are in the same room making decisions for the future of the sport. And tennis beats every other sport. That's the goal.

Host: Get around the table, guys. We can host it if you want. [laughter] Look down the camera for that.

Host: I look forward to ATP Ventures. Thank you so much for coming on the show. You've been fantastic.

Andrea: Thank you, guys. It's been a pleasure.
