## 一、这份访谈真正的"反常识":网球不是在争夺份额，而是在"富裕中窒息"
最让我意外的，不是 Gaudenzi 说网球估值被低估一半（$4B 应该是 $8B+），而是他亲口承认的一件罕见事：**"我们有需求端在排队买，但我们卖不动。"** 这在商业史上是极反常的信号——绝大多数行业倒在供给过剩、需求不足；网球却倒在"七个卖家挤在同一个柜台，各自打着不同的价签"。
这让我想起克莱顿·克里斯坦森的"成功者悖论"：音乐产业之所以被迫在 2003 年整合到 iTunes/Spotify，是因为 Napster 让所有人一起流血。而网球没有 Napster。七个利益体——四大满贯、ATP、WTA、ITF——正因为**每家都过得挺好**，所以永远凑不齐改革的痛阈。他说得极坦白："改变是痛苦的，而我们没有被迫改变的危机。"
**跨领域连接**：这几乎是央行政策里"债务通缩螺旋"的镜像——不是因为穷而改革不了，是因为富而改革不了。网球需要的不是更多的钱，而是一次人为制造的"压力测试"。沙特的入场、Netflix 的试探、Break Point 的失败——这些其实都是潜在的"温和版 Napst

item.title: [a16z] Andrew Huberman on Focus, Energy, and Performing at Your Best
item.dc:creator: a16z
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一、冥想的"乳酸悖论"：Huberman 悄悄颠覆了整个东方传统的西方理解

最惊人的不是他讲了什么，而是他用生物化学术语重新定义了冥想——"心智的乳酸"（lactate of the mind）。

通常我们以为冥想是"让心平静下来"，但他从威斯康辛的脑成像数据里拿到的结论恰恰相反：冥想的收益不来自宁静，而来自观察混乱时那种"几乎受不了但不动"的张力。这与肌肉训练中乳酸堆积触发肌肥大的机制在信息结构上完全同构——不是去除刺激，而是承受刺激而不反应，由此激活适应回路。

这里埋着一个反直觉的推论：那些自称"冥想从来静不下来"、因此放弃的人，其实一直处在最高训练强度区而不自知。他们以为自己失败，实际上是在做深蹲时抱怨"腿很酸"——那个"酸"就是训练本身。

二、他身上藏着一个认识论级别的时间悖论：实践比机制早了 15 年

他顺口提到一件被低估的事：90 年代中期，斯坦福睡眠实验室的研究员们——包括 Howard Hughes 研究员和美国科学院院士——每天从地下室走到屋外看日落。他们不知道为什么有效，但他们做。直到 2000 年代初，视网膜里那群感知环境光并校准昼夜节律的神经元才被发现。

这是一个极少被明说的跨领域规律：

实践 使用时间 机制阐明
柳树皮镇痛 公元前 1899（阿司匹林）
水手吃柑橘防坏血病 16 世纪 1930（维生素C分离）
发酵食物助消化 几千年 2010s（肠道菌群）
日落光照 1990s 实验室 2002（ipRGC 细胞）

身体的集体直觉系统性地领先实验室 100-500 年。Huberman 真正打破常规的建议其实不是"去晒太阳"，而是一句隐秘的方法论：不要等机制。身体已经知道的，比我们能验证的多得多。

这反过来对 a16z 的听众——一群以第一性原理为旗帜的投资人和创业者——其实是个尴尬的提醒：第一性原理有时候是最慢的路径。

三、神经科学家把手机锁进监狱级保险箱——系统失败的隐喻

最值得玩味的坦白：研究注意力机制的神经科学家，自己需要一个连写代码都解不开的保险箱来对付 X 和 Instagram。

人们通常把这当成"连他都这样，所以我没事"的自我安慰。但真正的意思截然相反——

如果连全世界最懂多巴胺回路的人都无法用意志力对抗推荐算法，那么"自律"作为解决方案已经在架构层面失效了。 这不是个人缺陷，而是系统性失衡：一端是一个受过神经科学训练的大脑，另一端是数千名博士+强化学习+ A/B 测试日活数十亿的优化机器。个体 vs. 群体智能的较量从一开始就定下了结局。

这跟心脏病医生抽烟不是一回事——心脏病医生的香烟没有在实时学习他的弱点。

跨领域连接：这个现象其实解释了为什么过去十年几乎所有"数字极简主义"的畅销书都不管用——它们把一个架构问题误诊为习惯问题。真正起作用的从来不是"少看手机"的念头，而是那个物理保险箱——空间上的不可达，而非心理上的克制。这与瑞·达利欧的"原则 vs. 情绪"、丰田的"防呆设计"（Poka-yoke）、甚至中世纪修道院把钟摆放在钟楼顶的物理隔离，在思想上同源。

四、一个藏在细节里的反主流观察："吃得太干净，我反而变弱"

这句话一闪而过，但它在悄悄炸掉一整个 wellness 产业的核心教义。

Huberman 发现：长时间严格清洁饮食后，他力量下降、情绪变差、进展变慢。偶尔吃两片 pepperoni 披萨反而像是"给营养加峰值"。

这和免疫学里著名的卫生假说（hygiene hypothesis）结构完全一样：过度无菌的环境培养出过度反应的免疫系统。延伸一步：代谢系统也许同样需要"扰动"才能保持韧性。零糖、零酒精、零炎症食物的极致洁癖，可能生产的是一种"代谢上的玻璃人"——指标漂亮，适应性却脆弱。

Mark Andreessen 完全戒酒、Huberman 近乎不吃糖，但他们都在某种意义上为这种"洁癖优化"付出代价。真正的健康也许不是消除扰动，而是管理扰动的频率与幅度——就像心率变异性（HRV）高才是健康，心率恒定反而是濒死信号。

五、一个让投资人应该竖起耳朵的信号：下一波神经技术在哪里

他几乎顺口预告了一个方向，但如果你听进去，这是一个明确的投资纲领：

"眼罩，通过控制眼动把你送入睡眠，再通过前庭电刺激把你唤醒。"

为什么睡眠会是神经技术的第一个商业突破口？因为：

  • 目标函数极其明确（要么睡着，要么醒着——不像"专注"那样模糊）
  • 生理路径短且已知（前庭神经、动眼神经、迷走神经分支都在耳朵附近浅表处）
  • 效果可即时验证（6 分钟内睡着，用户自己能感受到）
  • 市场规模无需教育（全世界失眠的人都知道自己失眠）

对比之下，"注意力增强设备"的失败率会很高——因为我们还不知道"专注的理想脑电模式"是什么（倒 U 型，但峰值因任务而异）。

这是个关键的 insight：技术突破的顺序不是由"问题的重要性"决定的，而是由"目标函数是否足够二元"决定的。 睡眠>清醒的二元清晰度，让它必然先于"心流诱导"商业化。同样的规律解释了为什么自动驾驶在高速公路（二元：在道/不在道）比在城市（无数灰色决策）更早落地。

📝 转录文本

Cold Open

Huberman: If you take yourself and your work really seriously, you need to organize your day that way.

Host: If you had to recommend three things to people to live a healthier life, what would those be?

Huberman: Do the weight training protocol I talked about earlier. It will completely change your life. Figure out some way to make the sleep you can get the highest quality sleep.

Host: Did you take any supplements or medications yesterday?

Huberman: Loads. [laughter]

Host: What's something you recommend to others but are not that good at following yourself?

Huberman: I think the social media thing might be the biggest one. I recently moved X and Instagram to a separate phone and then I keep that phone in a lock box. You can't actually code out of it.

Host: A lot of founders listen to our podcast. If you had to narrow it down to three pieces of evidence-based habits for cognitive performance, what would those things be?

Huberman: Um…

Welcome & Framing

Host: Dr. Huberman, welcome to the a16z show.

Huberman: Thank you. Delighted to be here.

Host: Your podcast launched in January of '21 and has changed the way millions of people live their lives. This morning I got my son. I delayed my caffeine a little bit, probably not as much as you would like. Um and you famously got our firm's founder Mark Andreessen to stop drinking alcohol. I'm not there yet. But I'm wondering if looking back you remember a moment where you were like, "Holy cow, people aren't just listening to me. They're like changing their daily habits because of what I say."

Huberman: Well, it's been a wild ride. I didn't anticipate any of it. But I'm delighted that people are doing things for their health, and I don't know whether to accept — by saying thank you — or apologize that Mark stopped drinking. I know he enjoyed the occasional drink. I want —

Host: Grumpy about it.

Huberman: Yeah. Well, I want to be very clear. The data say zero is better than any. Two per week is probably the upper limit for an adult non-alcoholic, and I don't think Mark is alcoholic. He could in theory have two drinks. But when — he goes, "No." You know, he kind of did what many people do, which is sometimes none is easier to stick to than some. And I do think that alcohol can be enjoyed, and if one wants to do that, just think about doing some of the other things that can be beneficial.

But to directly answer your question, I didn't anticipate any of it. As I said, I'm delighted people are taking measures for their health. At some point I realized, "Whoa, people are starting to do things." And I couldn't tell whether it was because of the science that we were presenting or because the protocols I know work extremely well. The nice thing is I don't take credit for the actual protocols, because in most cases — with rare exception, like some things related to stress mitigation — the protocols come from other people's science.

So in looking at the fields of science and health education, most people out there have been talking about their own science. Doing it this way affords me a certain amount of freedom. I have to be careful too, because I'm talking about other people's science often. But I love to learn and I love to teach. Nothing makes me happier than reading papers and sharing what I think is interesting information and trying things out and seeing what works. And the people close to me will tell you that for my whole life, when I've learned something I thought was cool, I'm out there teaching about it, whether people want to listen or not. So they just kind of stuck a microphone in front of me, and here I am.

A Day in the Life: Wake-Up

Host: Amazing. You've been very transparent about your daily protocols — sun in your eyes, delaying caffeine, rotating exercise by day, cold plunge and sauna, doing yoga nidra, taking a variety of supplements. Maybe you can just walk us through yesterday. What did you eat? What exercises did you do? What supplements did you take? What of your advice did you follow and what did you not?

Huberman: A single day. So I wake up, I use the bathroom like everybody else. I —

Host: Do you get on your phone while you're in bed?

Huberman: No.

Host: Okay.

Huberman: No, phone's out of the room while I sleep. If I didn't love-love-love my Eight Sleep so much, I would figure out a way to have no Wi-Fi on in the house at all at night.

Host: Interesting.

Huberman: So I woke up, I'm groggy like everybody else. My mind starts going places that are — it's discombobulated on waking. I don't think I've ever woken up and just done a big yawn and been like "life is so good." I wake up and I think, okay, I have this to do, I have that to do.

Meditation: "The Lactate of the Mind"

So the first thing that I do is get up, use the restroom, and then these days I do a 5-minute meditation. I set my phone for 5 minutes. And I do a standard meditation of just breathing.

This, I think, is an extremely important practice that I haven't talked a lot about. If for no other reason than it gets you very aware of what the inputs to your brain are about to be. And it also makes you very aware of how chaotic it can be in our minds.

After talking to a number of people who worked on the science of meditation — in particular folks out at University of Wisconsin who've done a bunch of the brain imaging — it's very clear that the real benefits of meditation come from not quieting the mind, but from being able to just observe how chaotic it is. And see that as something slightly separate from the quote-unquote observer. And we have circuits that we think underlie the observer versus all the monkey-mind stuff, as they call it.

But I always thought that meditation was about achieving a really peaceful state. Turns out it's about observing the chaos. And so the best way I can describe this practice in terms of its utility is: just as with exercise, if you get a burn in your legs or the final repetitions of lifting weights, that's what triggers the adaptation. With meditation — in terms of consciousness and focus and awareness — I think the lactate of the mind, as it was described to me (I didn't come up with that phrase), the lactate of the mind is to be able to experience that chaos, observe it, and not do anything with it. That's what allows you to move into your day with more awareness of what is a meaningful thought or reaction and what isn't.

Okay, so I do that 5 minutes. These days I find the buzzer goes off without me, you know, "When is this over? When is this over?"

Morning Light

And then I get sunlight in my eyes. I'm absolutely religious about that. Sometimes I go up on my roof, sometimes I go for a walk.

Host: Were you home yesterday?

Huberman: I was, yeah.

Host: Okay.

Huberman: Yeah, and I take some water with me usually, drink some water, get some sunlight in my eyes. Today I woke up in a hotel. I was facing east in the morning, so it was great, got to actually see the sunrise. But cloudy day, overcast day, I'm getting sunlight in my eyes first thing. If I wake up long before the sun is out, I have a 10,000 lux artificial light, and I'll get in front of that thing just as I make coffee in the morning or do my thing.

Caffeine & Exercise

I then, if I'm going to exercise, I drink caffeine right away. I think this is something that I've tried to be clear about, but hasn't always been clear. If I'm an exercise [sic], I need caffeine, so I'm not waiting even 30 minutes. I'm going to drink caffeine, so I drink yerba mate, which is my preferred source of caffeine, for a long time now.

And then I exercise. My exercise routine is very simple, and I might just share it, because I've found that it's been very beneficial not just for me, but for women I've trained with, men, people of all ages. I've followed it for 35 years, and I think it's the most time-efficient and effective exercise program.

The Framework: Weights + Cardio

It's really straightforward. 3 days a week lifting weights, two to three days a week doing some sort of, quote-unquote, cardio.

The cardio first. Something where you get your heart rate way, way up, safely. Could be the rower, could be the Airdyne bike (the one with the push-pull with the arms while you're pedaling), could be running. Pick something that you can go close to max effort without hurting yourself. This is a really big deal, especially now that I'm 50. I feel quite proud of the fact that I've never had a major injury and I feel great at 50 — mostly because of what I didn't do. A lot of people are telling me all the things they did do. It's all the things I didn't do. I never hopped on someone else's workout just because I was challenged. That's how you hurt yourself. I picked things that felt right to me. Cycling doesn't feel good to me. Running and the Airdyne bike do.

So: warm up for a minute pedaling easy, then go 20 seconds all-out effort, 10 seconds rest, repeat that eight times. You're done. That's one cardio workout. You're getting close to max heart rate. This is VO2 max type stuff, and it's so fast.

The Weekly Split

Host: So, yesterday was Sunday. What is Sunday?

Huberman: Day one — this could fall on a Sunday or a Monday for someone, doesn't matter. But the first day of the week I train my legs with resistance training. Takes about an hour. That's the hardest work of the week. And if I were to only do one workout per week for the rest of my life, it would be that. For lots of reasons: largest musculature, systemic effects on hormones and metabolism, etc.

After leg day, I typically take the day completely off. I'll try to do some sauna–cold alternation on those days for recovery. We can talk details there. Then, depending on how well I've recovered, it might be just one day off, might be two days off.

Then I do some sort of push-pull thing for the torso. So, some chest presses, some shoulder presses, a pull-up or pull-down type thing if someone can't do pull-ups, and some sort of row. Maybe some stuff for the neck if somebody has bad posture — oftentimes men's shoulders will start getting wider and they're not training their neck. First of all, it looks kind of disproportionate, but then they'll start getting rotator-cuff stuff. Training the neck is very important for stability of the entire shoulder girdle.

And then I'll take a day off and then I'll do some arms, calves, abs — smaller body parts. So those are three separate weight-training days.

The Set Scheme

All of them follow the same approach, and this is where I think people go badly wrong, but the data and what you're hearing online is starting to finally catch up.

You could warm up for a couple minutes on the bike or some jumping jacks if you wanted, but I recommend doing one light set — 10 or 12 repetitions very light, just to get blood flowing — for the first movement. Then the second set is a moderate set: a set that you probably could do 10 repetitions, you do three. You're just preparing the nervous system for the heavier load. Then you do two work sets, spaced maybe 3–4 minutes rest in between, which is long, but those work sets are all-out work sets in perfect form taken to momentary muscular failure. Two sets only.

This might be a leg extension for the quads, and then you would move to something else — some sort of movement you can do safely, a squat, a front squat, a leg press — some compound movement. And then the same thing for the hamstrings.

The point here is: light set, medium set with many fewer reps than you could do, then hard work for two sets. Write down what you did and either increase weight or increase repetitions every single workout. And I do this for every single thing I just described regardless of body part. It ends up being two exercises per body part, maybe three. So the total volume of work is very low. You leave these workouts even on leg day feeling not completely rejuvenated, but you're not crushed. Your recovery is very fast. Your nervous system isn't as taxed, and you make progress at an amazing rate.

A woman I suggested this to — a D1 athlete who played soccer for years — came to me the other day and she's like, "I can't believe this works so well. It's a third of the volume I was doing before." You can just put more into these individual sets.

Then somewhere in the week I find a way to do the 6-minute — turns out to be about 6 minutes of the 20 seconds all-out, 10-second rest. And I find another day to do some sort of long hike. It used to be a jog. Nowadays I like to throw on a weight vest or a backpack and hike where my heart rate's up and I'm breathing a bit. And if I'm really ambitious and I'm getting enough sleep every night, I might also do a 20- to 30-minute run in the middle of the week.

But those three weight workouts will get most people what they want in terms of body recomposition, strength, not just offsetting muscle loss and strength with age, but feeling much better posturally, mobility-wise. And of course you can always stretch — you can do that while you watch TV in the evening.

That's the framework. I've been doing that for 35 years. Everyone I've given it to is positively shocked by the brevity, the results, most importantly, and the fact that it's fun. When you are looking forward to a really 45- to 60-minute hard work, it's fun. It actually starts to become a pleasure to do.

A Note on Fibrous Foods

I'm a big believer in fiber, but I want to make a point that I think doesn't get discussed enough: many people get gastric distress from certain fibrous foods. It's very important, I think, that people find foods that are good for them, but that they feel good eating and after they eat. So for instance, you're not going to see me eating broccoli. It makes me feel kind of not well. It doesn't digest well no matter how much I chew it. I'm not alone in this. There's some foods like onions that generate histamines. And so some people just don't feel good after eating certain foods.

You have to experiment and see what works for you. And the only way to do that really is for a short while to start experimenting with single-ingredient foods. Just having some broccoli. You can put some olive oil or butter on it. Just seeing what works. If people are constantly eating sandwiches and stews and pizzas and soufflés and lasagnas, you don't know what works for you and what doesn't. So a lot of developing really healthy eating habits with foods that you love — and having a lot of choices — is to figure out what you can eat and feel really good eating after you eat as well.

Evening Light

And then in the later afternoon, I make it a point to get a walk before the sun goes down. Or if I don't have time and I'm on a phone call, I'll just step outside and watch the sun go down if I can, or just look in the direction of the sun in the overcast sky.

I actually learned this practice from the sleep lab at Stanford down the road from here when I worked there during a summer in college. This was before the discovery of the neurons in the eye that register ambient light and signal to the brain's circadian clock. So this is in the mid-90s. Those cells weren't discovered till the early 2000s. And what's interesting is all the staff of the sleep laboratory would go outside from the basement and would look at the sunset. And I was like, "Why are we doing this?" And they said, "Oh, this sets your circadian rhythm. It's well known. Ideally, you do it in the morning as well." And that's when I started the practice.

These are serious scientists — Howard Hughes investigators, members of the National Academy. Now we understand all the mechanisms, but I point that out because I think a number of people think that you need all the mechanistic science worked out first. There are certain practices that are so very clearly good for us where the mechanistic data come later.

So I try and do that in the afternoon. Sometimes I'll stand outside with a cup of tea or something. I do stop drinking caffeine about 2:00 p.m. That's about the latest. Otherwise, I do have trouble falling asleep.

Blue Light: Individual Variation

Here's an important thing that also came out of a conversation between Elon and Mark online. I think — oh no, it was Alex and Mark. And Elon jumped in. Mark said, "I stopped drinking because of Huberman, but I'm not going to do any of that blue-light [stuff]" — that's what he said. So —

Host: That sounds like him.

Huberman: His words. There is huge variation in terms of people's sensitivity to blue light at night. A lot of people think the lights have to appear blue, but bright lights, white lights, yellow lights all have short-wavelength light. So that's what we're talking about when we're talking about "blue."

Some people are very sensitive to it. It spikes their cortisol. It disrupts their sleep even as little as 100 lux, which is very dim through closed eyelids. Other people are less sensitive to it. We don't know how that works. It doesn't seem to be related to how light or dark somebody's eyes are. My eyes are just very sensitive to light, so that at night if I get a lot of bright overhead light, I have trouble falling asleep, or I fall asleep and wake up in the middle of the night. So if I dim the lights or wear wind-down glasses, I feel much better.

I think there is a split. We don't really know what the underlying reasons are.

Huberman: You need some short-wavelength light during the day on your skin and in your eyes to generate vitamin D, for instance. UV light is not across-the-board bad.

I should mention that when the sun is low in the sky, the UV index is very low. One of the reasons that you can look at the rising sun or the setting sun and it doesn't hurt your eyes is because of this phenomenon of atmospheric Rayleigh scattering, where the short wavelengths including UV are filtered out. When the sun is overhead, it's extremely bright. It's painful to look at. That's because you're getting a lot more of the shorter-wavelength light reaching your eyes. So if people are concerned about UV exposure, morning and evening or late-afternoon light exposure is very low UV — or you can just look at the UV index with a Google search or something.

Three Habits for a Healthier Life

Host: Okay, you do still health research for a living, and it's resulted in a lot of recommendations and protocols. If you had to recommend three things to people — ranked, no more than three — to live a healthier life, what would those three things be?

Huberman:

  1. Morning bright light, ideally from sunlight. In the first 30 to 60 minutes after waking. If you can't get it from sunlight, get a 10,000 lux artificial light, then get some sunlight if and when you can.

  2. Do the weight-training protocol I talked about earlier. It will completely change your life. If women are concerned about being too bulky — it's not going to do that. In terms of body recomposition, mood, brain health, you're not going to find a more potent stimulus.

  3. Figure out some way to make the sleep you can get the highest quality sleep. I sometimes get appropriately attacked for — "Hey, I've got kids, I've got a busy job, the neighbors are always making noise, what do I do?" Find a bedtime to shoot for most nights that allows you to get the most deep sleep. Don't miss that window.

And here I'm lumping in a fourth, but really: learn to get to sleep and fall back asleep. I'm not going to say "get perfect sleep," because you'd have to organize your whole life around that. I'm going to say do long-exhale breathing to slow your heart rate. Learn how to close your eyes — and this sounds so kooky, but it's grounded in what we understand about the underlying circuitry — moving your eyes back and forth and up and down when you're having a hard time falling asleep because your mind is racing will greatly help you fall asleep. And it's not mysterious why: in order to fall asleep you need to forget about your body position, and this confuses the vestibular system.

In fact, if I may — one of the technologies that I'm most excited about (and I'm hoping a16z will invest in this; I don't have a company related to this): sleep masks that induce sleep by controlling eye movements in certain ways.

Huberman: How cool would that be? And measure rapid eye movement sleep and slow-wave sleep. I think that's the next wave of technology that we all desperately need.

But the three things are, as I said: morning bright light, resistance training (still do cardio if you want to; the resistance training is the really sharp blade of health improvement), and find a way in your current circumstances each night to get the highest quality whatever — 5 hours, 6 hours, ideally 8 hours. Know that the things you can do in the context of the hotel room, the airplane you happen to be on — figure those things out. Then you'll start to experience the flexibility that comes from not fearing that you didn't get the perfect night's sleep. Like, I'm fine on 6 hours, because I know how to regulate my energy during the day if I just got 6. I would love to get eight, but I can't tell you the last time I got eight solid hours without getting up once or twice. It just doesn't happen.

Three Habits for Cognitive Performance (For Founders)

Host: We have a lot of founders who listen to our podcast. If you had to narrow it down to three pieces of evidence-based habits for cognitive performance, for founders or anyone, what would those things be?

Huberman:

1. Know Your Windows of High Cognitive Capacity

First one: know when your windows of high cognitive capacity are. This is different for everybody.

For me, I can feel 11:00 a.m. come around. I wish it was 7:00 a.m. when this happened — and I get up pretty early. I tend to get up between 6:00 and 7:00 a.m. Sometimes if I go to sleep at 9:00, I wake up at 5:00. If I go to sleep at 10:00 or 11:00, I tend to wake up at 7:00. And I wake up in the middle of the night, like I think most normal human beings — I use the restroom and get back into bed, 90% of the nights in my life.

So I know that in the morning I tend to have a lot of sleep inertia. I need to do these things — I'll do the exercise, etc. Part of the reason I do that is I know if I exercise before 9:00 a.m., I have a lot more energy and focus for the rest of the day. If I exercise at 11:00 a.m., which is kind of peak of my morning energy, at 3:00 in the afternoon I'm exhausted. This is just me, but other people might be different.

Some people find that peak for work lies at a certain time of day. For me, there are two times. It's really between the hours of 9:30 a.m. and 12:30 p.m. That window is crucial. So I have to be very careful that I'm not exercising in that window, because, like most founders, I don't get paid to exercise. This is very important. If you're going to do things for your health, they have to support the other areas of your life in a way that feed back onto something where your company succeeds, and then you actually have the resources to maybe change your schedule someday. Otherwise, if people are trying to just pack all these protocols in, they're just going to deplete themselves.

So for me, it's 9:30 to 12:30. That's one key window. Then I tend to have a little bit of dip in focus and cognition. And then somewhere in the late afternoon, right around 4:30–5:00 p.m., I start to get another window that lasts until about 7:00 p.m. or so, right before dinner. And I have to capture that. I've learned that my mind is better at certain things in those two windows.

Again, this is highly individual. For some people it might be the middle of the night. So knowing yourself — and this might change across stages of life or life circumstances — but knowing yourself and really capturing those two and protecting those times as if they were the most important times of the day. Maybe only your family members and co-workers can access you with emergencies during those times. For most people, it's going to be about twice a day. You might say that's not enough time. That's 3 hours of focused work, and then maybe 3 hours again in the afternoon or two or three. I don't know many people that are completely focused for 8 or 9 hours a day without the next day being completely shot.

Host: I agree.

Huberman: Especially if you use pharmacology — and we could talk about pharmacology. Caffeine I sip on throughout the day as I said till the afternoon. If I exercise in the morning, I tend to not need as much caffeine in the afternoon. I'll just hydrate — electrolytes. A lot of people will find that just hydrating better will increase their alertness.

So figure out when you can exercise so that it gives you more energy, and protect those — I call them "work bouts." I literally think of real work as a fight.

My friend Rick Rubin likes to wake up and move into the day with a lot of peace and calmness, and then his work block generally is in the afternoon. I know this because I've spent a lot of time with Rick. That's when his mind is sharpest, and then he tapers off in the evening, but he's working extremely hard in those hours, and he knows when those fall. I'm a little different. Mine come in two bouts. But they are like bouts. You should think of them as a fight.

Here's the real danger. If you're in one of those windows and you allow your attention to be captured by something that's not worthwhile toward your company build, you're not just losing that three or four hours, because the productivity that comes in those three or four hours is exponentially greater than the productivity that comes from doing that work at some point later, or the catch-up work. It also prevents you from having a healthy personal life. So you have to protect that time as if it were the most important thing, with the exception of family emergencies.

2. Daily Internal Check-In (Not Quite Meditation)

Okay, so that's number one. The other one is — it used to be in the valley (I grew up down here) that everyone said no successful founder is a non-meditator, or they all meditate. I said, "Can that really be true? Are they all these meditators?"

I think what that's really about is that you need to be pretty good at being in the whole stimulus-response mode of living life. You have tasks, you're handling tasks, you're organized. But I think once a day it's very valuable, even if it's for just a few minutes, to just get out of stimulus-response and going kind of inward and checking with yourself whether or not you're allocating your energy properly.

Some people are more prone to getting pulled into conversations and dramas and what they see. Sometimes people will see things online that has a long tail in their nervous system. And there's data on this, showing that your thoughts in 2 hours are sort of seeded by what you saw in previous hours. Some people are more of like square waves when they compartmentalize better. Other people, like myself, if I have a conversation earlier that's of interest to me, it sort of lingers, and it will impact the next thing that I do.

So I think these moments where you just kind of check in and separate yourself from all the inputs allows you to pivot more effectively. We don't really have formal protocols for task switching, but this is extremely important for company founders and employees across the board. You have to be able to cognitively task-switch. We need more data on how that's done, but it certainly involves returning to some state where there aren't any inputs. I think this is very important.

In fact, Rick and I have been kicking around some tools that are not meditations, not yoga nidra, that would allow you to kind of program your mind for what comes next. If you think about it, it's 2026 — why in the world are we sitting down to do work and just going, "Okay, now I'm going to be focused. Now I'm going to be creative"? We should have ways to control neural activity that would allow us to access those circuits more quickly and more deeply.

When it comes to "okay, now we're going to sit down and do this type of task" — we're still not clear what the patterns of brain activity that you want really are. For focus, you want to be alert but not too alert. It's the inverted-U-shaped function: over that hump you're highly distractible; too sleepy, you're highly distractible. It's that sweet spot. So that's a really exciting area of neurotechnology. It'll happen first with sleep. And with AI, it will be able to calibrate and say, "Oh, we need to make the eye deflections broader in order to induce [sleep] when you're in this particular state."

3. Organize Like an Athlete; Build Non-Destructive Recovery

So, you asked about tools for founders. I think organizing your day in a way that is tailored to what's most important to you — setting personal life differences aside, you need to get your best work done twice a day. You need to treat yourself like an athlete.

It occurred to me when I was running a lab, but also when I was a postdoc — if I get to bed earlier at a conference, I'm going to be sharper the next day at the conference. Conferences were really important to me then. Likewise with doing experiments: I can get twice as many experiments in as everybody else. Not just by working really hard one day, but I'm getting an extra hour of work done.

Of course, I was also the person who'd sometimes bring my experiments to seminars. I was like, "This is crazy. I need to run some immunochemistry. Why wouldn't I bring it to the seminar?" I'd heard someone else did that. I was like, "I'm going to just bring my trays and transfers." If everyone started doing that, it'd be problematic. But the point is that if you take yourself and your work really seriously, you need to organize your day that way.

I do think having one day per week where you just completely disengage from things can be very beneficial for your ability to re-engage. My dad's a scientist and he worked at Xerox PARC for a long time, and now he's doing other things. Long ago he said, "You have to be a long-distance runner. This is an endurance event."

Host: I agree.

Huberman: The best advice I ever got — and this will be the last piece on this — is from a neurologist at UC Berkeley and UCSF, Bob Knight. Some years ago, very talented. I asked him for advice as I was starting graduate school, and he said:

"Figure out the maximum amount of real work that you can do every day consistently, and then figure out some non-destructive way to reset yourself every single week."

I thought, "Okay." For me at that time, I could work very, very long hours. I said, "How do you reset?" He said he likes fishing. I'm okay with fishing, but I'm not into — I know what I like. I like to hike. I like to get into nature and spend time with people while I do it. So I figured out I could work X number of hours per day 5 days a week, sometimes a little trough in the middle of the week, and I just stuck to it for 25 years.

People who take a ton of stimulants and just blitz, blitz, blitz, blitz — these are the same people that crash and disappear. So you have to figure out and build your capacity. I think we don't talk about that enough, because people really differ in this regard. Yes, you have to work extremely hard. You have to be extremely focused. But you also have to figure out how long you can keep this up.

item.description:
## 一、冥想的"乳酸悖论"：Huberman 悄悄颠覆了整个东方传统的西方理解
最惊人的不是他讲了什么，而是他**用生物化学术语重新定义了冥想**——"心智的乳酸"（lactate of the mind）。
通常我们以为冥想是"让心平静下来"，但他从威斯康辛的脑成像数据里拿到的结论恰恰相反：**冥想的收益不来自宁静，而来自观察混乱时那种"几乎受不了但不动"的张力**。这与肌肉训练中乳酸堆积触发肌肥大的机制在信息结构上完全同构——不是去除刺激，而是**承受刺激而不反应**，由此激活适应回路。
这里埋着一个反直觉的推论：那些自称"冥想从来静不下来"、因此放弃的人，其实一直处在最高训练强度区而不自知。他们以为自己失败，实际上是在做深蹲时抱怨"腿很酸"——那个"酸"就是训练本身。
---
## 二、他身上藏着一个认识论级别的时间悖论：实践比机制早了 15 年
他顺口提到一件被低估的事：**90 年代中期，斯坦福睡眠实验室的研究员们——包括 Howard Hughes 研究员和美国科学院院士——每天从地下室走到屋外看日落。他们不知道为什么有效，但他们做。**直到 2000 年代初

item.title: [Lex Clips] Infinity explained: It broke mathematics | Lex Fridman
item.dc:creator: Lex Clips
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

瑞士奶酪：一个被双重借用的隐喻

说话者用"瑞士奶酪"来形容学生在微积分前崩溃的知识结构——几何 81 分、三角 75 分，每一科都有洞，当这些洞在某一刻对齐时，整堵墙塌了。

但他可能没意识到：这正是航空和医疗事故学里最著名的"Reason 瑞士奶酪事故模型"——重大灾难从不是单一失误造成的，而是多层防御上的孔恰好对齐。换句话说，一个学生在微积分课上的崩溃，和一架客机的坠毁，在结构上是同构的事件。这暗示了一件更深的事：数学教育的失败机制不是"没学会"，而是系统性脆弱——它需要被当成风险工程来设计，而不是当成知识传递。

牛顿的"离世幽灵"与量子场论的虚粒子

牛顿说的"ghosts of departed quantities"——那些"除完零之后才有意义"的东西，被当时的人嘲笑为神秘主义。可仔细看：这几乎就是现代物理里"虚粒子"的直觉——存在于过程之中、不存在于端点之处的实体。

这里有个让人脊背发凉的跨领域呼应：人类数学直觉领先严格形式两百年。牛顿"错"的方式，后来成了量子场论"对"的方式。这说明一件被职业数学家极少承认的事——有时候直觉的分辨率高于当时可用的符号系统，而历史的工作就是追上那个直觉。Lex 的嘉宾用"infinity had to get professionalized"轻描淡写地带过了这件事，但那是一场认识论意义上的驯化。

数学的多次死亡：一个被遗忘的库恩式真相

嘉宾最惊人的一句话是："So it turns out math has been killed multiple times before"——而且"it's only a scratch"。

这里藏着一个数学共同体不愿公开承认的秘密：数学的自我叙事是"累积的真理"，但它的实际历史是库恩式的范式革命——比物理学的革命更彻底，因为连"证明"这个最底层的概念本身都被重写过。Cauchy 和 Fourier 证出互相矛盾的定理，不是哪个错了，而是"连续"和"极限"这两个词的社会契约还没建立。

更出人意料的是：19 世纪对无穷的职业化，和同一时期医学、法律、心理学的职业化是同一场运动。韦伯称之为"理性化"。换句话说——Weierstrass 的 ε-δ 定义，和现代医院的病历格式、现代法庭的证据规则、现代公司的会计准则，是同一股历史力量的不同切片。数学看似最超脱、最永恒，却恰恰在那个世纪被迫完成了它的"科层化改造"：从绅士之间的直觉共识变成对陌生人也能成立的证明。

今天博士一年级的课程，几乎全部是 19 世纪那场屠杀留下的尸检报告。这是数学界的"创伤后应激"——只不过装帧得很优雅。

📝 转录文本

On the Reality of Infinity

— What's your relationship like with infinity? Is it real to you, or is it a nice thing to have as part of proofs?

So much of modern mathematics is exactly dealing seriously with infinity, right?

The Calculus Wall

One of the first times people really start to hit a wall in their mathematical education is when they hit calculus, and there's sort of several reasons for it.

One is they probably have a lot of gaps in their understanding in previous — you know, they got an eighty-one on geometry and a seventy-five in trigonometry or whatever. Those are pointing to gaps in their understanding that all of which is gonna come together in one fell swoop, and the Swiss cheese is just, you know — not, they're not able to cross that threshold. That's one issue with calculus.

The other issue with calculus is the first time you deal seriously with infinity. You have to add up infinitely many infinitely small things and get a finite number and have that number make sense.

Newton's Ghosts of Departed Quantities

Human beings — Newton and Leibniz — did not understand infinity the way we understand it today. They had an intuition for what it's supposed to represent. But if you read Newton, I mean, Newton in his time was ridiculed for the way he wrote about, you know, the ghosts of departed quantities.

You have to divide zero by zero — and have it make sense, and you don't do it when they're zero. You do it after they become zero. I mean, the way that he was trying to write about these things turned into the crisis in the nineteenth century when Cauchy and Fourier proved conflicting theorems.

The Cauchy–Fourier Conflict

Cauchy said: you have a sequence of continuous functions, and you take the limit of continuous functions, you're gonna get a continuous function, right? Limits are a continuous process. Continuous functions are continuous. The answer has to be continuous.

And Fourier says, "I'm gonna add up a bunch of sines and cosines. Doesn't get more continuous than sines and cosines, and I'll get a sawtooth. I'll get whatever you want. I'll get a discontinuous function in the limit."

They broke math.

The Professionalization of Infinity

— So that's when we had to start facing — it was no longer okay to think about infinity the way Newton and Leibniz and the entire — Euler's entire, what, thousand some odd papers lived in a world where infinity was something you play with, and in the nineteenth century, infinity had to get professionalized.

Math Has Been Killed Before

— So it turns out math has been killed multiple times before.

— That's right. And somehow it's only a scratch. The vast majority of our first-year PhD courses are the result of crises that happened in the nineteenth century. And math — where math was destroyed and had to be rebuilt from scratch.

item.title: [Lex Clips] The hardest problems AI can't solve yet - mathematicians explain | Lex Fridman
item.dc:creator: Lex Clips
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

当"奖项"消失时，佩雷尔曼并不古怪——他只是提前到达了

这段对话里最耐人寻味的反讽是：数学界正在讨论"菲尔兹奖是否还有意义"，而佩雷尔曼早在二十年前就单方面退出了这套奖励契约。大家把他当作"怪人"，但从系统论上看，他不是异类，他是时间旅行者——他现在的状态，正是整个共同体即将被迫进入的状态。当 AI 能日常地解决重大问题时，奖项作为"稀缺性仪式"的功能就坍缩了，只剩下 Alex 所说的"庆祝活动"本身。换句话说，佩雷尔曼不是拒绝了奖金，他是在示范一种后奖励时代的职业身份——价值由做本身构成，而不是由共同体颁给你的徽章构成。整个数学界正在被迫学习佩雷尔曼早已内化的态度。

一个被颠倒的 Anna Karenina 定理：难题都难得一样，易题各易各的

Tao 顺口引用托尔斯泰"幸福的家庭都相似，不幸的家庭各有不幸"，但他真正说的其实是它的反转版：难题之所以难，结构上都一样（都能被嵌入密码学那种被精心设计的最坏情形）；而在实际中出现的"容易的 SAT 实例"，却各自容易得完全不同——编译器寄存器分配的容易和图着色的容易毫无关系。这一点跨到生物学会非常震撼：进化空间也呈现同样的不对称性。致死的突变大多以相似方式致死（蛋白质无法折叠、关键酶失效），而"成功的生命"却以千奇百怪的路径幸存。换句话说，自然界和算法界共享一条隐藏法则——失败具有共同结构，成功各有其巧。P vs NP 真正的突破也许不来自证明 P ≠ NP，而是来自分类学：建立一种"容易性的本体论"，像林奈给物种分类那样给"可解性"分类。

"乘法表—计算器"这个类比其实偷换了维度

Alex 用七十年前的计算器争论来安慰自己——"当年没学乘法表的孩子吃亏了，所以今天的孩子也该学"。这个比喻听起来温和，但它藏着一个未被察觉的维度错位：乘法表位于认知的地基，LLM 位于认知的穹顶。计算器把一个"低于你理解力上限"的任务外包；LLM 却把"高于你当前理解力上限"的任务外包。这在心理学上是两种完全不同的依赖——前者释放工作记忆去做更高阶的事，后者跳过了形成更高阶思维所必需的"挣扎窗口"。更深一层的跨领域联想：柏拉图在《斐德罗篇》里反对文字的发明，理由一模一样——"人们将不再记忆，只会查阅"。两千四百年来我们反复进入这个循环，而每一次新工具真正改变的，不是人学不学得会，而是谁被允许挣扎。富裕家庭的孩子依然会被要求背乘法表、手推证明、读完一整本难书，因为挣扎本身被重新定价为奢侈品。AI 时代真正的分化，可能不是会不会用 AI，而是谁还被保护在'必须自己想'的温室里。

隐藏的洞见：我们正在要求 12 岁的孩子具备中层管理者的能力

Tao 一句话带过——"我们要求本科生具有 critical advisor skills"——但这句话应该被放大。所谓 advisor skills，是你不是专家时如何从专家那里获取信息、识别胡扯、知道什么时候该追问。这在传统上是 CEO、董事会主席、资深记者、博士生导师才需要的能力。我们正在把管理学最硬核的一项技能——"管理比你聪明的下属"——下放给 12 岁的中学生，而且是在他们的前额叶还没发育完的时候。这是人类教育史上从未试过的实验。它要么会制造一代"认知经理人"（擅长协调、鉴别、提问），要么会制造一代"认知消费者"（只会点头、点赞、复制粘贴）。中间地带几乎不存在——这就是 Lex 直觉里"中学问题比大学问题更难"的真正原因。

📝 转录文本

On the hardest unsolved problems

Lex: Um, what do you think are the hardest problems before us right now in the space of mathematics — or, maybe for Steve, more in the space a little bit broader outside of mathematics? What do you think is the problem that's unlikely to be solved in the next year or two?

Steve: I'm still going with P versus NP.

Lex: You think that? By the way, do you think it's possible it turns out that P equals NP?

Steve: Sure. Anything's possible.

Lex: What does that world look like to you?

Steve: So it depends on what the running time of the algorithm is. So it could be so large that it's impractical, and then it doesn't really matter that much. It's more of, you know, a tidal wave for the theory research.

Tao: Yeah, but that seems like a very important problem and very hard to solve. In fact, I remember back when I was a graduate student, there was an attempt on P versus NP, which was actually semi-serious. Some people started — all having rumors that, "Hey, has it been solved?" And my first reaction was, "No, it has not been solved." And I remember spending an afternoon thinking about — the betting markets were still pretty new then, so it wouldn't let me take a counter bet to "P versus NP has not been solved." So instead, what I did was I bet on all the other Millennium Prize problems, 'cause that seemed like a good way to hedge, because the question was: which Millennium Prize problem will be solved first?

Lex: Mm-hmm. But is it possible that P equals NP in the real way? So there's something deeply that we don't understand about complexity theory, about computer science, about algorithms, where there are fast algorithms for satisfiability?

Hard problems vs. easy instances

Steve: So I think there are two threads in there that are important to tease out. So first, it seems — at least so far — that you can always manufacture hard instances of problems, and we use that to great effect for our cryptography systems. But it does seem like in practice, a lot of problems are much easier than we give them credit for.

So for things like SAT, one of the places where they come up is in compilers and register allocation, and SAT solvers are amazingly effective at solving those kinds of SAT problems. Now, we don't really know what makes those problems so eminently solvable compared to the other hard problems that come out of cryptography or other areas. But it could be that in practice, a lot of the problems that we model in the worst case are secretly easy, and that the harder part is articulating what kinds of structures they have that makes them eminently easy — but that there are still a rich source of hard problems that we can do a lot of things with, like building cryptographic systems out of. That would be my bet in the world we live in, but that's just a guess.

Lex: So maybe there's some, um, way to basically quickly classify that this particular example of the problem is easy. So, like, be able to identify quickly that this is one of the easier instances. Like, there's a whole, like, set, subset.

Steve: It could be. So I'm reminded of the opening line for Anna Karenina. You know, every happy family is happy in the same way, and every unhappy family is unhappy in their own way. I think my worry is that, you know, many problems are easier than we make them out to be — but they're easy for very different reasons. Now, that doesn't mean that algorithmic perspectives aren't useful in trying to classify or developing an ontology of what those structures are. But I think the types of SAT problems that come out of register allocation are very different than the other SAT problems that come out of other domains, even though they might be easy too. I just think they're easy for very different reasons.

Lex: So to you, the hard problem's P = NP. So you'll be impressed if that, within the next couple of years, that falls—

Steve: I would be pretty impressed.

Lex: Alex, what's the hard problem that you'll be impressed by?

Alex: Well, I'm already impressed with quasi-RH, but it's not RH. You know, it's hard to think of a more iconic problem to say this is the hardest, you know, one of the hardest problems in mathematics. It's been around for so long and—

Perelman and the question of prizes

Lex: What do you think on that — uh, sorry, it just made me think of Perelman. Credit — like, uh, the Perelman — what did he say? He said, "If the proof is correct, that's all the credit I need." He famously turned down the Fields Medal. What do you think he would say about all this, the OpenAI drop?

Alex: I mean, I have a very hard time predicting what Perelman will do or say. I did not know he would decline the Fields Medal. I did not know he would decline the million-dollar Clay Prize, so—

Lex: What do you think about that in general, like turning down a prize? A few folks have done that in, in history of prizes. They're all about prize—

Alex: He's the only one who has turned down a Clay Prize — and the million dollars. Uh, what do I think about it? Mathematicians are weird.

Lex: Okay. Yeah.

Alex: We — to each his own. We love diversity of opinions and thoughts, and that's what makes the world of mathematics so wonderful: there's so many different kinds of people, and we let them all in.

Lex: I mean, these questions are kind of coupled with what the mathematics community is dealing with now and the value of prizes. Because in some sense, what his particular world view is aligned with this new world view that the mathematics community is entering, which is, like, it doesn't even make sense — the Field— I don't know if there'll be ever another Fields Medal given. And so you're like, "We're entering Perelman world."

Is this the last Fields Medal era?

Alex: We were talking about that explicitly this summer when the Fields Medals — you know, the last round of Fields Medals was given out in Philadelphia — and there was definitely a question, you know, 'cause people were following the progress. There hadn't been this latest bit of progress that really puts the question in the most powerful way possible. But already this summer, we were thinking, "Is this the last time that a Fields Medal is awarded?"

I sure hope not. But we have to figure out what that means, you know? You have to think more sociologically about what do prizes accomplish. Why have these prizes? The people who win these prizes are already, you know, tenured professors at top places, and they're gonna be doing mathematics for the rest of their lives. Well, Perelman being one very—

Lex: Yeah, exception.

Alex: …very well-known exception. So what do the prizes accomplish? They celebrate the activity. They celebrate. They say, "This is what we think is important. This is, you know, the highest instance of something." And there will still be activities that we wanna celebrate. I don't know if right now they're given out for solving major problems. Uh, solving major problems is something AI systems can do. That's not something that will be rare, and hence, it won't be nearly as valuable as it was in the past.

Centaur math and learning with LLMs

Tao: I would like to think that despite our earlier discussion about the solved axiom — again, I don't believe the solved axiom — and I believe centaur math will be a very—

Lex: Centaur math, okay.

Tao: …like, great way to do math. I mean, that's how I currently feel now. I'm constantly talking to AI systems, and I'm learning a lot of math a lot faster than I'd be able to. Because the way math is written, you know, I sometimes give a paper to a grad student to read, and they come back a week later, and I say, "So how far did you get?" "Well, I didn't really get past the first page, to be honest." "Oh, really? Tell me." "Uh, well, actually, I didn't get past the first paragraph." I say, "Okay, fine. Why not?" "Well, the first sentence is 'by the perturbation theory of non-local systems,' and I don't know what any of that means, so that's, that's kinda where I'm stuck." I'm like, "Okay. You don't know how to read a math paper. You don't — you skip the first couple of paragraphs. Go straight to, you know, Lemma 3. And that's where you can start working and work your way backwards to what the thing is doing."

But in the future, there is no "I don't know what this means," 'cause you just upload it to an LLM, and you start asking it questions, and it will zero in on the zone of proximal development — the place where here's everything that you know, and here's the next thing you need to hear so that you start learning. And if people use that effectively, they can really supercharge their education. I don't just mean kids. I mean old fogies like me can learn new fields.

Um, you know, to learn a field — like this is what our graduate students are going through — they have to completely rewire their brains. Like, learning math is still hard. Up until past the master's level into the PhD level, you are not expected to produce new mathematical theories. Everything that they can do is something that is in a textbook somewhere. And yet it's still extraordinarily, extraordinarily difficult for people to learn to solve problems that are solvable by lots of other people, never mind problems that aren't solved. So learning math is hard. Learning new math is even harder — discovering math, whatever — working out solutions to math problems. But I think it's going to get easier, and this tool is gonna be an amazing resource for people to be able to get to that zone of proximal development much more rapidly and develop their understanding much more rapidly.

Learning by construction, and the motivation problem

Lex: Yeah, I've been having so much fun on topics I'm not even… And I would love to go back to grad school with the tools we have now. But one of the ways my brain likes to learn is constructing visual examples — toy examples, the simplest possible example that still contains the insight there, and especially if it's interactive. Like, if I can, like, move stuff, it's like, oh, you immediately, like, get it.

All these words that the community agreed mean something — you're supposed to know all the notation, all that kind of stuff. If I can just know that this little symbol means this, oh, okay, cool, all right — and just everything kind of falls into place. Also, you fall in love with the subject, and I feel like I can take on any problem that's completely outside of my field. Like, I can understand, like, protein folding. I can, like, play with the parameters and play. I can take a DeepMind paper and actually understand by taking any aspects of it and playing with it — and what's a simple example? Ask crazy, aforementioned pothead questions. So yeah, this is super fun.

The question is whether people will be motivated to learn. This is the problem — the problem of human motivation. That's the real question.

Critical advisor skills, and the middle-school problem

Alex: Well, the key ingredients there are curiosity, asking good questions, and being able to call bullshit. Like, the critical advisor skills of, like, getting information where you're not the expert, and knowing if you need to dig deeper or push back. And I think, you know, there will always be people who are curious and not curious, and who ask good questions and don't. We need to be really promoting that more than we ever have.

It's a little scary to me that we're expecting our undergraduates, our young students, to interact with these tools when they're learning, when their brains aren't fully formed. We're asking them to have critical — not just critical reasoning skills themselves, but, like, advising skills. How do you take in information and tell if it's true or not, or how to question it? And that's a huge task for us in education: how do we train people to have good advisor skills when they're kids?

Lex: Yeah, I think the hardest problem isn't undergrad. The hardest problem is, like, middle school. 'Cause, like, that, I… What is the point at which homework starts getting hard? That, at that point, why do the homework?

Alex: There's the temptation, right?

Lex: That thing will just… At first, I'm saying — see, I've come to appreciate the value of doing difficult things because of all the suffering, but I think because I was forced to. But if you're not forced to do it because LLM can, AI can just help you, I don't know what that, what kind of society that creates.

The calculator analogy — and why mastering it yourself still matters

Alex: But math has the longest head start on that question, because calculators came out, what, 70 years ago? And we still ask kids to learn their times tables. At least some of us do, and those who said, "No, kids don't need to learn times tables," you know, to the extent that teachers listened to that and kids listened to that and didn't learn, they really suffered. There's a great, great amount of human suffering resulting from people saying, "You don't need to know times tables, 'cause calculators can do it."

And my hope is that we can learn from that and say: just because a calculator can do it, you're gonna be much better off if you can also do it yourself. Doesn't mean — if I have to do some calculation, obviously I'm reaching for a calculator. But I could in principle do it myself, and that's what allows — every time you give yourself that skill and master a skill…

Kids love mastering skills. How happy are they when they learn to tie their shoelaces for the first time? You would think it's like, "It's just shoelaces. Who cares?" No, it's the greatest thing ever. You wanna celebrate every little bit of independence, and you want to be able to think. You wanna be independent from the machines. Just 'cause the machine can do something doesn't mean you don't wanna have the capacity to do it yourself.

item.description:
## 当"奖项"消失时，佩雷尔曼并不古怪——他只是提前到达了
这段对话里最耐人寻味的反讽是：数学界正在讨论"菲尔兹奖是否还有意义"，而佩雷尔曼早在二十年前就单方面退出了这套奖励契约。大家把他当作"怪人"，但从系统论上看，**他不是异类，他是时间旅行者**——他现在的状态，正是整个共同体即将被迫进入的状态。当 AI 能日常地解决重大问题时，奖项作为"稀缺性仪式"的功能就坍缩了，只剩下 Alex 所说的"庆祝活动"本身。换句话说，佩雷尔曼不是拒绝了奖金，他是在示范一种**后奖励时代的职业身份**——价值由做本身构成，而不是由共同体颁给你的徽章构成。整个数学界正在被迫学习佩雷尔曼早已内化的态度。
## 一个被颠倒的 Anna Karenina 定理：难题都难得一样，易题各易各的
Tao 顺口引用托尔斯泰"幸福的家庭都相似，不幸的家庭各有不幸"，但他真正说的其实是它的**反转版**：难题之所以难，结构上都一样（都能被嵌入密码学那种被精心设计的最坏情形）；而在实际中出现的"容易的 SAT 实例"，却各自容易得完全不同——编译器寄存器分配的容易和图着色的容易毫无关系。这一点跨到生物学会非常震

item.title: [Lex Clips] Optimal dating strategy - mathematician explains | Lex Fridman
item.dc:creator: Lex Clips
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

婚姻与最坏情况分析：一个被忽略的隐喻滑坡

Lex 自己笑着承认"用最坏情况分析婚姻不是好策略"，但他没意识到的是——秘书问题恰恰是最坏情况分析的伪装形式。表面上它谈"最优停止"，内核却是"假设输入顺序随机、目标是对抗那个全知的 oracle，使我的 regret 最小化"。换句话说，37% 法则并不教你如何幸福，它教你如何在被一个想象中的上帝比较时不至于显得太蠢。这是一种隐秘的防御性数学：我们以为自己在追求最优，实则在购买一份针对"完美的平行宇宙"的保险。

跨领域的奇袭：秘书问题就是机器学习的验证集

这里有一个让大多数人没察觉的同构：秘书问题中那段"概率窗口期"——前 37% 的候选人被强制牺牲以做校准——与机器学习里 train/validation split 的逻辑在数学结构上完全一致。都是：用一部分数据建立一个 baseline 阈值，然后在剩余数据上据此做决策。更惊人的是，交叉验证中"K-fold"的思想也可以回流到人际关系——人之所以会反复陷入类似的恋爱模式，不是因为愚蠢，而是因为单次采样的 37% 太小、方差太大，大脑在无意识地进行自我 bootstrap。所谓"渣男恒定律"，其实是统计学上必然的 overfitting。

真正的反直觉：真实世界中的顺序是对抗性的，不是随机的

Guy Rothblum 在原片中反复强调"假设输入按均匀随机顺序到达"——这是定理成立的命门。但现实恋爱中，候选人会自我筛选自己出现的时机：ta 等你有空、等你脆弱、等你刚失恋。这意味着你面对的根本不是一个 i.i.d. 的序列，而是一个对抗性在线算法问题（adversarial online algorithm），其 competitive ratio 的下界会立刻崩塌。这解释了一个古怪现象：学过秘书问题的人在实际约会中并不更成功。因为他们在用一个假设"宇宙中立"的工具，对抗一个本质上在策略性布置输入的对手。

悄悄埋下的更深命题

Rothblum 提出的"beyond worst-case analysis"其实是在说：最聪明的研究者正在从"我不知道输入长什么样"退回到"我愿意为了多知道一点而承担建模风险"。这是一个认识论的转折——从康德式的先验怀疑论，转向贝叶斯式的温和承诺。而这恰恰是成年人成熟的定义：不再为所有最坏情况做准备，而是敢于对世界下有限的赌注。数学家们正在经历的，其实是心理学上的"从焦虑型依恋走向安全型依恋"。

📝 转录文本

开场：复杂度理论与婚姻的奇妙类比

Lex: when we say a certain problem is hard, you're actually talking about worst case. It's like analyzing, I don't know, I don't know why that popped into my head, but like marriage. It's like analyzing whether I should marry this person or not by saying, "Well, what's the worst thing that could possibly happen?" I think that's for human relationships, maybe it's not such a good strategy. Maybe the average case is a better guide for making decisions. Anyway, I don't know why I brought that up.

Guest: Okay, I have no advice about who you should marry.

Lex: This is com— yeah, complexity theory does not give you. I think there is some— Isn't there a dating is it like an optimal stopping theory of the optimal—

Guest: Secretary problem.

Lex: The secretary problem. There's a lot of different names for it— ... but there is a mathematical way. There's an optimal strategy.

什么是最坏情况分析

Guest: So first, so what is worst case analysis? So—

Lex: Yes, please.

Guest: ...you know, I was describing the SAT problem earlier, and the algorithmic problem you want to solve is, given any formula, you want to decide is it satisfiable or not. Now, what's crucial there is that when I'm asking to solve that algorithmic problem, I'm not telling you anything more about the structure of the formula. I'm not telling you, you know, these are the size of the clauses. They look like this. If I drew a graph connecting them, it would have this topology.

So that's what worst case analysis is about, is it's about the premise that you can treat all of these computational problems actually by ignoring a lot of the fine-grained detail about the individual structure, and you can try and solve them, you know, for all possible inputs. And that's been spectacularly powerful because we've identified lots of algorithmic problems that really can be solved in the worst case and can be solved really efficiently. You know, like finding the max flow, as an example.

超越最坏情况：一个被低估的方向

But the question is, you know, whether or not that's a useful abstraction. So sometimes maybe you really do need to know more about the structure of the instance you're faced with in order to solve it better, right? And that's really an open question. This is the area of what's called beyond worst case analysis, and I would sort of argue that, you know, it's a very important direction for theoretical computer science to go in.

It's hard to figure out what you should articulate about natural problems that is really the right level of detail that your algorithm can exploit it and can do better things than it can in the worst case.

秘书问题与在线算法

But let's use an example. So you were talking about the secretary problem. So the way that this works is it's an example of something called online algorithms. So you have a sequence of options coming. One through N. They come in each time step, and your goal is, you know, when someone comes along, you know their ranking relative to everyone else you've seen before, but you don't know their ranking relative to the people who are yet to come.

And your goal is to, you know, to make a decision when the person comes along, do you commit or do they move on, in such a way that you have a good chance of finding the absolute best candidate.

最优策略与"观察窗口"

And so the point is that you can actually get a constant competitive ratio algorithm that what you do, the best strategy is to wait some amount of the time, not make any decisions, don't accept anyone. And then once that probationary window has passed, you take the first person who's better than anyone you've seen thus far.

And that'll give you a good competitive ratio in the sense that you can prove theorems. Assuming the inputs arrive in a uniformly random order, you're likely to do pretty well compared to as if you knew what that sequence of inputs was in advance.

不确定性的面纱 vs. 建模的艺术

So there's, you know, under online algorithms, there's this veil of uncertainty, which is, I don't know what the sequence of inputs are gonna look like. I wanna do well no matter what that sequence is because, you know, I don't really know how to model what that sequence looks like.

Now, you can instead say, "Hey, maybe the algorithms I derive aren't good enough for my applications. Can I do better by trying to model more of the world around me?" And then there's kind of an art to figuring out what you should model, what you should build into your model, and what you shouldn't. And that seems to me like a tremendously important area, to explore. So for example, one other variant

item.title: [Lex Clips] Do numbers exist? - mathematician explains | Lex Fridman
item.dc:creator: Lex Clips
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一个被你忽略的认知悖论：越"真实"的数字，越晚被发明

这段对话里埋着一个令人毛骨悚然的时间线：复数（想象中的"虚"数）在西方数学家眼中，比负数更早获得合法性。这不是历史的偶然，而是一个关于人类心智的深刻揭示——我们对"抽象"的接受度，竟然高于对"反向"的接受度。一个商人可以想象 √-1 作为中间步骤的符号游戏，却无法接受"欠债 3 块钱"是一个"数"。这暗示：人类的抽象能力是拓扑式的（可以跳跃到遥远的概念空间），而不是线性式的（沿着数轴稳步外推）。换句话说，你的大脑宁愿接受一个外星人，也不愿意承认镜子里的自己。

跨领域连接：石头的"不存在"，与大语言模型的 tokenization 是同一件事

Lex 说的"一块石头不是一块石头，而是一堆原子的集合"——这个观察在三个看似无关的领域中是同构的：

  • 佛教的"缘起性空"：没有自性的"石头"，只有因缘聚合的现象；
  • 量子场论：没有"粒子"，只有场的激发模式；
  • LLM 的分词（tokenization）：没有"词"，只有被人为切分的字节序列，而不同的切分方式会让同一个模型输出完全不同的结果。

整数就是宇宙的 tokenizer。你数"三块石头"的那一刻，你已经在对连续的物质世界执行一次有损压缩——把一个无限维度的原子云，强行投影到一个一维的计数空间。数学不是发现，而是宇宙的 JPEG 算法。而更惊人的是：这个压缩算法工作得如此之好，以至于我们开始以为压缩后的像素就是原图。

出人意料的观察：零的难产，不是数学问题，而是语法问题

人类用了几千年才"发现"零——这往往被解释为"抽象思维的进步"。但真正的瓶颈可能在语言学而非认知。观察一个事实：几乎所有古代语言的句法都要求谓语必须有主语，"有东西"是默认，"没有东西"需要被标记。零不是一个数字的缺失，而是一个需要被语法"命名"的在场的缺失——这是一种二阶抽象。

更妙的对照：婴儿先学会"三个饼干"才学会"零个饼干"，这个个体发育过程精确复刻了人类文明的发展史（haeckel 的重演律在此意外成立）。而在今天，我们正在用 LLM 重演同一个过程——现代大模型在算术任务中，对"没有"的推理能力依然显著弱于对"有"的推理能力。零在硅基智能里，依然是最后一块拼图。

所以当你问"数字是否存在"时，你其实在问一个更深的问题：存在本身，是否也只是人类为了处理稀疏数据而发明的一种默认值？

📝 转录文本

数字的"真实性"悖论

Numbers are a good example — integers. We all fundamentally feel like, you know, counting numbers are real in a very essential way. I can have one rock and two rocks and three rocks, and that is a number of rocks. It is a real number of rocks.

But those are absolutely abstractions that I have created. A rock is not a rock, is not a rock. It's a collection of atoms. It's a different collection of atoms. There's not one rock or two rocks.

数字究竟存不存在？

Do numbers even exist? I wrestle with this. I don't know. Like, do we actually believe that integers are a human creation to interact with our symbolic abstraction of what we observe — quantities?

零与负数的漫长旅程

— I mean, it took humans thousands of years to discover the number zero.

— Right.

— And then negative numbers. Negative numbers were actually accepted by mathematicians in the West after complex numbers...

...were accepted as a mechanism for study, which seems insane, but there's a whole story behind that.

item.title: [Latent Space] Building Legal Agents When You Can't See the Data — Jacob Lauritzen, CTO of Legora
item.dc:creator: Latent Space
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一、最反直觉的洞察：看不见数据，反而是护城河

Jacob 在采访中几乎是"抱怨式"地提到一个现实——Legora 完全看不到用户的真实 trace。律师的数据往往不是律师的，是客户的，受制于层层保密义务。他说这"super annoying"。

但这里藏着一个被所有人忽略的反转：在 AI 时代，"数据盲区"正在悄悄成为战略资产。

  • 绝大多数 AI 公司陷入"数据过拟合陷阱"——看得见用户在做什么，就会不断去 patch 眼前的具体场景，最终做出一堆高度特化的小功能。
  • Legora 被迫走向反方向：他们必须先构建原语（primitives）——list、agent、project、tabular view——因为他们只能通过抽象去逼近用户，而不是通过观察去模仿用户。
  • 结果：Jacob 下意识把自己的 CTO 工作定义为"how do I build a system where we can build a lot but actually only build a few things"。这是被"看不见"倒逼出的架构哲学。

对比：OpenAI 之所以发布 ChatGPT 后一度陷入"做什么都是功能，什么都不是产品"的困境，恰恰是因为他们看得太清楚了——所有用户的 prompt 都在眼前，于是每个 case 都想处理。而 Legora 的"盲"反而让他们像一个必须依赖公理系统的数学家，而不是依赖显微镜的生物学家。

二、跨领域连接：律所合伙制 = 没有区块链的"人力资本代币化"

Jacob 突然冒出的一段话值得反复咀嚼：律所合伙制存在，是因为你不能拥有"人"（slavery is abolished），但你必须让产生价值的人拥有公司，否则他们会走。合伙制本质上是一种"把人力资本证券化"的变通机制。

现在把这个框架和三个看似无关的领域叠在一起：

领域 "不可被拥有"的核心资产 当下应对机制
律所 / 咨询 律师/顾问的脑子 合伙制（让产生价值的人成为股东）
加密世界 社区的"信任"与"注意力" DAO 代币（把社区贡献代币化）
开源软件 维护者的时间与判断力 GitHub Sponsors / Protocol Labs 的 "intangible capital" 实验

三者解决的是同一道题：如何让"长在人脑里的东西"沉淀为可继承的资产？

而 Legora 真正押注的——Jacob 自己说得很委婉但指向很清楚——是用 AI 把律所的"tacit knowledge"（师父心法）变成一套可运行、可迭代、离职带不走的 agent/knowledge graph 系统。一旦成立，律所的合伙制根基就被釜底抽薪了：因为公司第一次拥有了"不随人走"的 durable capital。

这不是"用 AI 替代律师"，这是"用 AI 让律所第一次具备资本主义意义上的资本"。整个西方职业服务业的组织形态可能因此被重写——不是因为律师失业，而是因为激励结构失效。

三、一个让人脊背发凉的用词转向："meat proxy" 与新式奴役

采访里有一个几乎被笑过去的词：meat proxy（肉身代理）——指"坐在机器前把别人告诉你的话输入，再把机器告诉你的话复述出来"的人。Jacob 用它形容"退化后的初级律师"。

但如果你把它和"paralegal gone, junior lawyer gone"的焦虑并置，一个幽灵浮现出来：

AI 并没有消灭初级白领，它把初级白领重新定义成了一种新型的、合法化的、被工具穿透的"中介人"。

这和 18 世纪英格兰纺织业的 "putting-out system"（分散加工制）在结构上惊人相似——不是工人消失，而是工人从拥有判断权的工匠，退化成在家织布但完全依附商人订单与原料的半无产者。随后才是工厂制度，才是工人的组织化反抗。

有趣的是，Jacob 下意识给出了"好 meat proxy"的洗白定义："当你真的懂工具、能主动选择怎么用它，你就不再是 proxy，而是在做 meaningful work。"——这句话听起来励志，但其实是今天所有知识工作者的新型分水岭：要么成为工具的主人，要么成为工具的传声筒。没有中间态。

四、一个几乎没人注意的产品哲学线索：Agent 本身能否就是 API？

Jacob 几乎是半自言自语地说出一句颠覆性的话：

"Can the agent be the API?"

这句话如果成立，会打穿过去 20 年 SaaS 的全部假设。REST、GraphQL、Webhook，本质上都是确定性的、可预测延迟的、无状态的契约。而 agent-as-API 意味着：

  • 契约从"schema"变成"intent"
  • 延迟从"可估算"变成"可能是 3 秒也可能是 3 分钟"
  • 幂等从"由状态机保证"变成"由 2% 的概率失败兜底"

这和 Bezos 的 AWS mandate（所有团队必须通过 API 对外，没有后门）构成鲜明对立。Bezos 当年要求的是确定性契约，Legora 在摸索的是概率性契约。

这里的意外结论是：如果 agent-as-API 真的成立，那么未来 B2B 软件的定价单位也会从 "per seat / per API call" 转向 "per attempted outcome"。这不只是技术变化，是定价本体论的变化。而律师行业——那个全世界最早按"outcome"（contingency fee / project fee）定价的职业——反而可能是最先走通这条路的测试场。

It's not like a software engineering firm or a manufacturer where you have physical assets or some sort of intangible assets that you accrue over time and they pay dividends to the shareholders. In professional services, consultancies, whatever — all of your value is in your people, and you can't really own human capital. Slavery is abolished. You can't own people — but you can rent them, you can pay them money. And so partnerships essentially is a structure where you make the human capital the owners of the company so that they stay.

You can build a system that learns how you work. A lot of firms right now think about: there's the X law firm way of doing things, and we can codify that. We can build a system — whether that's a self-improving knowledge graph or precedent files and documents, where there's a way of working that produces a really good output — and that can be their IP.
