That's changed over the past two years. Now people understand: okay, we need to get on cloud, we need to do all this kind of stuff. There was also a lot more people talking about on-prem back then — that's disappeared completely. People understand that you should just do it in the cloud, and it's safe, and it's probably safer than what you're doing.

So that's changed a lot, but it's only been three years.

Open-Weights Models & Multilingual Transcription

Host: Open source models now are getting really good. How are you thinking about that?

Jacob: We're thinking about — to your point — just bring our clients along on the Pareto frontier, the map of all the models and what they're good at and their latency and their cost and their governance and their regional availability. How do we just optimize across all of that? Some open-weights models are great for certain tasks and then we'll use them there. Some we'll post-train, and some we'll just use the frontier models.

Host: You did some research on this where you were firmly Anthropic at the start of the year. Grok is improving a lot. You want to give an example of a model that wasn't ranked highly overall but you want to shout it out as surprisingly good?

Jacob: Not overall good — Gemini. One of the early Geminis is extremely good for certain types of transcription and speaker attribution. So we use that for transcription.

Host: Oh, so you have a transcript, like a Granola?

Jacob: We actually probably will build a meeting thing, but this is just speech to text, text to speech, like in any other app. And we do also transcribe files if you upload hearings or whatever — we'll transcribe them, put them into text so we can do all of our analysis on it.

Host: No Eleven Labs?

Jacob: No, Eleven Labs for DPA reasons — Data Processing Agreement. Our DPA has very few vendors on it, because we need to keep it super tight on where any data goes. One of the benefits of a Gemini or OpenAI is: they're like, "you come to us, we have most of the things that you need," and that is actually very valuable. Even if it doesn't have to be state-of-the-art — as long as it's mostly good enough for all tasks, then who cares. I should actually shout out also Microsoft's transcription model.

Host: They made one? MyTranscribe?

Jacob: Yeah. It's great. Better than the old Gemini.

Host: At this point, speech-to-text models are pretty much good enough — one word here or there if it's off, that's —

Jacob: No, for sure. Particularly in legal — we had this thing where (I forget if it's in Australia) there's a certain name for a person in court, and it would consistently transcribe it as "condom." There are certain things that you don't want there. So usually you run an LM layer on top of it, you extract some keywords, and then you run the transcription model again with the keywords. That's kind of my workflow.

If you've done this on any large scale, you will pick up tons and tons of transcription errors on any domain that is not average day-to-day conversation. Any sort of jargon — it's going to be tough. Whisper and Eleven Labs still transcribe "Claude Code" as "cloud code." That's actually very common. So there's a lot more to improve.

Deep Dive: Tabular Review

Host: I do want to cover a little bit on the agent product side. We've already name-dropped tabular review, we've name-dropped intake. Let's call it the big two — agent and tabular review. Is that fair?

Jacob: And our Word add-in — a lot of people work inside of Word, so our Word add-in is huge. And Outlook add-in also.

Host: Tabular review is basically a fan-out of a lot across each document. You can ask the same question across all documents, collected on the table, and then work back and forth. A million is impressive. What's hard about this, engineering-wise?

Host: Before we do that, can you just walk through — what is the user experience for a lawyer, and then the flow?

Jacob: A good example is just a due diligence. We need to review all employment contracts, all the supply contracts, etc. So — employment contracts, you put 10,000 employment contracts in there. Each row is one employment contract. For cells, you ask questions. The first column might be "what's the termination period?" And then it's going to fill out for everyone — 30 days or whatever. The next question is "is there an IP assignment clause?" Next one is "how much do we have to pay them if we fire them?" And then it's going to fill out the entire thing.

You can also just ask the agent to do this. If you just drop 10,000 files into the agent and say "do a due diligence on this," it will spin up a tabular review, run all of them, wait for it to be done, then analyze the results and highlight red flags — "okay, the CEO is getting paid an outrageous amount," or "there's this weird bonus structure." Then the agent can draft a memo to send to the client, or it can just do the review and have the user say, "okay, let's look at this — here are the red flags." It's also collaborative so that you can comment on it for other people to look at.

Host: Why do you choose that spreadsheet format?

Jacob: It's super easy to work with. It's really easy to get an overview super quickly of what's going on and to review it. All of the stuff that we produce also has citations back to source documents, so you can review it super easily. You can highlight "these are reviewed," or "these are the ones that are flagged," and you can comment and collaborate. That's much easier than any other form factor that we've tried.

Host: The spreadsheet form factor has a lot of pull in some areas but somehow hasn't really spread. Clay is another one on the GTM side, very known for the spreadsheets. You guys — I don't really know if anyone else does a large spreadsheet AI thing.

Jacob: There was V7 that tried to launch sheets. Even in finance domain I don't really have a top name that does spreadsheets really well. If you have fan-out and you're doing the exact same thing, extracting stuff, it's such a great form factor to understand what's going on.

Host: Do people export to Excel, or are they happy to live in your spreadsheet?

Jacob: People are happy to live there.

Host: Do you use AG Grid or your own?

Jacob: AG Grid — that seems to be the leading one. They've done this for 15 years.

Host: The only other interesting thing for me engineering-wise is the fan-outs. Engineers are well equipped to understand the trade-offs — well, okay, before you fan this thing out on a million documents, maybe test it on two. Does it work before you go nuts?

Jacob: Our tabular view actually will run the first 10 rows. Does this make sense? Did it show us what we thought it was going to show us? That's really good. Also, for people building this, it's really good for them to iterate quickly on the first 10 rows until they're getting the results that they want. Then they can go ham.

Intake, Lists, and the Agent Swarm

Host: Intake — which is your Slack bot. Everyone has a Slack bot. What's different about yours?

Jacob: Ours is just legal specific. What happens with ours — it might also be an interface to the agent, but it's actually specifically to kick off an agent that then adds a task to our lists. So we have this "lists" thing which is like Linear. It will add it to a specific intake list, and then lawyers and agents can go into Legora and be like: okay, these are the things that people are sending to us as our law firm or as our legal team in a big corporate. We can kick off agents for them, we can collaborate on them, we can just mark them as done, and then it gets sent back in Slack.

So it's more of a storefront thing — hey, here's the ticket, I want this thing reviewed. Okay, now here it is. It's back. No one needs to change anything. The legal team just sits in Legora and manages the agents and everything there.

Host: The data structure for this is really interesting — it's like the inbox for all these kinds of queries that can potentially translate into a thing, into something else. Is it hard to integrate all these with all the other features?

Jacob: It's not. We have some primitives that work really well. Lists is a great primitive because it's essentially extremely flexible — it's like a Notion database. You can configure it for whatever you want. We invest a lot into making this super scalable. You can have triggers on them, automations on them. It's a great glue — you can kick off an agent run based on a list if something happens, and then that comes back and populates a field, or adds new documents, whatever.

Just like you might coordinate a bunch of coding agents with Linear or some task management tool, we can do it similarly with lists. Agents can create lists, and lists can create agents, and agents can read lists. So the agent swarm comes alive.

Host: Do people get excited or overwhelmed by that? This is basically end-user programming. You can let people set up crazy automations.

Jacob: Some people get super obsessed by it and they become like influencers. It'd be cool to have Legora influencers. We need the flexibility even if we don't actually expose it to the end user. Let's say this was just all internal — then it's a really fast way for us to utilize people like our legal engineers to build a lot of products extremely fast. You can build custom fund management dashboards. We can have a marketplace of specialized products that we can scale super quickly, because all of our legal engineers can just build new ones. If they're out with a client — "oh, you want your own X, easy, we'll just fix one for you." It's like a Lovable inside Legora a little bit.

If we don't want to expose it, that's also how we build our own custom features. We made another acquisition in the UK called Wexler, and they're doing fact intelligence — mostly for litigation. You upload a million documents for a lawsuit, we extract facts from those with named entities and dates, and then when you have all the facts you can hold them up against each other and see which ones are corroborated and which ones are in disagreement. That's extremely powerful, because then you can also transcribe a court and be like, "oh, he said this thing, but actually the email over here..." If you see it live, it's cool. We can also build on this primitive.

So we can build a lot of really cool things on this one primitive. That's how we think about it: as we scale the company, we have to solve so many things — so I think a lot about how do we build a core primitive that we can scale to many different end products and create very customizable experiences.

Host: So what core primitives do you have, let's just restate for people?

Jacob: Lists is a core one, configurable. Projects, basically containers of files, file systems. The agent, of course — you can kick that off and run that in very different configurations.

Host: Do you have a name for the agent, by the way?

Jacob: No. We called it like "Leia" or we gave it a name — "Legora" would be cool. People used to talk about Legora as a named entity. But yeah, we stopped that. May well bring it back. It might be confusing.

So: list, agent, tabular view — which is arguably an instantiation. You can take this as far down as you want. But those are probably the big ones.

Forward Deployed Engineers

Host: I wanted to talk a little bit about FDEs. Max has talked about that — when you onboard a new big customer, you want to get them value ASAP. How has that evolved?

Jacob: We hired our first forward-deployed engineer — that was our first hire in New York, also YC founder — nine months ago maybe. I'm not actually sure.

Host: Are they considered as legal engineers?

Jacob: No, engineers. But I think about: how do we enable that at scale? A core thing is how can we empower our legal engineers and our power users to customize the product in a powerful way. And then of course we'll still have forward-deployed engineers help out — custom integrations, scoping, figuring out what's possible, feed all that back into core product development. It's almost a first-line / second-line defense: legal engineers should be able to customize a lot of stuff and build a great experience, and then where they can't — or we need to make core product changes or custom integrations — we have FDEs, who also cycle in a little bit behind. Sometimes they'll just work on the product and sometimes they'll work with clients.

Host: Can you walk through an example? You just got this new client — what's step number one?

Jacob: It's very different client to client. If it's a big client and they're super engaged and they have all these dreams of things that they would want to do — or they already have, typically they have already tried to build something and it's failed, "this is a problem that we'd like to solve" — then we'll staff them with legal engineers and a forward-deployed engineer potentially, depending on what the thing is. Then we'll be like, "hey, these guys will come, they'll make you successful. They will sit with all your lawyers and teach them how to use it, figure out all the workflows that you have right now and build them into Legora." Some of that will just be a legal engineer, and some will require a forward-deployed engineer.

Host: What is that separation?

Jacob: Legal engineers configure the product as a power user would. They don't write code.

A forward-deployed engineer writes code into production, basically.

Host: What kind of background do the FDEs normally have?

Jacob: Founders, regular engineers, they're old-school.

Host: D was your —

Jacob: D was our first — two YC companies and worked on search at Meta. She's awesome.

Host: That's a high bar. First boots on the ground in the US. What are some examples of workflows these people are building for clients?

Jacob: It's very different. Some core workflows everyone has, and we can just build in Legora — that could be anything from "this is how we handle these types of NDAs" — you activate it. For most of the FDEs, it's more: there's something that we can't do yet, we need some more flexibility in some of the primitives, or we have this really complex system we need to integrate into, and then they'll build the integration against our APIs, maybe expand our APIs to make that work.

Host: How does the legal structure work there? Because you said you guys yourselves can't even work on deals.

Jacob: So they don't touch the data still. They'll just build the system. But they will also be onboarded like an employee sometimes — they might get a laptop and everything, if they need to. That doesn't happen very often, because usually they'll just build an integration and it works. But they can if they need to.

And we only onboard FDEs into a customer if they're a certain size. It needs to make sense, because our FDEs can also work on core product — it's a constant prioritization thing.

Host: Is there a rule — like Palantir famously had four days on site, one day back contributing to product?

Jacob: No, we don't. To be fully honest with you guys, it's still early days in a lot of this.

Host: Where do you see it headed?

Jacob: I do think it's going to be more — maybe not exactly like Palantir — but we will have a larger, in-constant-circulation group of FDEs that maybe sit with a client for two months to build out this one thing and then go to the next one. I do imagine us rolling in with legal engineers and forward-deployed engineers to work on specific projects.

The API (and the Agent-as-API Thought Experiment)

Host: The API business is actually interesting — because, like you said, you are the CTO / maintainer of the Legora platform. Will we offer everything that we have in the Legora web app as an API?

Jacob: That's not something we're promising now. We do have APIs that you can build against, but not the entire surface of the product.

Host: That's the curious thing. Is that the strategy? Some people will love it, because — I don't have to learn a new tool, I can just use the existing tool I have, and then I just install Legora like the Word document stuff. Other than that, you have to maintain it.

Jacob: Exactly. That's been my thing — that's why we've tried not to do it. We haven't had APIs until — I mean, we started our APIs like six months ago. We fought it for a very long time, mostly because I don't want to be slowed down by having to maintain old API versions for a data model that we've changed. Now we're bigger and things are different. So now it's a cost that we can take on. But when we were 20 engineers, we moved so quickly that we couldn't do this.

Host: It's generally good for all companies to have a platform team and a product team, because then the product team — you have one, but you can easily spin up a second one as long as the platform is not super tight to product. A very simple one is web app, mobile app, right? And then your FDEs are just one more client to the overall platform.

Jacob: Yes. Even the agent, you can think about it this way. There's a harness team that runs the agent, and then you can build a product around it with skills and automations and whatever else.

Host: This is very famously the Amazon / AWS mandate — Bezos was like, "no more back-door access. You only offer other teams your APIs, the same APIs you offer customers. If you don't have it, you build it. And then the customers also get it."

Jacob: I think that's also changing a little bit. One thing we're toying with is: can the agent be the API? I know it sounds weird, but for some of this stuff, what they actually want to do is trigger certain things to happen. It could just be — I'm not saying we're doing this, but it's a thing I'm toying with in my head — could that just be: okay, you trigger the agent and ask it to do this thing? Obviously it's way less efficient than if you just had an API, but something I'm toying with is: how much of our product can just be the agent versus all the other stuff?

Host: You get unbounded execution, cost, and latency. That's the only holdback?

Jacob: And then determinism — maybe 2 out of 100 times it's going to do something whack that we didn't want it to do.

Restraint: The 20 Engineers Fantasy

Host: We're going to go into harness and model fine-tuning in a bit, but there's a product question about restraint — what you don't do. Because there's a prioritization issue. Are you more at a point of "let's say no to most things and only do a short number of stuff," or "no, we want to do more things and we just need to hire 100 people"?

Jacob: I was very strongly the first thing for a very long time. Let's just say no to everything. Keep the engineering team small. One of our presentations — after I'd been at Legora for half a year — I pulled up this slide of the 300 Spartans and said: we're just going to be 20 engineers for the rest of the company's history and we're going to beat everyone who's much bigger. And we're 100 engineers now and it feels like we're way too small.

I wanted to do that. But in the real world, we're in fierce competition. People want so much stuff. I could be a Puritan and be like, "no, we have to stay 20 people and we can only build whatever" — but then we just lose, people would go elsewhere. So we have to build more. My job is to figure out: how do I build a system where we can build a lot but actually only build a few things? That's how I think about my job right now.

Host: Primitives is right.

Jacob: Exactly.

Host: Testing new products, just seeing if there's any pull here — or do you just focus on your main thing?

Jacob: We've made certain strategic bets, but we've not tried anything that we don't have a lot of confidence in already — mostly because we just have a mountain of demand. We want all of these things, so it hasn't really made sense for us to be like, "hey, maybe this thing could work." There's so many people screaming for the other things, so we mostly build those. Sometimes we'll disagree with clients and we'll be like, "actually, I think this thing over here will make a lot of sense strategically," and we'll try to build that anyway.

Host: Strategically for you?

Jacob: Exactly. One of those things was the agent. No one was actually asking for "I want the assistant I'm using to have more agency and do things without me asking it." No one ever. But we were just like: this is definitely where the industry is going; this is going to empower you to do so much cool stuff. Collaboration was another one — we think the industry is going to a place where you can collaborate inside of where you're working, which is Legora, and not in emails and text messages.

Fine-tuning, Harness, Search

Host: You guys said previously — I think Max said this — that early on specifically you guys weren't fine-tuning your own models. Is that still the case?

Jacob: We haven't fine-tuned any models up until now. In the past few months open-weights models have become extremely capable, and so we will do it for certain tasks where we think there's a huge delta between what a frontier model can do at the cost and latency versus what we think a post-trained model can do. Legal research is a great example — it's a fan-out retrieval problem, and you can make a really effective model do those queries super quickly and super cheaply at low latency.

Host: So specifically, you're post-training them to be better at very specific bounded tasks.

Jacob: Exactly. We're not trying to train our own Fable to be the main agent. We won't win that versus Anthropic most likely. There's still a lot of search and retrieval research — or RAG research — to do, which is maybe less glamorous. It's not even model training; sometimes it's just architecture and pipelines.

Host: You did a case study with Turbopuffer. There's also late interaction — do you do that?

Jacob: We actually don't do that, but you're completely right. There's one guy on the team, Son, who just really cares about search, and he comes to me all the time: "we should do these things, there's these new embedding models, we can do late interaction." He actually talked to the Turbo team to get them to build multivector so that we could do these types of things.

But there's loads of low-hanging fruit generally, even before models and even in the harness. If you just want to create a better output for our clients, there's so much stuff that we can do that has immediate impact before training models.

Host: What makes a good harness for the law industry? I'm assuming you guys are making your own custom harness.

Jacob: Of course. The way that we edit files is important. The way we do analysis is important. The way you do legal research is all baked into it. You might have a problem that comes up, see something, then it knows how to go and do the legal research to figure out what the answer is, what the precedent is. That's all very important. Then of course there's all the governance stuff around it as well.

Host: It seems like search is probably the most important tool that you guys are really customizing — because if you can't pull in the right information, you're screwed.

Jacob: It's search, it's analysis, and it's drafting, probably — because drafting a huge contract is actually also not super trivial.

Host: Like what about it is not?

Jacob: You're drafting a huge contract from scratch — then you have to find precedent of how do we do this previously. Do we need this type of clause or not? Specific law firm — how did they do it previously? So I am the law firm, I'm about to draft a huge NDA. NDAs are very simple, but there are contracts that are way more complex, and then you need to find the right precedent first. Lawyers don't just sit and start typing stuff. They figure out what clauses have we used in similar deals — "similar" can mean a lot of different things, as I'm sure you know in search: same industry, same type of companies, same whatever. So you need to identify the right precedent, you might have multiple documents, then you figure out which part should I take from what document. That's actually non-trivial. So it's essentially also a search problem.

Which Model Is Best at Drafting?

Host: Which model's best at drafting?

Jacob: I was faring this yesterday. Definitely Fable and Opus are extremely chatty. I'm sure you guys have known this — they're very verbose. That's generally not good. I've noticed Astra is pretty good at writing. Much more concise.

Host: Are you running like 100 different prompts to —

Jacob: Yeah, sure, we can do certain things. But I think the chattiness / verbosity is actually a little bit difficult for us to do. Probably the next model from Anthropic is going to be much better at this. Astra is actually very concise.

Host: I assume they all have a Slack channel with you and you're telling them this, right?

Jacob: They know this.

Then the other thing that I really care about is hallucination. Do they make stuff up? We have a citation system where we basically check what they're writing has a link. The user has a link they can click, and it highlights with a bounding box in the PDF or whatever where this information was taken from. We can make sure that what it says always is citable somewhere, even multiple layers down. If the agent writes something based on a tabular review, it can cite the cell or the row in the tabular view. You can click multiple layers down and validate it all the way up.

Host: Are you finding that lawyers are verifying that these citations are correct or not?

Jacob: Initially they did, but now — exactly, like hallucinated links to Supreme Court. They don't care. That happens.

It's like coding. You have engineers that just don't give a f and just send agents, and you have people that sit and read every comma. Same. There's just so much — how can one human do that? But I think they probably know, okay, these are the red — this is the thing that's important, let me just double-check these things. "These sound reasonable, so it's probably fine." Just like if you receive something from a junior lawyer — I should double-check this, and this probably is fine.

Host: Any other elements of legal reasoning, or the legal frontier that models are not good enough at yet that you want from the next generation of models?

Jacob: Nothing I can think of specifically right now. Long document reasoning is still difficult. You have a huge contract and you're making edits across it. It's a difficult thing to do for a model today — remember that you changed all these things up here, and the definitions changed, and the ordering changed. The simplest would be one-shot: you feed everything in, one-shot output. You don't do that. You break it up into chunks and then you orchestrate edits.

This is one of those things that are fun to be part of in this industry. For our Word add-in, we've done map-reduce, and there was one big one, and multiple big ones — we keep changing the scaffolding we build around as models change.

Host: I've recently shifted from map-reduce to throw everything into context, and it's better. But it's also different. We had this problem with search — you're searching for certain things in huge contracts, you can map-reduce it, but it might lose some important nuance between the chunks if you just summarize the individual parts up. There are documents where they talk about something at length over two pages, and each individual chunk is not necessarily relevant to the search term, but together it's extremely relevant.

Host: And you guys are planning on how many in New York?

Jacob: A lot. As many as you can. It's aggressive.

Host: That's the whole of corporate law as far as America's concerned. I'm looking forward to you buying a law firm. It's super exciting. Every industry, especially the top like doctors, lawyers, coders, they all have to have two or three agent labs that completely dominate the space. So you guys have a great market.

Jacob: Yeah, I think so. And I think it's only going to get much bigger as law changes and becomes more available to more people.

Host: Also, the problems that you work on are very the frontier of knowledge work. Unless you're literally doing Navier-Stokes and science, other than that most work basically converges to legal.

Jacob: Yeah. Hiring, finance, everything. I just have to consult my lawyer. Which is why I think it's a really exciting thing to work on — because modern society runs in some way on legal.

Host: Cool. All right, that's it. Thank you.

Jacob: Thank you. Thanks.

观看原视频 →
item.description:
## 一、最反直觉的洞察：看不见数据，反而是护城河
Jacob 在采访中几乎是"抱怨式"地提到一个现实——**Legora 完全看不到用户的真实 trace**。律师的数据往往不是律师的，是客户的，受制于层层保密义务。他说这"super annoying"。
但这里藏着一个被所有人忽略的反转：**在 AI 时代，"数据盲区"正在悄悄成为战略资产**。
- 绝大多数 AI 公司陷入"数据过拟合陷阱"——看得见用户在做什么，就会不断去 patch 眼前的具体场景，最终做出一堆高度特化的小功能。 - Legora 被迫走向反方向：**他们必须先构建原语（primitives）**——list、agent、project、tabular view——因为他们只能通过抽象去逼近用户，而不是通过观察去模仿用户。 - 结果：Jacob 下意识把自己的 CTO 工作定义为"how do I build a system where we can build a lot but actually only build a few things"。这是被"看不见"倒逼出的架构哲学。

item.title: [Dwarkesh Clips] Why Old Buildings Were More Beautiful - Robert Caro
item.dc:creator: Dwarkesh Clips
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

美学的秘密不是"便宜劳力"，而是"被浪费的卓越"

Caro 没说出口的真正洞察藏在那段关于15楼雕花的细节里——有人花钱雕刻了只有邻居能看见的石头。这不是"低工资让漂亮变得划算"，而是一个更诡异的经济学现实：当技艺的供给远超可见的需求时，多余的技艺会自动溢出成不被观看的美。大萧条没有创造"美的消费市场"；它创造了一群走投无路的工匠，他们把过剩的手艺像汗水一样留在了城市的每一个缝隙里。换句话说，纽约20世纪初的美，不是被"订购"出来的，是被"挤"出来的。

跨界联想：15楼的石雕 = 哥特教堂顶上的滴水嘴兽 = 寿司师傅的隐秘刀工 = 没人读的开源代码注释

这里有一个横跨千年的系统性模式：凡是技艺过剩的时代，都会出现大量"只有上帝/邻居/后来人看得见的卓越"。中世纪石匠在尖顶上雕刻面朝天空的怪兽；日本寿司师傅处理顾客永远看不见的刀口角度；开源程序员在没人会读的函数里精心命名变量；Robert Caro自己花十年写一本大多数人只读摘要的1200页传记——这些都是同一种现象的不同切片。所谓"美的黄金时代"，从来不是审美意识更高，而是劳动市场更"低效"。20世纪下半叶城市变丑的真正原因，可能不是品味下降，而是劳动市场变得更"精确匹配"——每一份技能都被精准定价到了可见的ROI上，再也没有"看不见的角落"可供过剩才华流淌。效率杀死了隐形之美。

一个令人不适的预测：AI正在重演大萧条的美学逻辑

把 Caro 的观察往前推一步：纽约最美的那些建筑，本质上是人类苦难的结晶化产物。大萧条是一种隐形补贴——政府和开发商利用绝望的失业率，把崩溃的人力成本偷换成了永恒的石头美学。这意味着一个黑暗推论：我们在赞叹的美，其实是在消费前人的灾难剩余。而眼下AI正在对视觉与创意劳动做同样的事——供给过剩、单位成本坍塌、技艺从稀缺变得"用不完"。如果Caro的模型成立，那么未来十年我们很可能会进入一个"数字美学的黄金时代"：屏幕上、游戏里、无人打开的App深处将充满惊人的视觉过度装饰——相当于AI版的"15楼石雕"。只不过这次被挤压溢出的，不是失业建筑师的尊严，而是人类作为创作主体的位置。美再一次是别人痛苦的副产品，只是这次的"工匠"是我们自己。

📝 转录文本

On Moses, the Depression, and Cheap Labor

Interviewer: You're writing not the history of one man but of an era in America. And one of the most interesting things about The Power Broker is — especially in the period in which he's able to accomplish so much so quickly — what's happening, and you talk about this, is the Great Depression. You know, he's hiring thousands of architects, tens of thousands of linemen for pennies on the dollar to do big public works for the city. And so I wonder: how big a part of Moses's early achievements is just that the government, because of the Great Depression, could compete with the private sector for the top talent, and for lots and lots of labor working 24/7 through the winter, moving fast?

Caro: Yeah. Another great — yes. And the answer to your question is that played a big role. Because, like, he needed architects for something — I don't remember what it is, it's in The Power Broker — and they lined up on Fifth Avenue, thousands of out-of-work architects, you know, that he could hire for very low wages. But more than the wages, they were available, because they didn't have anything to do. He was able to hire so many people, and hire and fire them in a ruthless way, making the workmen work hard. You know, he could just fire them. It was the Depression and they didn't have other jobs to go to. I think he used that — yes.

Why Old Buildings Were More Beautiful

Interviewer: So, as somebody who has studied urban development so deeply, here is one thing I'm curious about. You look at the things that were built at the beginning of the last century or before the beginning of the last century — you know, Grand Central Station and all the beautiful architecture in New York — versus the things that are built in the second half of the century. They look a lot less beautiful.

Caro: Yeah.

Interviewer: And the earlier, more beautiful things were built by a much poorer country.

Caro: Yeah.

Interviewer: What changed? Why were we able to build more beautiful things before?

The 15th-Floor Carving

Caro: One thing that changed is you had all these out-of-work artisans who could — we'll just say — carve stonework on buildings.

Like, my apartment is on the 15th floor of an apartment house. Across the street is a building that's 15 stories or 16 stories high, and you say, "Look at all the beautiful carving that's done in the stonework of that building, up on the roof." I said, the only person who can see it is the people in my apartment and the people in the apartment next to him.

Someone was willing to spend that money because the builders who built that could hire skilled people at such low wages that they could make them do the decorations to make a building beautiful — up on floors that nobody's going to see. Nobody's going to see them, because people came cheap.

If you enjoyed this clip, you can watch the full episode here and subscribe for more clips. Thanks.

观看原视频 →

item.title: [Lex Clips] The Physics of Warp Drives: Faster-than-light space travel | Lex Fridman
item.dc:creator: Lex Clips
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一、被"pothead thought"标签掩盖的真实结构性洞见

最有意思的地方不是这个想法本身，而是说话者在陈述之前就先用"pothead thought"给自己打了标签。这是一种典型的"认知自我降级"——用社交性的自嘲来为智识上的大胆下注购买保险。但如果你剥开这层防御外壳，看他实际说的内容：

用 Navier-Stokes 方程的 blow-up（爆破解）奇点，来类比穿越一对相连黑洞时的时空流动控制。

这其实不是胡话。Alcubierre 的曲速度规在数学上本来就把时空当作一种可压缩介质来"塑形"——前方收缩、后方膨胀。这与机翼绕流的压力场重塑在偏微分方程层面具有同构性。Navier-Stokes 的千禧难题（光滑解是否永远光滑）与广义相对论里的奇点定理（时空在何时必然崩溃为奇点）问的是同一类问题：连续场论什么时候会在有限时间/有限区域内自我撕裂？ 他随口说的东西，踩中了两个未解之谜之间罕有人谈论的深层平行结构。

二、一个让我意外的观察：Alex 的"那个眼神"比任何论证都更有知识论杀伤力

注意这段对话的真实动力学：想法没有被反驳，它是被一个表情杀死的。"the look Alex just gave me, it hurts my soul." 然后说话者立刻说"okay, moving on"。

这揭示了一个很少被正视的事实——学术生态系统中的大部分想法并不是死于逻辑，而是死于微表情。同行评审的硬性标准之下，有一层流动得多也残酷得多的"眼神评审层"。这解释了为什么跨学科想法尤其脆弱：它们一定会在某个专家面前显得像 pothead thought，而那个专家只需要挑一下眉毛。

更微妙的是说话者的反击策略——"there's some non-zero probability that future AI will listen to this and say that guy was actually correct"。这是一次跳过当代评审、直接向未来索要认可的赌博。这种"诉诸未来 AI"的修辞，和历史上伽利略式的"诉诸后世"、19 世纪民科的"诉诸真理终会胜利"结构上完全一致——只不过裁判从上帝换成了 GPT。这本身就是我们这个时代一个值得被记录的认识论转变。

三、跨领域连接：厕所、机翼与奇点——为什么科学对话从不"收尾"

这段转录以一个厕所break突兀结束，这看似无关紧要，但其实是真实思维过程的化石证据。

对比一下三种流动： - 机翼绕流：气压场塑造升力，偶尔产生湍流奇点； - 曲速时空：能量-动量张量塑造度规，可能产生黑洞奇点；
- 人类对话：注意力流塑造想法，几乎必然被生理需求打断。

它们都是不可压缩流动被外部边界条件截断的例子。科学史上，牛顿因瘟疫回乡才想通万有引力，庞加莱在跨上公共马车的一瞬间顿悟 Fuchs 函数，凯库勒在火炉边打瞌睡梦见苯环。真正的突破从不发生在"让我们继续讨论"里，而发生在"a quick bathroom break"里——因为前额叶皮层终于松开了对默认模式网络的压制。

所以这段 2 分钟的转录，表面是一个被嘲笑掐灭的疯狂猜想，底下其实同时演示了三件事：一个可能真实的数学同构、一种眼神驱动的知识筛选机制，以及一次被生理终止的典型创造性思维周期。Lex 剪出这一段放出来，可能自己都没意识到他捕获的是什么。

📝 转录文本

Pothead Thoughts: Navier-Stokes, Black Holes & Warp Drives

Speaker A: Yeah. I have a couple of — I apologize — pothead thoughts, 'cause Alex mentioned black holes.

I have a fun thought that maybe the singularity observed with a blowup in Navier-Stokes equations comes into play when we're — as opposed to airplane wings on Earth — we're traveling through two connected black holes in a warp drive that we figure out, and then there's the flow control of spacetime, and that becomes relevant because now you're in a black hole, hence the singularity.

This is the—

For people just listening to this, the look Alex just gave me, it hurts my soul. Okay. So moving on to the next topic.

The Forcing Problem

Speaker B (Alex): But the forcing — you'd need the black hole vortex to also be forced at exactly the right —

Speaker A: The — yeah, the force. Where's the force? I mean, at that point —

Speaker B: How do you… Yeah. You could try to ride it.

Speaker A: Yeah. There's a way — you can make something out of this.

Appeal to Future AI

Speaker A: There's some non-zero probability that future ass that will listen to this, that guy is the one time he said something that was actually correct.

Okay. If it's okay, a quick bathroom break.

Speaker B: Yeah. Sounds good.

观看原视频 →

item.title: [All-In Podcast] Anthropic S-1 Shocker, Greatest Business Ever? Google’s $500B Wipeout, Midterm Predictions
item.dc:creator: All-In Podcast
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一、被忽略的"诡计"：Anthropic 的"末日论者不在场证明"

这期节目里最锋利但最被低估的洞察来自 Sax ——他捕捉到了 Anthropic 一个精妙的叙事结构：它一边喊着要"放缓竞速"，一边比任何人都更凶猛地在推进递归自我改进（RSI）。8 月的博客里已经承认 26% 的下一代模型任务由自家模型生成改进。

但真正值得玩味的是：这不是伪善，而是一种制度化的"不在场证明工程"（alibi engineering）。它和 20 世纪烟草巨头们一边在医学期刊上发警告、一边推广过滤嘴香烟是同构的；也和 Oppenheimer 在三位一体核爆后立刻呼吁国际管控、却继续推进氢弹研发是同构的。

关键识别点：当一家前沿技术公司主动呼吁监管时，监管的范围往往恰好画在它自己已经越过的那条线之内。Dario 的"pacing letter"不是刹车，而是一张提前写好的辩护状——"是你们不听我的，不是我停不下来"。

二、你可能没意识到的：这不是最大的 IPO，这是资本主权的转移

播客里反复提到 Anthropic 的债务和 AI 复合体占到美国国债同期发行量的 30%。所有人都把这当成"系统性风险"讨论，但没人指出背后更深的历史回声——

上一次七八家公司能和主权政府在债券市场正面抢资金，要追溯到 19 世纪的东印度公司和 1870 年代的美国铁路债券狂潮。那两次都以同一种方式收场：公司最终要么被国有化，要么反向把政府变成了自己的功能延伸。东印度公司最后拥有自己的军队和税收权，铁路巨头则在镀金时代直接写美国法律。

这里有一个让人毛骨悚然的跨界连接：七位创始人持有 50.1% 的 F 类投票权，其中 80% 的股份注入"非营利/利益公司"——这不是慈善，这是一个超越国家资产规模的、由七个人投票控制的准主权实体。沙特主权基金是 9000 亿美元，Anthropic 的非营利分支如果真的继承 80% 的股份，上市后将轻松超过。

我们正在实时见证的，不是一次 IPO，而是现代民主国家历史上第一次出现"由七人董事会控制的、规模超过中等国家 GDP 的准主权体"。而选民、监管者、甚至大多数硅谷人都还没意识到这一点。

三、Microsoft 图表揭示的"反鲍莫尔定律"：知识工作第一次被"工业化"

节目里 Jason 展示的图表看似普通：Microsoft 四年内营收从 1980 亿涨到 3320 亿，员工只增加 2000 人。但这张图是人类经济史上一个范式转折的早期证据。

经济学家 William Baumol 1960 年代提出"成本病"（Baumol's cost disease）：服务业和知识工作无法像制造业那样提升单人产出，所以医生、教师、律师的实际成本会永远跑赢工业品。这个定律统治了战后 70 年的经济学。

Microsoft 这张图可能是鲍莫尔成本病的死亡证明。更惊人的是：Freeberg 的"1 美元 Nvidia 成本→18 美元 Anthropic 收入"图谱里，每一层都保持高毛利，意味着这不是零和的边际替代，而是全链条的生产率净增。

跨领域连接：这和 1920 年代"电气化"进入工厂车间的那十年高度相似。电力一开始只是替代蒸汽机，产能提升有限；但当企业重新组织车间布局（从"中心轴驱动"改为"分布式电机"），生产率才真正爆炸。我们现在还处在"用 AI 替代单个白领任务"的阶段，相当于 1915 年的工厂——真正的爆炸要等到企业重新组织工作流。

而 Jason 说"每个员工都有五个 agent"的那一刻，就是 1925 年。

四、一个让 Sax 自己都没意识到的隐藏讽刺

Sax 本季多次强调"Anthropic 在搞 regulatory capture 不道德"，但他同时赞美 Anthropic 的"capital efficiency"。这两件事其实是同一枚硬币：

Anthropic 真正的护城河不是模型质量，而是它比 OpenAI 和开源阵营更早、更深地嵌入了联邦政府的 AI 政策制定机构——前拜登官员整批加入，现在开始挖特朗普政府的人。这种"旋转门套利"正是它能把 110 亿融资只花掉 9-10 亿、却估值 2 万亿的真正原因之一：监管优势让它拿到了别人拿不到的政府和军方合同、拿到了别人拿不到的能源审批优先权。

所以这不是"伟大的生意顺便有点监管捕获"——监管捕获就是这门生意本身的一部分。

📝 转录文本

All-In Podcast Ep. 295 — Anthropic S-1 Shocker, Google's $500B Wipeout, Midterm Predictions

Cold Open: Sax Returns, "Superintelligence" vs. "AI"

The "Phantom $80B Loss" Refuted

Now, there's a few other data points in this S-1 that I think reflected the strength here. Number one is that this $80 billion loss number that we've heard so much about — that the media has constantly been pumping and harping on as proof that Anthropic was either a fake business or that we were in this whole bubble — that narrative basically just got completely refuted. It turns out that that $80 billion loss is a phantom number.

It resulted from the fact that Anthropic had issued convertible notes — basically to their infrastructure partners like Amazon and so forth. And as Anthropic's valuation increased, those convertible notes got recorded as a loss on the balance sheet and that flowed through into the income statement. But it's not a real loss. If they had just issued equity, that loss wouldn't be there. So it was not a cash loss. It's basically a fake number.

And in fact, what was revealed in this S-1 is that Anthropic has been an extraordinarily capital-efficient business. They've raised something like, I think it was around 110 billion roughly, and they've only spent about 9 or 10 billion throughout the entire course of this business. And they still have, like you said, JCal, about 100 billion left of cash or cash equivalents on the balance sheet.

So everyone thought, based on the previous reporting, that this was a huge loss-making business. In fact, it ended up being a very capital-efficient business.

Margins, Compute Multipliers, Recursive Self-Improvement

Then the other thing you saw was that their margins have been improving. I think their gross margin is now something like 85%. And what you see is that for a given task or capability, they're showing roughly 10x improvement year over year in their ability to deliver that task — the cost effectiveness of that task gets 10x cheaper year over year. And that allows them to cut the cost of that model or that task by, let's call it, 50%. The consumer recognizes a huge cost savings, but they are able to realize an even greater savings because they're able to capture the rest of that efficiency in their margin.

That's what we basically saw: again, they're cutting the cost of their tokens significantly, but their margins are going up even faster, because they're able to produce these models that are more and more efficient. They call them compute multipliers. It's very interesting the way that Anthropic sees their business. The framework that Dario has is that there's raw compute, which is scaling very rapidly as a result of better and better chips and more and more of those chips. And then there's the compute multipliers, which are things like algorithmic improvements or better curation of the data, or it can be things like better architectures, more MOE architectures — things that make all these models more efficient. So they're able to give you the same answer for one-tenth the cost, or they can take those efficiencies and create greater capabilities.

This is what we're seeing: that business is actually improving. And I think it is a little bit of a refutation to all the people who've been saying over the past year that they're getting commoditized away, that open models are basically putting them on a hamster wheel where they're basically going to zero on gross margin, or that it's a business that only works because it's heavily subsidized by venture capital.

In fact, I think there's a lot of reasons to believe that Anthropic has a pretty big lead. And if you believe that recursive self-improvement has kicked in, as they are claiming it has, then their lead could actually grow.

Freeberg: Governments vs. the AI Complex

Freeberg, the other issue here is: if we are not spending enough building this out, and a large percentage of the country believes in socialism and is against the oligarchs — both Republican, independent and Democratic oligarchs — this is what they think of us and of the leaders in our industry and other industries. I have a view that humans try to organize into groups — organizations — to try and create power that benefits the members of that group. We form tribes, we form communities. In a sense, governments are a form of an organization. It's an organizational coalition of individuals to achieve an objective — for, in the case of a democracy, the majority of the voters.

As a result, organizations in a world of pseudo-limited resources compete with each other for those resources. Nonprofits, for-profits, governments — they're all effectively competing for resources, because the individuals they represent the interests of are going to be served if they get more resources, get more power, get more influence.

So to some extent, the power of AI — and the influence it enables in terms of media, in terms of capital accumulation, in terms of changing people's minds, in terms of aggregating resources through its competitive capacity, productivity, etc. — makes it a bit of a threat to government organizations. And so to Chamath's point: if one of the manifestations of that is that AI is now accruing more interest from capital than governments, governments aren't going to want to let that happen. The governments, whether they're right or left, are going to fight for the AI to become either part of the government and the government to subsume the AI, or control the AI organizations.

This is why I've kind of argued the case — I think that you're going to end up seeing compute get regulated in the future, where compute capacity is going to be assigned by government and they're going to pass laws to try and do that. Post-production, that is. Meaning they're not going to control the chips, they're going to control the actual compute layer, and they're going to determine who's going to get access to what amount of compute.

I think for governments to compete — I think one of the ways this is going to play out, to Chamath's point, is: in the near term in capital, there's more capital going to the AI organizations than the government. The governments aren't going to want to let that happen, so they're going to try and stop the data centers.

I've never seen something in my adult working life where a complex of a handful of companies are effectively competing with governments now for capital. You've never seen companies in an organized manner have one very narrow thing that they need money for — that is a one-way bet on something that attracts the same amount of money that would otherwise go to a traditional two, three, four, five-year, 10-year bond auction. It's kind of nutty, actually.

And by the way, the story you're going to hear from both sides is a story of which side benefits the people more. That's going to be the narrative argument — which is going to be: every side is going to say the other side's lying. Remember, if one side's lying and another side's not lying, the side that's not lying says, "Hey, those guys are lying," and they're correct. The side that is lying de facto says that the other side is lying because they're liars. So you'll hear both sides screaming, "We are the better path for society. We are the better path for humanity." It's either government or private market AI. And that'll be the huge battle that's going to brew over the next half decade. We'll see.

Max Anderson's Viral Thread: The Vickrey Auction Shift

So you have to go through transitioning out the folks that wanted to own a single-stock bet on search or ads or whatever it was, and now have to move to this other kind of business model. And when you switch buckets like this, a bunch of folks say, "Oh, it's too complicated."

So problem number one is: if you were Google IR, please read this and refute it, or try to figure out how to get in front of it, because every analyst now will try to figure out whether this is true. The second, though, is very narrow: how do you keep Demis at Google? That's it. That's the only task. Pay Thomas Kurian whatever he wants. How do you keep Demis at Google?

Sax: Google Not That Bad — Still Growing

Sax, looking at this business — it's been obviously a journey for the past 10 years to make Alphabet have resiliency in revenue streams, diversify the revenue streams. Do you think there's some great risk here? And would you be long, short, or neutral the stock?

Well, I'm seeing people post that Alphabet's Google search revenue dropped below 50% of total revenue for the first time, and they're making it sound like that's a catastrophic situation — basically playing into the narrative that the search business is going to be disrupted by SI. And that's what it seems like on the surface. But when I dug into the numbers, it didn't really seem that bad at all.

It's true that Google search's relative share decreased, but its absolute revenue still increased. If you look at Google search revenue year over year, it was still up 12%. It increased from 56 billion to 63 billion. So still a roughly $7 billion year-over-year increase in Google search. Google search is still thriving, I think you could say. It's not growing that fast relative to other businesses, but you're not seeing it deteriorate yet.

Again, the reason why the share fell below 50% is because other Alphabet businesses are simply growing much faster. The main one is Google Cloud, which basically doubled year over year to 30.7 billion. So it's the rise of the Google Cloud business that has made Google search seem like it's on the decline — but I tend to think it's a good thing that Alphabet is now finally getting some of these other businesses to really work and to grow fast and to finally diversify the revenue. Diversifying from search has been something they've wanted to do for a long time. They now have all these other segments. You've got YouTube, you've got G Suite subscriptions.

So in any event, I tend to think Google's a little bit oversold on this news today. I agree, although I'm certainly not telling anyone to buy anything.

Since inception and maybe past 10 years — you can pull both charts up, we'll go through them real quick here — but this is just this franchise. The number of searches is still going up. The revenue per search — that issue is obviously the one people are concerned with. But the other side of the coin is absolutely correct, David: the other businesses — they're now only 50% dependent on this business, and that will continue. So for me, I just literally bought some shares. So I'm long. I just bought more shares of Google while doing the show.

Just remember: Alphabet owns 6% of SpaceX and like 15% of Anthropic as well. I think 85% of Waymo as well, right? That's the other piece of this puzzle. Amazon also owns a big piece of Anthropic. They're going to be a big winner.

Midterm Predictions

All right, listen, that's our time here. Do you guys want to talk about the election ahead of Tuesday night and predictions or anything like that? You've been shepherding this guy. What are you guys watching on the midterms? Anything you're keeping an eye on? Chamath, any big contrarian predictions on what might happen on Tuesday?

Chamath: Expecting a Democratic Spritz, FUD Campaign Ahead

It's so interesting. I'm really confused. I've started to stop paying attention just because there's so much misinformation. I thought that we are going to have — and I still think — what Sachs called a "spritz." You know those spritzes? I think it's more of a Democratic spritz.

But when you look at some of the early data — and I don't know if Brett Baier was doing this just to kind of hedge his bets or not, but he did a clip which went viral on X where it just looked like it was going to be a bloodbath for the Republicans and they were going to lose both sides, both the Senate and the House. I think it's still set up to have the Republicans keep the Senate, and the Democrats to have a narrow majority.

Just going back to maybe where we started: the mandate from the Democrats then becomes obvious, which is how do you introduce FUD? And there's one way to do that, which is to start subpoenaing everybody and start to do disclosure, discovery, release document after document after document and let the masses start to churn through this stuff going into '28. So number one: create FUD. And then number two: I think a economic slowdown benefits the Democrats going into the '28 election cycle. So whatever they can do to influence power permitting and data centers — because as we talked about earlier, that's the lever.

So to me, it almost doesn't matter what happens at the federal level, except for the FUD part. I think we now should be paying a ton of attention to what's happening in these governorships and some of these other races.

Sax: Don't Trust the Polls

Zach, has your view changed?

Look, I think that you can't trust any of these polls. First of all, a couple of these polling firms have come out and admitted that they are fake. We literally have a couple of fake polls. There was literally a hoax, and those fake polls were included in those averages. So some of the polls are outright fraudulent, and then the rest of them are well known to have a bias. Patrick Ruffini just did a study of the last three elections and found that three quarters of the polls aired in favor of Democrats. We see this as a recurring pattern. We saw this in 2024 — you had Ann Seltzer, who is supposedly the gold standard, say that Trump was going to lose Iowa by like 10 or something like that, and it turned out to be total nonsense.

So the pollsters have a history of bias, of fraud — or you could just say, for some reason, oversampling progressives in their polls. So I think that people should shut that out. I think that some of them are a tactic designed to depress and suppress turnout.

Republicans just go out there and vote. The economy is not a disaster — that is total fake news. We know what the growth rates are. It was 2.5% in the last quarter, and it's tracking at 3.7% right now. Median household income is almost $90,000 — it's at an all-time high. Poverty is at an all-time low. I think the percent of people below the poverty line is like 12%. It's the lowest it's ever been. It's not just a K-shaped recovery. You're seeing real wage growth in real terms by the average household, which was not true during the Biden years.

So I don't think people should get psyched out by this media operation to make people super depressed about what's going on.

Jason: Trust Polymarket — Democrats Sweep Coming

JCal, any views?

Oh, well, I agree the polling data has been suspect for a long time now across many elections. Wedgewood did this — like they're claiming performance art but they were kind of serious. I don't know who they're working for or what the shenanigans are. But I do trust Polymarket. I think when you look at the Polymarket, pretty clear what's going to happen here.

And by the way, Polymarket was wrong on Bolsonaro — although I think maybe he got robbed. It was wrong on Netanyahu. So the Polymarkets are just a reflection of public sentiment, or public sentiment that's willing to place a bet. Yeah, that could be totally wrong. Yeah, so they were totally wrong about those two national elections.

By the way, I'm not predicting some sort of miraculous Republican win here. It would be very unusual for the Republicans to win a midterm election when they're in the White House. Remember that Bill Clinton and Barack Obama both suffered horrendous midterm losses. Bill Clinton — remember he lost in 1994, he lost to Newt Gingrich, the whole Contract with America. That was the first time Republicans took control of the House for the first time in 40 years. With Obama, one of his midterms was "the shellacking." So it's quite customary for the out-of-power party to do very well in the midterms. I'm just saying that the media is already portraying this as a tsunami or a bloodbath, and I think it might be a more normal midterm result. That's all I'm saying. So I, in any event, I think people should just go out and vote, not get depressed or psyched out by whatever the media is telling them, because the media has a long track record of being wrong and biased.

And JCal, any view that's different than where we've been in the past?

I think Polymarket is going to get it right. I think Democrats are going to win the Senate — 68% chance right now on Polymarket. I believe that. And House, obviously, everybody believes that — 92% chance. So when that happens, and the reason I'll back that up is: if you look at the net approval rating of Trump, all-time low, the country is very upset. And the libs are going to come out in force to vote anti-Trump. The moderates are either not going to show up, and they're not going to be Trump-curious like they were for the second term. "Oh, Kamala was such a disastrous candidate, they were like, 'Okay, I got to try something else here,' and they went for Trump reasonably." If you were going to have a choice between Kamala and Trump, I think Trump's the better choice for most Americans.

And then you have the fractured Republican party, where the America First people feel really like they got rug-pulled by Trump because of the economy — inflation didn't get solved, the wars didn't get solved, and he started another war. So that group's kind of pissed off. So when you put all that together, I think it's a very easy sweep for the Democrats.

What Happens Next: Impeachment, Chaos, New Candidates

Then, if we want to look at what the next two cards are: if you look at impeachment, that process, from what I understand, is a House and then Senate, and it's a legal proceeding. I think we're going to go right back to Trump being impeached, and then both houses are going to do that. It's going to be absolute chaos. And then the Dems are going to start putting legislation out there and force the Republicans to vote against it in order to scuttle JD Vance's chances.

So this is obviously going to be a chaotic two years. You and I — you let me finish. Your life, let me control them. So what's going to happen is to be a chaotic two years. And I think what will come out of that ultimately is: we're going to need some new candidates on the Republican side, and they're going to put the Trump era to bed. And then I think that means they put JD Vance and Marco Rubio to bed, and they're going to need a new champion that is more populist and actually executes on the populist agenda, which they feel Trump represented but didn't execute on. That's my — and that's not my personal belief, that's just my analysis.

Go ahead, Chamath.

No, I think what I'm saying is: you think there's going to be a Democrat flood campaign. They could control the House. They're just subpoena everybody. They're going to subpoena everybody. They're going to look into every single accusation of grift they can think of — and ones that are valid, ones that are not valid, everybody in between.

Join the All-In Live Stream

And so, yeah. We have a really good group, by the way, coming. So join us for the All-In Midterm Live Stream, 8 to 10 p.m. — YouTube, X, and Polymarket. Shane Copeland, Tim Dillon, Rahm Emanuel, Taylor Lorenz. It's going to be chaotic and fun. Taylor Lorenz — she's on a redemption arc, I have to say. She's actually been great on certain topics lately, I have to say. Wow. Base Lorenz coming on the pod. I love it. I love Tim Dillon — he's coming on.

I'm not going to be there. Where are you going to be? What do I need to do a midterm live stream for? Because you're going to lose. Your party's going to lose, so you're not coming. If we outperform, I'll pop in and spike the football. Otherwise, I'm not showing up. That's not cool. Wants to hear you come on. We can drink, we can drink some tequila, we'll have fun with the Sax. Come on, you can't cry. We should all be drinking, by the way. Maybe we should get together at Chamath's house and drink and do it live.

Sax's Closing Warning

I agree with a lot of your analysis about what will happen if the Democrats win, JCal, because they have not changed their stripes. Okay, people are just forgetting who the Democrats are and what they were like during COVID — all the lawfare that they perpetrated, all the crazy woke stuff. It's all there ready to come back. They have not really analyzed why they lost in 2024. They have not really changed or adjusted anything. If anything, they've become more extreme. The DSA is ascendant in their party, as even Gavin Newsom acknowledged. So I think that if the Democrats do take Congress, you're likely to see how nutty they are, and the American public will be reminded of that, and that will be really interesting to see. But that's why there's a pendulum in politics, right? There is a pendulum.

Um, I think we need a — yeah. I mean, I'm wondering who the champions are. If it's not JD and Rubio, I wonder who the champion on the right will be. I think it's going to be somebody we can't even name right now is going to emerge. And I think the same thing on the left.

Anyway, it's going to be exciting. We're going to get Sax to show up, and we'll see you all next Thursday night for our live stream. Love you besties. Bye-bye. Bye-bye.

Brain Man, David Sacks. Oh man. We should all just get a room and just have one big huge orgy, because they're all just like this — like sexual tension, but they just need to release them out.

## 一、被忽略的"诡计"：Anthropic 的"末日论者不在场证明"
这期节目里最锋利但最被低估的洞察来自 Sax ——他捕捉到了 Anthropic 一个精妙的叙事结构：**它一边喊着要"放缓竞速"，一边比任何人都更凶猛地在推进递归自我改进（RSI）**。8 月的博客里已经承认 26% 的下一代模型任务由自家模型生成改进。
但真正值得玩味的是：这不是伪善，而是一种**制度化的"不在场证明工程"**（alibi engineering）。它和 20 世纪烟草巨头们一边在医学期刊上发警告、一边推广过滤嘴香烟是同构的；也和 Oppenheimer 在三位一体核爆后立刻呼吁国际管控、却继续推进氢弹研发是同构的。
关键识别点：**当一家前沿技术公司主动呼吁监管时，监管的范围往往恰好画在它自己已经越过的那条线之内**。Dario 的"pacing letter"不是刹车，而是一张提前写好的辩护状——"是你们不听我的，不是我停不下来"。
## 二、你可能没意识到的：这不是最大的 IPO，这是**资本主权的转移**
播客里反复提到 Anthropic 的债务和 AI 复合体占到美国国债

item.title: [Lex Clips] Computation in nature: Slime mold, fruit flies, and turbulence | Lex Fridman
item.dc:creator: Lex Clips
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一、果蝇的秘密不是"算得少"，而是"根本没在算"

视频里最反直觉的一点藏在那句"strain-sensitive neurons fire ... local computation is happening in that shoulder muscle"。表面上这是在说果蝇用更少的信息做出更快的决策，但真正惊人的事实是：果蝇的翅膀肩部肌肉在信号到达大脑之前就已经完成了"计算"——这意味着它根本没有把问题形式化为我们理解的那种"求解 Navier-Stokes"。

它不是在用更小的模型逼近同一个问题，而是把问题本身替换成了另一个问题：不是"预测气流"，而是"响应形变"。这就好比你问围棋 AI 怎么下，它却告诉你"我根本不下，我让棋盘自己震动，然后让石头落到低处"。果蝇把流体力学从"预测问题"变成了"物理反射问题"——这与现在最前沿的 neuromorphic computing / physical reservoir computing（物理储备池计算）惊人地同构：让物理介质本身承担计算，大脑只做读出。

二、Kamal Jain 那句玩笑话其实是宇宙级物理定律

"If my laptop can't find it, then neither can the market." 这句引用在视频里是作为博弈论的注脚出现的，但如果把它推到极限，它暗含一个让物理学家都会不安的命题：

计算复杂度，可能是和热力学第二定律同级的宇宙硬约束。

想想看——Navier-Stokes 的 blowup 之所以能通过图灵机构造出来（Terry Tao 的工作），恰恰说明"不可计算性"可以物理地嵌入在流体方程里。换句话说，宇宙并不会"替你"去完成 NP-hard 的优化。那么当一只椋鸟群在空中瞬间转向、当一个黏菌找到最短路径、当市场完成价格发现——它们都没有在"解问题"，它们都在用物理过程绕过问题。

跨领域连接：这与经济学里 Hayek 的"知识分散"命题、神经科学里 Friedman 的"自由能原理"、以及深度学习里 lottery ticket hypothesis（彩票假设）其实共享同一个骨架——可计算性决定了什么样的解会在自然中存活下来。

三、棒球外野手的曲线，是物理学里一次失传的发明

视频里一笔带过的那个外野手案例是整个对话里最深的宝藏。为什么外野手不走直线？Steve Brunton 的解释是"持续重估轨迹"，这当然对，但还可以更锋利：

外野手在跑一条让自己的视觉信息增益最大化的路径。 直线路径的代价不是跑得慢，而是在那条路径上，球相对于他的视角几乎不变，等于主动丢弃了传感器数据。曲线路径强迫球的视差持续变化，从而让每一步都在采样新信息。这其实就是机器人学里的 active perception / informative path planning，也是贝叶斯推断里"探索 vs 利用"的运动版本。

最意外的连接：这和果蝇翅膀的 strain neuron 是同一枚硬币——果蝇让翅膀的形变做"被动数据采集"，外野手让身体的轨迹做"主动数据采集"。两者都拒绝"先建模完整系统再决策"的 Laplace 式方案，而是把身体本身当成测量设备。

四、一个贯穿黏菌、果蝇、外野手、湍流的隐藏原理

把视频里所有例子并排看，会跳出一个被忽视的共同点：它们都不是在"解方程"，而是在"让环境替它们解方程"。

  • 黏菌：让化学梯度在物理介质中扩散，物理过程就是算法。
  • 果蝇：让空气在翅膀上留下压痕，形变就是答案。
  • 外野手：让自己运动，视差变化就是观测。
  • 湍流控制：让涡旋碰撞，流体自己完成了维度塌缩。

这其实挑战了视频里那个"好坐标系应该多小"的提问方式。真正的问题也许不是"多少个变量够用"，而是——哪一部分可以外包给物理本身？ PV=nRT 之所以好用，不是因为它压缩了信息，而是因为它承认了平衡态物理已经替我们完成了压缩。而天气之所以不可压缩，不是因为变量太多，而是因为没有任何自发过程愿意替我们做这件事。

所以 Alex 问的那个"涡旋碰撞能做什么计算"的问题，可能有一个让所有人都没想到的答案：它能做的计算，恰好是我们不愿意自己做的那种。

📝 转录文本

一、自然界已经在"解"哪些计算问题？

  • So one of the things I would wonder, you know, scientifically, I mean, these are really interesting problems, and that was a great explanation.

So I'm always curious about what computational problems nature can solve already, right? And there are a lot of examples of this. You know, there's a famous one with like slime mold finding shortest paths and mazes. In fact, some of the precursors to Navier-Stokes were, you know, like some of Terry Tao's work on showing that you can have blowup for Navier-Stokes-like equations because they can simulate Turing machines.

So I guess I would also wonder what sorts of computational tasks these computations with vortices colliding can do, and how that imposes limits on what sorts of coordinate systems ought to exist. 'Cause, you know, you mentioned PV equals nRT. That's an amazing dimensionality reduction —

... because you don't keep track of all of these positions and velocities of particles, but there's just, you know, a small list of numbers that describes a meta state, and that's it. But if I really had a tremendous reduction, you know, like that in the case of turbulence, then it would seem to me very difficult to compute very interesting things too.

二、Game of Life 式的类比与"算法透镜"

  • Could it be like the game of Life, where you have this very simple cellular automata system, and it's a universal Turing machine, and you can cook up whatever behavior you want in it?

  • Yeah, that's right. I mean, so game of Life, a lot of times people think about, you know, what are minimal rules to have all of these exotic behaviors, and it's really shocking how small the rules need to be to get that, right?

But I guess, you know, I'm a theoretical computer scientist. One of the biggest exports from our field is really the algorithmic lens. So it's not just about, you know, computation where you have a well-defined problem and a laptop and you wanna solve it, but it's also about, you know, computation in the natural world, you know, and what that teaches us about what the rules of nature might be.

So, you know, some famous examples of this are things like equilibria in multiplayer games, and Nash equilibrium is a great solution concept. But of course, the fact that it's hard to compute Nash equilibrium, you know, throws into question, is it really a universal mechanism that explains how people play games?

There was this amazing quote by Kamal Jain that I really like, which is, "If my laptop can't find it, then neither can the market." And, you know, to me, what's really exciting is the nexus of a lot of these different perspectives. When you were describing it, it sounded to me like there are very interesting computational problems under the hood, and that one can kind of get a dual perspective on these things by thinking about how that computation imposes limits on what a good coordinate system ought to look like.

三、两个极端：地球气候 vs 果蝇飞行

  • So I think that's a really nice way of framing the problem. Uh, and I would take two extreme examples.

So Earth's weather and climate systems are actually just complex. They — all the scales do matter. The weather in this zip code matters to me. Um, you know, everything matters. All the variables matter. And you're right. Like, if I over-reduce that system to, you know, five numbers, then I lose the descriptive capability of what I actually care about. That's one extreme.

The other extreme, let's think about how, you know, a moth flies or a butterfly or a fruit fly. They are proof by existence that you can interact with an extremely complicated turbulent flow and do very advanced engineering control. They can control their forces and moments in gusts, in rain. They can live very rich lives, and they presumably don't have a PhD in fluid dynamics —

... or know the Navier-Stokes. They're probably not running supercomputer simulations. There might be five or six numbers that actually matter to their daily life of maintaining a leading-edge vortex and, you know, stalling their wings to perch and to land.

And those are kind of two extreme examples, and I really want to be able to handle both of those. We want to be able to handle the full complexity of truly complex systems, and we want to be able to distill down the absolute bare minimum essentials for fast decisions in those kind of insect extreme cases. And biological flyers still dramatically outperform, you know, human-designed, fluid systems in many regimes, so we still have a lot to learn about, about these simple systems.

四、不确定性下的鲁棒解：外野手的曲线路径

  • So maybe we're, like, veering into research now, but, you know —

... to me, it's always amazing how nature not only solves very hard optimization problems, it seems to find very robust solutions. And I'm always struck by the fact that, you know, when we model it, we tend to model it assuming we have full knowledge, you know, about what the boundary and initial conditions are for things like Navier-Stokes. But when a bird flies, you know, it doesn't know all of that.

And to some extent, you know, modeling things with uncertainty is really how you reframe the optimization problem to get very, you know, rich and robust solutions. And it's kind of amazing to me how a lot of everyday examples sort of fit into this.

I remember, you know, I'm a big baseball fan, and I remember reading a math paper about baseball that when you've got an outfielder, you know, once the ball has been hit, a lot of stuff is known. You know, the velocity, the trajectory. You would think the outfielder would just take a straight-line path to where they expected the ball to be. But when you observe outfielders, they don't take straight-line paths. They take a slight curve to it.

So why is that? You know, at least one way to wrap your head around it is that that's actually a very robust strategy, 'cause when you're taking a curved path, you can continually reevaluate —

... the trajectory of the ball and then adjust as needed. So there are very interesting solutions that nature finds, but it's not always obvious what is the right formulation for the optimization problem in the first place, and sometimes modeling it in the case of uncertainty so that you can design solutions that are robust to the fact that you don't have full system knowledge seems to be an important piece of the picture.

五、果蝇翅膀上的"边缘计算"

  • So there's a fun aside related to this. Um, insects in particular don't have the ability to measure their full flow field. Um, they can react to gusts of wind faster than the information that hits their wings, goes to their brain and back to their muscles.

So researchers have studied this for decades in biology. And what they've found is that there are strain-sensitive neurons embedded on the wings, maybe a few dozen to a few hundred of these in very stereotypical locations. So brother fruit flies will have the same locations of these strain-sensitive neurons, and those strain-sensitive neurons fire when the wing bends in a certain temporal pattern.

So it gets hit by a gust of wind, the wing bends, neurons fire, and a local computation is happening in that shoulder muscle of this insect that goes directly back and corrects robustly based on partial information of a system it doesn't have equations for that is nonlinear and turbulent. So it's like, again, proof by existence —

... of exactly what you're saying is maybe the robust strategy of actually relying on partial information and uncertainty. They can do more than we can at this point, with way less information.

六、彩蛋：黑洞奇点与 Navier-Stokes 的玩笑

  • Yeah. I have a couple of — I apologize — pothead thoughts, 'cause Alex mentioned black holes. I have a fun thought that maybe the singularity observed with a blowup in Navier-Stokes equations comes into play when we're — as opposed to airplane wings on Earth — we're traveling through two connected black holes in a warp drive that we figure out, and then there's the flow control of spacetime, and that becomes relevant because now you're in a black hole, hence the singularity.

This is the — For people just listening to this, the look Alex just gave me, it hurts my soul. Okay. So moving on to the next topic.

  • But the forcing, you'd need the black hole vortex to also be forced at exactly the right —

  • The, yeah, the force. Where's the force? I mean, at that point —

  • How do you... Yeah. You could try to ride it. Yeah. There's a way — You can make something out of this.

  • There's some non-zero probability that future ass that will listen to this, that guy is the one time he said something that was actually correct. Okay. If it's okay, a quick bathroom break.

  • Yeah. Sounds good.

## 一、果蝇的秘密不是"算得少"，而是"根本没在算"
视频里最反直觉的一点藏在那句"strain-sensitive neurons fire ... local computation is happening in that shoulder muscle"。表面上这是在说果蝇用更少的信息做出更快的决策，但真正惊人的事实是：**果蝇的翅膀肩部肌肉在信号到达大脑之前就已经完成了"计算"**——这意味着它根本没有把问题形式化为我们理解的那种"求解 Navier-Stokes"。
它不是在用更小的模型逼近同一个问题，而是把问题本身替换成了另一个问题：**不是"预测气流"，而是"响应形变"**。这就好比你问围棋 AI 怎么下，它却告诉你"我根本不下，我让棋盘自己震动，然后让石头落到低处"。果蝇把流体力学从"预测问题"变成了"物理反射问题"——这与现在最前沿的 **neuromorphic computing / physical reservoir computing**（物理储备池计算）惊人地同构：让物理介质本身承担计算，大脑只做读出。

item.title: [Lex Clips] The hardest physics problem in fluid dynamics: Turbulence explained | Lex Fridman
item.dc:creator: Lex Clips
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一、这段对话真正讨论的，不是湍流，而是"可简化性"的边界

Brunton 丢出了一个被大多数听众忽略的炸弹：房间里的气体有 10²³ 个分子，比任何湍流都"复杂"，但它反而是湍流的反面。为什么？因为气体的所有尺度之间是解耦的——分子的疯狂运动在宏观上塌缩成三个数字（温度、压强、密度）。而湍流之所以是千年难题，不是因为它"复杂"，而是因为它的尺度彼此纠缠，不允许信息向上塌缩。

这是一个让人不安的洞察：复杂度不是问题，耦合度才是。一个有一万亿参数但层级清晰的系统，可能比一个只有五个变量却彼此反馈的系统更容易被理解。这解释了为什么大脑的 860 亿神经元可以被意识统摄，而只有少数几个变量的 2008 年金融系统却崩塌到无法预测——危机时刻，正是宏观与微观尺度突然"耦合"的时刻，正如层流转捩为湍流的瞬间。

二、意外的观察：物理学的所有重大突破都是"换坐标"，而不是"算得更快"

Brunton 说了一句很容易被滑过去的话："牛顿的 F=ma 出现在我们把太阳放到宇宙中心之后。"把这句话推到极致，你会得到一个颠覆性的历史模式：

  • 牛顿革命 = 日心坐标系
  • 相对论 = 时空坐标统一
  • 量子力学 = 希尔伯特空间
  • 傅里叶分析 = 从时域到频域
  • 深度学习 = 从像素空间到潜在空间（latent space）

AI 的本质工作，不是"思考"，而是在数据中寻找一组让问题变得平凡的坐标。 ChatGPT 的 Transformer 做的事情，和寻找湍流坐标是同一类事情——它找到了一个让"下一个 token"变得可预测的高维表示。所以当 Brunton 说"这是一个完美的 AI 问题"，他其实在说：凡是 70、80 年代被卡住的问题，本质都是坐标问题，而 AI 刚好是一台坐标搜索机器。

这也给我们一个可怕的启示：你人生中反复解不开的难题，很可能不需要"更努力"，而需要"换坐标"——换一个描述问题的变量，换一个看待关系的维度。

三、跨领域连接：鱼、章鱼、与"身体即坐标系"

Lex 问了一句很关键的话："可是鱼已经解决了（湍流）。" Brunton 轻描淡写地认同——但这里藏着一个更深的裂缝。

鱼没有解微分方程，鱼也没有大数据集。鱼是用身体本身作为坐标系解决了湍流预测问题。它的侧线、鳞片、肌肉张力分布——这些不是"传感器"，而是与流体耦合的物质本体。这呼应了 Rodney Brooks 的话："The world is its own best model."

把这个思想推到极致，就会撞上章鱼之谜：章鱼三分之二的神经元在它的触手里。它不是中央集权地"计算"湍流，而是让每条触手自己与水流共振、协商、决策。

于是产生一个异端的猜测：湍流也许根本没有一组"数学上的"简洁坐标，它只有一组"形态上的"简洁坐标——需要一个会流动、会变形的身体来表达它。这意味着未来破解湍流的，可能不是 Transformer，而是软体机器人 + 具身学习：让一个人工鱼在水里游一百万年，它找到的坐标，可能是任何方程都写不出来的。

这又反过来逼问一个哲学问题：如果一个解只能被身体表达、不能被符号表达，它还算"理解"吗？ 这正是数学与生命之间最深的那道裂缝。

📝 转录文本

The Big Puzzles in Fluid Dynamics

Lex: Can you speak to some of the maybe beautiful, fascinating phenomena in the space of fluids that you've been thinking about? You mentioned turbulence. What are the big puzzles to sort of solve in this space to understand? You've mentioned drag, like air, fluid. What are like the big Millennium Prize type problems that people are thinking about?

Brunton: I mean, there's so many. You can break them down into a few categories. So turbulence is very hard because it's multi-scale.

Lex: What is turbulence?

Turbulence as a Multi-Scale Phenomenon

Brunton: Turbulence is this phenomena that when you have a complex fluid roiling or mixing and moving — kind of like a Da Vinci's… he has these beautiful drawings of fluids at all of these different scales. All of the scales matter: the big vortices, and the medium vortices, and the little vortices — all of them actually matter to predict the lift and the drag and the thing.

So the gas in this room is a great counterexample. It's the opposite of turbulence. It is complicated — the molecules are all moving around in a very frenetic way, and there's a lot of molecules. But that, you know, ten to the twenty-three number of gas particles — all of those individual configurations don't matter. We know from thermodynamics (this is like the great success of classical physics) that there's a small handful of numbers that actually determine how this gas behaves — you know, temperature, pressure, density.

That simple description doesn't exist for turbulent fluids: for the flow over a wing, the flow inside your heart, for, you know, any — for the flow on a river. All of the scales actually matter. All of the numbers in that simulation actually matter to predict the next, you know, behavior — to predict what's gonna happen. And that makes it fundamentally challenging.

Is There a Coordinate System for Turbulence?

So this is actually a great AI problem: Is there a coordinate system? Is there a set of numbers just like we have for gases — you know, temperature, pressure, density? Is there a set of numbers or some representation of a fluid, of a turbulent fluid, that allow it to be simply described in a way that is useful for engineering — to build, you know, motors and engines — just like we have for gas dynamics?

Lex: So then the interesting question, if it's a problem for AI (and AI is listening, I'm sure)… um, the solution to that problem, would it — would the path lie through mathematics or through having the AI system sit there and watch some fluid for a while?

Brunton: I think yes to both.

Lex: 'Cause fish, they figured it out.

Coordinate Transformations as the Prelude to Breakthrough

Brunton: They figured it out. Well, so I think you have the right keyword — coordinates. And I — so that's kinda why I said both. And I'm not trying to be trite, but all of our great physics breakthroughs were predated by a coordinate transformation. So Newton's F = ma came after we put the sun at the center of the universe instead of the Earth, right? You had to do that coordinate transform first.

So I think what — the way I see it is: we need to take all of this data, these simulations, these observations of fluids, and what we're looking for is a simple coordinate system so that the description of that fluid becomes very simple and generalizable, beautiful in a physical sense. And that is both a brute force — you know, get a lot of data, try a bunch of different coordinate transformations and representations until you find the simplest one that generalizes the best. But there's also a lot of deep mathematics in what the form of that coordinate transformation might take.

In general, if you find a question that really smart people asked, you know, in the '70s and '80s, but they hit a wall computationally — that's very fertile ground right now. So like, we know what the form of these coordinate systems probably should take from some fundamental principles. We've just never been able to write them down. They're too complicated to write down. That's like a perfect problem for AI: you know, now let's give it a lot more data, a lot more compute, and see if we can start learning these transformations we know should exist.

Vortices: Structured Chaos

Lex: Just so I understand, the formation of vortexes — so that's like a, like, little, like, tornadoes.

Brunton: Little tornadoes.

Lex: Their formation is — is that part tricky to understand?

Brunton: Uh, yeah, absolutely. And it's beautiful too. Like, I love watching these videos of, you know, if you shoot two vortices together, they'll, you know, influence each other and then merge in these very interesting ways — that you have like a red vortex and a blue vortex, and you can see where they merge and join.

But they also stretch and fold, and, you know, turbulence is chaotic, so the trajectories get tangled like spaghetti. It's not random. There's a huge amount of structure — but it is very multi-scale, very, very tangled.
